name: Dot Physical Exam Decoder
q: Use this skill when the user asks how to interpret a DOT medical examiner's findings — what restrict
body:
# Decoding the DOT Physical Exam Result

A driver completes the medical examination under `§ 391.43` with an FMCSA-certified examiner. The result lands as a **Medical Examiner's Certificate (MEC)** with one of several outcomes. This skill helps carriers interpret what the certificate says, what restrictions mean, and when a re-exam is required.

## The five possible outcomes
1. **Qualified** — 2-year certificate, no restrictions
2. **Qualified with restrictions** — certificate issued but limited (e.g., "corrective lenses," "hearing aid," "intrastate only")
3. **Qualified with shorter certification period** — 1 year, 6 months, 3 months — typically for conditions requiring monitoring (e.g., hypertension, diabetes)
4. **Temporarily disqualified** — current condition prevents certification; driver can re-test once resolved
5. **Permanently disqualified** — condition that doesn't meet `§ 391.41` standards (e.g., uncontrolled seizure history, recent heart attack)

## Common restrictions explained
- **Corrective lenses** — driver must wear glasses/contacts during operation. `§ 391.41(b)(10)` requires 20/40 vision in each eye.
- **Hearing aid** — required for the hearing standard in `§ 391.41(b)(11)`
- **SPE (Skill Performance Evaluation) certificate** — needed for fixed impairments of extremities
- **Driving within an exempt intracity zone** — limited to a defined area
- **Wear corrective lenses, hearing aid, and SPE** — combined

## Shorter certification periods — what's happening
- **Hypertension stage 1** (140-159 / 90-99) → 1-year cert
- **Hypertension stage 2** (160-179 / 100-109) → 3-month cert if treated
- **Diabetes** on insulin → typically 1-year cert
- **Sleep apnea** with treatment → 1-year cert
- **Cardiovascular** post-event → varies, often 1-year with cardiologist sign-off

## What the carrier does with the result
1. Verify the examiner is on the **National Registry of Certified Medical Examiners** — `§ 391.43(g)`
2. Verify the certificate date and expiration
3. File the certificate and the **MER (Medical Examination Report)** in the DQF
4. Update the driver's CDL state with the medical card status (most states require this)
5. Calendar the **expiration** — set a renewal trigger 60 days out

## What invalidates certification
- Driver develops a disqualifying condition after exam — driver must stop operating, report
- Examiner is removed from the National Registry — cert remains valid but new certs must come from a current examiner
- Driver lies on the MER — automatically disqualifying

## Federal vision exemption
FMCSA's **vision exemption** lets some drivers who don't meet the standard in one eye operate with documentation. Cert will note "meets federal vision exemption" — DQF must include the exemption letter.

## Common errors
- Treating a 1-year cert as a 2-year cert (calendar wrong)
- Filing without verifying National Registry status
- Not flagging restrictions on dispatch assignments
- Missing the MER report (separate from the certificate)

name: Dqf Application Validity Window
q: Use this skill to understand how current a driver's employment application must remain in the DQF
body:
# DQF Application Validity & Currency

The employment application is one document in the DQF — but its currency matters. Carriers often miss the requirement to update or refresh.

## Initial application requirements (§ 391.21)
Application must include:
- Driver's name + present residence
- Date of birth
- Driver's license info (number, issuing state, type, class)
- Names + dates of medical examiner if cert exists
- 10 years of employment history (any DOT-regulated employer in past 3 years)
- 10 years of accident history (DOT-recordable)
- 10 years of CDL violation history
- Driver's certification of accuracy (signed)
- Employer's date of receipt

## When to require update
- Driver's residence changes — update within 30 days
- Driver's license number/state changes — update immediately
- New employment history (driver had other jobs since hire) — update in performance review
- Driver answers misleading information uncovered — investigate + document

## Re-application triggers
- Acquired by new carrier (depending on transfer method)
- Returned after extended absence (over 12 months)
- Driver claims information was missing from original

## Retention
- DQF copy: duration of employment + 3 years
- Prior applications (superseded): may be archived to closed-files but not in active DQF

## Common errors
- Application is 5+ years old without updates
- Driver's residence on the application does not match driver's record
- Application not signed by driver (or signed without date)
- Employment history blank or incomplete

## Auditor's question
"Show me the driver's application." → must produce immediately. The application is the legal record that this driver is who they say they are, has the qualifications they claim, and has authorized the carrier to verify.

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 391.21**
- **49 CFR § 391.51(b)(1)**

name: Dqf Audit Self Assessment
q: Use this skill when conducting a self-audit of your DQF library before an FMCSA compliance review
body:
# DQF Audit Self-Assessment Workflow

A self-audit catches DQF issues before FMCSA does. Run quarterly or before any expected compliance review.

## Step 1: Driver list verification
- Pull list of all drivers active in past 12 months (including terminated)
- Cross-reference against your DQF library (should have a file for each)
- Flag missing DQF files immediately

## Step 2: Per-driver completeness check
For each driver, verify these 12 documents are present:
- [ ] 1. Employment application (§ 391.21) — date hired, complete signature
- [ ] 2. Prior employer inquiries (§ 391.23) — sent + responded OR documented attempts
- [ ] 3. MVR — current (within last 12 months) + 3-year history
- [ ] 4. Annual review of driving record (§ 391.25) — within 12 months of hire/last review
- [ ] 5. Annual driver's certificate of violations (§ 391.27) — within 12 months
- [ ] 6. Medical examiner's certificate — current (not expired)
- [ ] 7. Medical examiner verification — National Registry number on file
- [ ] 8. Road test certificate OR equivalent — at time of hire
- [ ] 9. Safety performance history — completed at hire
- [ ] 10. Medical variance — if applicable
- [ ] 11. CDL copy — current
- [ ] 12. ELDT certificate — for drivers with first CDL after 2/7/2022

## Step 3: Document quality check
- Signatures and dates legible
- All sections completed (no blanks)
- Documents are signed by authorized parties (medical examiner from National Registry)
- Certificates not expired
- Old certificates archived (3-year retention for replaced documents)

## Step 4: Cross-reference with HR system
- Hire dates match between DQF and HR
- Termination dates flagged for 3-year retention countdown
- No "ghost drivers" in DQF without HR record (or vice versa)

## Step 5: Generate audit report
- Total drivers in DQF library
- Total drivers with complete files (target: 100%)
- Drivers with at least 1 missing document (action items)
- Drivers with expired documents (urgency)
- Average DQF "completeness score"

## Documentation
Save the self-audit results — at the next compliance review, demonstrating self-audit shows continuous improvement intent.

## How Compass automates this
Compass DQ Files module runs this audit continuously. Each driver has a "compliance score" based on document presence + currency. Daily digest surfaces the top 5 driver files needing attention.

- **49 CFR § 391.51**
- **49 CFR § 391.53**
- **49 CFR Part 385 Subpart B**

name: Dqf Personnel File Vs Dqf
q: Use this skill when sorting paperwork between a driver's personnel file and the regulated DQ file
body:
# Personnel File vs DQ File — What Goes Where

The Driver Qualification File (DQF) and the personnel file are separate documents with different purposes, regulators, and retention periods. Mixing them is the #1 cause of DQF audit findings.

## DQF (regulated by FMCSA)
Per § 391.51(b), exactly these 12 documents:
1. Driver's employment application (§ 391.21)
2. Inquiry to prior employers (§ 391.23)
3. Inquiry to state driver licensing agencies (§ 391.23(a)(1) for MVR)
4. Annual review of driving record (§ 391.25)
5. Annual driver's certificate of violations (§ 391.27)
6. Medical examiner's certificate (§ 391.43) — current
7. Medical examiner verification (§ 391.51(b)(7)) — National Registry number
8. Road test certificate OR equivalent (§ 391.31, § 391.33)
9. Safety performance history (Previous Employer Information Request)
10. Medical variance/exemption (if applicable)
11. Driver's license copy
12. Entry-Level Driver Training certificate (§ 380.609) — post-2/7/2022 hires

## Personnel file (HR / state law)
- Pay rate, payroll history
- Tax withholding forms (W-4, I-9)
- Health insurance enrollment
- 401(k) records
- Performance reviews
- Disciplinary actions
- Driver bonus + incentive history
- Personal information (emergency contact, beneficiary)
- Workers' comp claim history
- ADA accommodation requests

## What does NOT go in either
- Drug & alcohol test results → separate file under § 382.401(b) (retention 5 years)
- Workers' comp claim documents → separate per state requirements

## Retention
- DQF: Duration of employment + 3 years after termination
- Personnel: State law varies (typically 3-7 years post-termination)
- D&A: 5 years (longest), 1 year for negatives

## Audit consideration
At an FMCSA compliance review, auditors request DQF. They do NOT have authority to review personnel files. Keeping them separate protects both your driver privacy and audit clarity.

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 391.51**
- **49 CFR § 391.53**
- **29 CFR § 1602**

name: Dqf Returning Driver Rehire
q: Use this skill when re-hiring a driver who has been away from CMV operation for 1+ years
body:
# DQF Re-Up for Returning Driver After Long Absence

Drivers returning to CMV operation after extended absence (1+ years) need re-qualification. The DQF mechanics depend on absence length.

## Absence 0-12 months
Treated as continuous employment for FMCSA purposes:
- Existing DQF stays in place
- Annual MVR + annual driver's certificate of violations resume on schedule
- Medical certificate must be current
- Drug/alcohol pool participation resumes

## Absence 12-36 months
- Pull new MVR within 30 days of re-employment
- New road test (or equivalent) if 24+ months since last
- New medical exam if expired or not current
- New annual driver's certificate of violations
- Driver's safety performance history may need re-confirmation if missed during absence
- Re-enroll in random testing pool

## Absence over 3 years
- Treat substantially as a new hire
- Full new DQF (all 12 documents fresh)
- Pre-employment drug test required
- Prior employer inquiries for entire 3-year period preceding return
- All new documentation as if first hire

## Special case: military leave
USERRA + Part 391 allow military returning drivers to resume qualification:
- Re-validate medical and MVR before driving
- Document military service period in DQF (e.g., copy of DD-214 or active duty certificate)
- Random testing pool resumes immediately

## ELDT consideration
- Pre-2/7/2022 license holder: no new ELDT required (grandfathered)
- Post-2/7/2022 license holder: ELDT certificate stays on file regardless of absence (one-time event)

## Common compliance pitfall
Re-hiring a driver after 14 months and assuming "they're qualified" because the old DQF exists — must pull fresh MVR + run prior-employer inquiry for the absence period.

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 391.27**
- **49 CFR § 391.31**
- **49 CFR § 391.43**

name: Dqf Successor Carrier Transfer
q: Use this skill when buying another carrier and inheriting their drivers' DQF library
body:
# DQ File Transfer in Carrier Acquisition / Merger

When a carrier acquires another carrier, the driver qualification files transfer with the driver. The acquiring carrier inherits responsibility for verifying records.

## Permitted transfer methods
1. **Original files transferred** physically (or digitally) at acquisition
2. **Acquired carrier provides documents** for the acquiring carrier to create new DQFs

The acquiring carrier becomes responsible from the acquisition date forward. Prior period responsibility stays with the prior carrier's records.

## Required verification by acquiring carrier
- All 12 documents present (per § 391.51)
- Documents are current (not expired)
- Documents are properly executed (signatures, dates)
- Driver's safety performance history covers the acquiring period if needed

## Common gaps in inherited DQFs
- Missing prior-employer inquiries for older hires
- Missing road test certificates for drivers hired before § 391.31 was clarified
- Medical examiner verification missing for pre-2014 drivers (National Registry didn't exist)
- ELDT certificates missing for drivers with CDLs predating 2/7/2022 (exempt — note in file)

## Inheriting non-DOT drivers
If acquiring a carrier with both DOT and non-DOT drivers (e.g., property-only intrastate), only the DOT-qualified drivers need DQFs under federal rules. State rules may differ.

## Reporting obligations
- Acquiring carrier inherits the prior carrier's DataQ-eligible inspection history
- Acquiring carrier inherits CSA score (50% of acquired carrier's score weight typically merges per FMCSA SMS rules)
- File FMCSA Form MCS-150 within 30 days of acquisition

## Remediation steps for incomplete DQFs
- Document the gap (note "inherited file — document not available from acquired carrier")
- Re-create what you can (re-pull MVRs, re-do prior employer inquiries)
- Update medical exam if current cert has passed
- The acquiring carrier cannot be cited for the prior carrier's documentation gaps, but YOU must remediate from date of acquisition forward

## Best practice
Audit each acquired DQF within 60 days of acquisition. Set up the acquired carrier's drivers in your Compass DQ Files module — Compass scans for missing slots and surfaces remediation actions.

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 391.51**
- **49 CFR § 390.21**

name: Driver Coaching Conversations
q: Use when a manager, dispatcher, or safety director needs to have a coaching conversation with a driv
body:
# Driver Coaching Conversations

Coaching sits between dispatch communication and formal discipline. Done well, it corrects behavior and retains the driver. Done poorly, it accelerates turnover or escalates without basis. This skill covers a practical coaching framework for safety managers and dispatchers. The trigger is often a vehicle inspection issue under `Part 396` or a roadside violation feeding the CSA BASICs.

## When to coach (vs warn vs discipline)
- **Coach** — single low-severity issue, recoverable behavior, first time. Examples: minor speeding, missed pre-trip item, late delivery.
- **Warn** — pattern of low-severity OR a single moderate issue. Document in writing.
- **Discipline** — high-severity (e.g., positive D&A test, OOS violation, at-fault crash) OR repeated warnings.

## Coaching framework (SBI + COACH)
**SBI** — describe the situation, behavior, impact.
- **Situation** — "On Tuesday's run from Dallas to Houston..."
- **Behavior** — "...you logged 11 hours 15 minutes of driving..."
- **Impact** — "...which put us over the 11-hour limit and shows up in our HOS BASIC."

**COACH** — collaborative resolution.
- **Connect** — "I want to understand what was going on."
- **Observe** — listen without interrupting
- **Action** — agree on what changes
- **Confirm** — driver repeats the agreed action
- **Hand-off** — document and follow up

## Tone rules
- Private, not in front of other drivers
- Calm and specific
- Driver does most of the talking
- Focus on the behavior, not the person
- End with clear next steps

## Documentation
Every coaching conversation gets a one-line note in the driver file:
- Date
- Topic
- Driver's commitment
- Follow-up date

This isn't discipline — it's a paper trail that shows the carrier acted on patterns. It also protects against "no one ever told me" claims.

## What drivers actually hear
- "I'm not in trouble, but my boss noticed."
- "There's a specific change they want."
- "They'll check back."

Get to those three things and you've coached effectively.

## Common errors
- Coaching by text — loses tone and context
- Coaching publicly — destroys trust
- Coaching without specifics — driver doesn't know what to change
- No follow-up — driver concludes it didn't matter
- Letting the conversation drift to unrelated complaints (the laundry list)

## Escalation triggers
Move to formal warning if:
- Same issue recurs within 90 days of coaching
- Driver disputes the underlying facts and isn't open to discussion
- Severity is higher than first thought after investigation

name: Driver Discipline And Progressive Correction
q: Use this skill when the user asks about driver discipline — when to coach vs warn vs suspend vs term
body:
# Driver Discipline and Progressive Correction

A written **progressive discipline policy** protects the carrier in three ways: it ensures consistent treatment of drivers, supports the safety management defense in litigation, and frames lawful termination decisions. The hiring-side baseline is `§ 391.21`. This skill covers the step ladder and where to skip steps.

## The standard ladder
1. **Verbal coaching** — documented as a one-line note
2. **Written warning** — signed by driver and supervisor, in personnel file
3. **Final written warning** — last chance, may include suspension
4. **Termination**

## When to skip steps
Some conduct goes straight to termination regardless of prior record:
- **Positive drug or alcohol test** or test refusal under `Part 382`
- **Falsifying logs or DQF documents**
- **DUI / CDL disqualifying offense**
- **Violence, theft, drug use on duty**
- **At-fault fatal crash with proven preventability**
- **Abandoning a load**

This short list should be written into the policy as **"immediate termination offenses"** so it's predictable.

## Key documentation rules
- Every written warning describes the **specific behavior**, the **policy violated**, and the **expected change**
- Driver signs to acknowledge receipt (signing doesn't mean agreement)
- Written warnings go in the **personnel file**, NOT the DQF
- Coaching notes stay separate from formal discipline
- A discipline event referencing safety should reference the related safety policy

## Patterns of bad practice
- Inconsistent enforcement — one driver fired, another warned for same offense
- Skipping warnings when convenient (you'll lose the wrongful termination case)
- Verbal-only documentation
- Discipline files mixed into the DQF — auditors see HR matters they shouldn't

## The safety management defense
In a serious-injury or fatality case, plaintiff's counsel will subpoena the driver's full personnel and discipline history. The carrier's defense is stronger when:
- Policy is written
- Enforcement is consistent
- Documentation shows the carrier actively managed performance
- Termination decisions match the policy ladder

A driver with three written warnings on speeding who then causes a fatal crash creates a negligent retention exposure — unless the policy at three warnings is termination.

## At-will employment overlay
Most US states are at-will, meaning the carrier can terminate for any non-discriminatory reason. Progressive discipline doesn't change that — but skipping the ladder against your own policy creates legal exposure.

## Driver communication
When a driver is terminated:
- Conduct the meeting privately
- State the reason factually
- Process final pay per state law
- Notify the **Clearinghouse** of any related D&A events per `§ 382.705`
- Update prior-employer inquiry response per `§ 391.23`

## Common errors
- No written policy
- Termination without a documented prior warning when policy required one
- Pre-employment inquiry returns that don't match the actual termination reason — creates litigation evidence

name: Driver Fitness For Duty
q: Use this skill when the user asks about driver fitness-for-duty programs — pre-trip readiness assess
body:
# Driver Fitness for Duty

Fitness for duty (FFD) is the carrier's program to confirm — before each shift — that a driver is medically, mentally, and operationally ready to operate safely. It overlaps with `§ 391.41` medical qualification but operates at the daily level. A robust FFD posture is also a CSA-friendly position under `Part 385`. This skill outlines what a working FFD program covers.

## What FFD includes
1. **Medical certification status** — current MEC per `§ 391.45`
2. **Hours of Service availability** — enough hours to legally complete the assigned trip
3. **Fatigue self-assessment** — driver attests they're rested
4. **Substance / alcohol** — no use within the prohibited window per `§ 382.205-207`
5. **Vehicle qualification match** — driver licensed for the equipment assigned
6. **No active disqualification** — Clearinghouse not in prohibited status
7. **Personal issues** — significant life events that may impair concentration

## Pre-shift FFD process
A typical small carrier flow:
1. Driver logs in to ELD; carrier verifies HOS availability
2. Driver completes pre-trip inspection per `§ 396.13`
3. Driver attests in writing (or app) to: rested, no impairment, no medical issues
4. Dispatcher confirms no Clearinghouse hit
5. Load is released

## Special situations that affect FFD
- **Return from leave** — after a medical absence, confirm MEC still valid
- **Post-accident** — driver may be off-duty until cleared
- **D&A test pending** — driver typically off until result
- **CDL suspension/restriction** — must catch via MVR monitoring
- **Recent ELD malfunction** — verify resolution before next shift

## Programmatic elements
- **Reasonable suspicion training** for supervisors (`§ 382.603`)
- **MVR monitoring** beyond the annual review (`§ 391.25`) — many carriers run monthly
- **Clearinghouse limited query** annually + new hire full query
- **Fatigue policy** — when a driver shuts down, dispatch supports it
- **Confidential reporting channel** for drivers to flag fitness concerns

## Reasonable suspicion under Part 382
If a supervisor observes specific physical, behavioral, speech, or performance indicators of drug or alcohol use, they document observations and direct the driver to immediate testing per `§ 382.307`. The observation must come from a supervisor who has completed the required training.

## Common errors
- Treating FFD as a one-time event at hire
- No supervisor training on reasonable suspicion — can't act when it matters
- Annual MVR only, missing in-year suspensions
- Pressuring fatigued drivers to continue
- No documentation of FFD attestation — undermines the carrier in litigation

name: Driver Leasing Arrangements
q: Use this skill when the user asks about carrier-driver relationships — Independent Contractor (IC /
body:
# Driver Leasing Arrangements: IC, Lease-Op, Company Driver

A motor carrier can engage drivers under three primary structures: **Independent Contractor (IC)**, **Lease Operator**, or **Company Driver**. The structure affects taxes, insurance, equipment, control, and FMCSA compliance responsibility. The classification question is policed by IRS, DOL, state agencies, and `49 CFR Part 376` for the FMCSA side.

## Company driver
- W-2 employee of the carrier
- Drives carrier-owned equipment
- Carrier handles insurance, fuel, maintenance
- Carrier pays per mile, hourly, or salary
- Full FMCSA compliance is the carrier's responsibility

## Lease operator
- Owner-operator with their own truck, leased ONTO the carrier's authority
- Operates under the **carrier's MC number**
- Lease agreement governs the relationship per `§ 376.12`
- Carrier still responsible for FMCSA compliance (DQF, D&A, HOS)
- Owner-op handles truck maintenance, insurance options vary by lease
- Typically paid percentage of linehaul or flat per-mile

## True independent contractor
- Operates under their **own MC number**
- Engages with the carrier as one business to another
- Each party handles its own compliance
- IRS / state may still reclassify if the relationship looks like employment

## The Part 376 lease — what it must include
- 30+ day minimum term
- Compensation methodology
- Equipment to be used
- Identification (sublease, exclusive use)
- Receipt of equipment
- Charge-back items (fuel advances, etc.) disclosed
- Insurance responsibility
- Final lease settlement procedure

## Misclassification risk
Federal and state agencies use multi-factor tests (IRS 20-factor, ABC test in CA/MA/NJ, FLSA economic realities). Red flags:
- Carrier dictates routes, dispatch, schedule
- Driver wears company uniform, drives only for one carrier
- Carrier controls how the job is done, not just outcomes
- Driver has no real opportunity for profit/loss
- Long-term exclusive arrangements

Reclassification triggers back-payroll-tax, workers' comp exposure, unemployment liability, FLSA wage-and-hour claims.

## State-specific
- **California AB5** — narrow ICs; B2B exemption requires careful structuring
- **Massachusetts ABC test** — among the strictest
- **New Jersey** — similar
- **Federal** — DOL rules have swung; current guidance is still tight on trucking

name: Driver Onboarding Process
q: Use this skill when the user asks about onboarding a new CDL driver — pre-hire process, day-zero req
body:
# Driver Onboarding Process

Onboarding a new CDL driver is part regulatory compliance, part operational orientation. The regulatory bar is the **Driver Qualification File** under `§ 391.51` — built before the driver moves a single load. This skill covers a practical, defensible workflow.

## Pre-hire phase
1. Driver completes the **driver's application for employment** per `§ 391.21`
2. Carrier obtains a **signed release** for prior-employer inquiries and Clearinghouse
3. **MVR** pulled from each state where the driver held a CDL in the last 3 years
4. **Clearinghouse full query** per `§ 382.701`
5. **Prior-employer investigation** per `§ 391.23` — 3 years back, DOT-regulated employers
6. **PSP report** (Pre-Employment Screening Program) — optional but standard
7. **Background check** if used by the carrier

## Hire decision
If any step returns disqualifying info → run **FCRA adverse action** before declining.

## Day-zero requirements
- **Road test** per `§ 391.31` (or equivalent — CDL acts as substitute under `§ 391.33`)
- **Medical examiner's certificate** (current)
- **ELDT certificate** (`§ 380.609`) for post-2/7/2022 first-time CDL holders
- **Pre-employment drug test** — negative result before driving
- **DQF assembled** with all 12 documents

## Day-one orientation
- Carrier-specific HOS policy review
- DVIR process
- Cargo securement training (if hauling secured loads)
- ELD operation
- Hazmat awareness if applicable
- Customer / dispatch procedures
- Pay structure
- Personnel-side: W-4, I-9, benefits enrollment

## First-week mentoring
- Pair with a veteran driver for first 2-5 days where possible
- Check ELD events daily; coach on form-and-manner
- Review pre-trip / post-trip walks in person
- First week of dispatch with extra dispatcher attention

## What goes where (file separation)
- **DQF** — the 12 regulated documents
- **Personnel file** — W-4, I-9, benefits, signed handbook
- **D&A file** — pre-employment test, Clearinghouse query — separate per `§ 382.401`
- **Training file** — completed orientation modules

## Common errors
- Letting the driver run before pre-employment D&A result is back
- Missing prior-employer inquiry (#1 audit finding for small carriers)
- ELDT not in DQF for post-2022 hires
- Annual MVR clock not started
- Clearinghouse query not done or not documented

name: Driver Pay Models
q: Use this skill when the user asks how to pay CDL drivers — cents per mile (CPM), percentage of reven
body:
# CDL Driver Pay Models

Driver pay structure affects recruiting, retention, dispatch behavior, and HOS compliance under `Part 395`. There's no single right model — each has tradeoffs. This skill covers the main structures and where each fits.

## Cents per mile (CPM)
- Most common OTR model
- 2025 typical range: $0.55-$0.85/mi for company drivers
- Per-diem split available (portion as non-taxed per diem under IRS rules)
- **Pro** — simple, scales with productivity
- **Con** — driver loses pay on detention, traffic, weather. Encourages HOS pushing.

## Percentage of revenue
- Driver gets a % of the linehaul (typically 25-30% for company drivers, 65-72% for lease-ops)
- Often used with owner-ops and premium lanes
- **Pro** — driver shares upside on premium freight
- **Con** — exposes driver to rate swings, complex settlement

## Hourly
- Common for local drivers
- Required for non-DOT drivers under FLSA
- 2025 typical: $22-$35/hr depending on market
- **Pro** — fair pay for stop-and-go, detention, urban work
- **Con** — overtime exposure unless driver qualifies for motor-carrier exemption (`29 USC § 213(b)(1)`)

## Salary
- Used for dedicated/regional lanes with predictable volume
- Often combined with productivity bonuses
- 2025 typical: $65k-$95k
- **Pro** — driver predictability, retention
- **Con** — overtime exposure for non-exempt; doesn't scale with volume

## Daily / load-pay
- Flat per-day or per-load
- Common for short-haul, hub-and-spoke
- **Pro** — administrative simplicity
- **Con** — driver behavior issues if rates don't match effort

## The Motor Carrier Exemption
Under FLSA, drivers whose work affects interstate commerce safety and who are subject to FMCSA jurisdiction are typically exempt from **overtime** requirements. Important caveats:
- Doesn't exempt from **minimum wage**
- Doesn't apply to drivers exclusively under 10,000 lb GVWR (Corrections Act 2008)
- Some state laws override (CA, others)

## Accessorial and bonus structures
- **Detention** pay (after free time)
- **Stop pay** (per stop beyond first)
- **Tarp pay** (flatbed)
- **Hazmat** premium
- **Safety bonus** — quarterly/annually for clean record
- **Sign-on bonus** — paid over 6-12 months typically
- **Referral bonus** — common retention tool
- **Per diem** — non-taxed portion of pay

## How pay structure interacts with HOS
Pure CPM with no detention pay creates pressure to push HOS limits. Salary + bonuses tied to safety record realign incentives. Many fatigue-related crashes can be traced to pay structures that punish stopping.

## Common errors
- Misclassifying drivers as overtime-exempt under state law
- Per diem improperly structured (IRS rules require substantiation)
- Bonus formulas drivers don't understand (recruiting tool that turns into retention problem)
- 1099 driver pay with no W-2 backup when DOL audits

## How Compass surfaces this

- **IRS Publication 463** — per diem rules

name: Driver Qualification File
q: Use this skill when the user asks about Driver Qualification Files (DQF) — what must be in a DQ file
body:
# Driver Qualification File (DQF)

The **Driver Qualification File** is the regulated record proving a driver meets FMCSA standards under `§ 391.51`. It's the single most-scrutinized document set in any FMCSA audit. This skill covers exactly what belongs in the DQF, retention rules, and common audit findings.

## The 12 required documents (`§ 391.51(b)`)
1. **Driver's employment application** — `§ 391.21`
2. **Inquiry to previous employers** (3 years back, DOT-regulated employers) — `§ 391.23`
3. **Inquiry to State driver licensing agencies** — MVR for each state held in last 3 years
4. **Annual MVR review** — `§ 391.25(a)`
5. **Annual driver certificate of violations** — `§ 391.27`
6. **Medical Examiner's Certificate** — current — `§ 391.43`
7. **Medical examiner verification** — National Registry number — `§ 391.51(b)(7)`
8. **Road test certificate** — OR equivalent under `§ 391.33` — typically CDL acts as substitute
9. **Safety performance history records** — Previous Employer Information Request response
10. **Medical variance/exemption** — if applicable
11. **Driver's license copy** — current
12. **Entry-Level Driver Training certificate** — `§ 380.609` for first-time CDL holders post-2/7/2022

## What does NOT go in the DQF
- Drug & alcohol records — separate file under `§ 382.401`
- W-4, I-9, payroll — personnel file
- Performance reviews, discipline — personnel file
- Workers' comp records — separate per state
- ADA accommodation requests — personnel file

## Retention
- Active driver: maintain the full DQF for **duration of employment**
- After termination: retain for **3 years**
- After termination, items 1 (application), 5 (cert of violations), 9 (safety history): retain for at least 3 years
- MEC: retain at least 3 years from expiration

## Annual maintenance
Each year on the anniversary:
- Pull a fresh MVR
- Review the MVR (signed/dated review)
- Obtain driver's annual certificate of violations
- Document the annual review per `§ 391.25(c)`

## When to update
- New medical certificate issued → update DQF immediately
- Driver moves states → new MVR
- Driver gains/loses endorsement → updated CDL copy
- ELDT only at hire (one-time document for entry-level drivers)

## Common audit findings
- Prior-employer inquiry missing or returned blank
- MEC expired (not pulled before lapse)
- Annual MVR/review missed in year 2 or 3
- ELDT missing for post-2022 first-time CDL holders
- Application missing residence/employment history detail required by `§ 391.21`
- DQF and personnel files mixed (auditor pulls confidential HR data)

## How Compass surfaces this

name: Driver Wellness And Retention
q: Use this skill when the user asks about CDL driver wellness, retention strategies, what causes drive
body:
# Driver Wellness and Retention

Trucking's industry-wide turnover rate at large fleets hovers near 90% annually. Retention is the single biggest hidden cost in carrier operations. Wellness — physical, mental, financial — is the strongest leading indicator. The records that document these efforts fall under `Part 379` for general carrier recordkeeping.

## What drives drivers out
- **Home time** — #1 reason cited in industry surveys
- **Pay shortfalls** — detention, deadhead unpaid
- **Dispatch treatment** — feeling like a number
- **Equipment problems** — repeated breakdowns
- **Long sit times** — between loads, at shippers
- **Health issues** — sleep, weight, diabetes risk
- **Family pressure** — divorce risk highest in OTR

## Physical wellness
- **Sleep apnea screening** — common, treatable, affects medical certification
- **Diet on the road** — limited healthy options at truck stops
- **Exercise** — minimal opportunity in OTR
- **Hypertension** — affects MEC renewal
- **Diabetes** — affects MEC renewal

Programs that help: gym partnerships (Anytime Fitness), telehealth, on-board fitness equipment, dietitian consult, partner with St. Christopher Truckers Relief Fund.

## Mental health
- Isolation in OTR
- Limited access to therapy on the road
- Suicide risk above national average for drivers
- Programs: telehealth, EAP, peer support groups, chaplain partnerships

## Financial wellness
- Direct deposit + same-day pay tools (Branch, MoneyNetwork)
- Per diem optimization
- Financial literacy modules
- Emergency assistance programs
- 401(k) match

## Retention levers (in order of impact)
1. **Home time predictability** — even 1 weekend in 3 beats unknown
2. **Pay floor** — minimum weekly guarantee
3. **Driver-facing dispatcher culture**
4. **Equipment age** — newer trucks reduce frustration
5. **Lane assignment** — consistent runs
6. **Recognition** — million-mile awards, safety bonuses
7. **Career path** — trainer, dedicated, supervisor opportunities
8. **Family-friendly** — ride-along programs, pet policy, etc.

## What recruiting can't fix
If the operating model creates 100% turnover, no recruiting funnel can keep up. Fixing retention is cheaper than out-recruiting churn.

## Measurement
- **Annualized turnover** — most common metric
- **First-90-day retention** — leading indicator
- **eNPS** for drivers
- **Exit interview data** — most carriers don't do this rigorously

## Common errors
- Sign-on bonuses without retention bonuses (hire, lose, repeat)
- Treating wellness as HR overhead, not operations
- Ignoring family communication (spouses influence retention)
- No formal exit interview process
- Driver communication only through dispatch — no separate driver advocate

name: Drug And Alcohol Testing
q: Use this skill when the user asks about commercial driver drug & alcohol testing under 49 CFR 382 +
body:
# Commercial Driver Drug and Alcohol Testing

FMCSA's drug and alcohol testing program for CDL drivers runs under **`49 CFR Part 382`** (the program rules) and **`49 CFR Part 40`** (DOT-wide testing procedures). It's the most enforced and most litigated FMCSA program. This skill covers the six test types, the panel, the Clearinghouse, and recordkeeping.

## The six test types
1. **Pre-employment** — before first dispatch, drug test only (alcohol optional). Negative required.
2. **Random** — annual rate set by FMCSA (currently 50% drug, 10% alcohol of the pool)
3. **Post-accident** — required when accident criteria in `§ 382.303` are met (fatality OR citation+injury OR citation+tow)
4. **Reasonable suspicion** — supervisor-observed signs, supervisor trained per `§ 382.603`
5. **Return-to-duty** — after a positive/refusal, before resuming safety-sensitive function
6. **Follow-up** — minimum 6 tests in 12 months after return, lasting up to 5 years

## The 5-panel drug screen
- Marijuana (THC)
- Cocaine
- Opioids (includes codeine, morphine, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, oxycodone, oxymorphone, 6-AM, since 2018 expansion)
- Amphetamines (incl. MDMA)
- Phencyclidine (PCP)

As of 2023, the **oral fluid** alternative to urine is approved (some labs implementing).

## Alcohol testing
- Breath test, EBT device
- Prohibited concentrations: **0.04+ BAC** disqualifies
- 0.02-0.039 BAC removes from safety-sensitive function for 24 hours

## Post-accident testing windows
- **Alcohol** — within 8 hours
- **Drugs** — within 32 hours
- Missing window: document why

## The Clearinghouse (`Part 382 Subpart G`)
- All carriers query pre-employment (full query) and annually (limited query) per `§ 382.701`
- All positive results, refusals, and return-to-duty events reported by MROs and carriers
- Driver must consent to a query
- Carrier cannot dispatch a driver in **prohibited status**

## Recordkeeping (`§ 382.401`)
- Positive results: **5 years**
- Negative results: **1 year**
- Random selection records: **2 years**
- Annual calendar plan: **5 years**
- Supervisor training: **for duration of employment + 2 years**
- These records are in a **separate file** from the DQF

## Substance Abuse Professional (SAP) process
A driver with a positive/refusal must:
1. See an FMCSA-qualified SAP
2. Complete the SAP's recommended program
3. Pass a return-to-duty test
4. Complete follow-up testing

## Common errors
- Mixing D&A records into the DQF
- Missing post-accident testing window
- Pre-employment query of Clearinghouse missed
- Random pool not properly maintained (consortium administrator handles for many small carriers)
- Supervisor reasonable-suspicion training never completed
- DOT vs non-DOT test forms confused

name: Ehs Emergency Environmental
q: Use this skill when the user asks about Environmental Health & Safety (EHS) for trucking — fuel spil
body:
# EHS Emergency and Environmental Response for Carriers

Environmental Health and Safety (EHS) for a motor carrier covers fuel spills, hazmat releases, on-site injuries, terminal hazards, and reporting to **EPA**, **OSHA**, and (for hazmat) **PHMSA**. Cargo securement under `Part 393 Subpart I` ties into this when securement failures cause environmental damage. This skill outlines the carrier's response and reporting framework.

## Fuel spill response
**On-road spill (truck involved in crash, ruptured saddle tank)**
1. Driver: stop, render aid, call 911
2. Notify dispatch + safety
3. Carrier notifies the **National Response Center (NRC) at 1-800-424-8802** if reportable quantity reached
4. Engage spill response contractor (e.g., Clean Harbors, US Ecology)
5. State environmental agency may require notification (varies)
6. Document quantity, location, time, response

**Reportable quantity** for diesel fuel under CERCLA is typically tied to the **harmful quantity** rule — any sheen on water, or any quantity that may damage public health, must be reported.

## Hazmat release (placardable material)
Driver/carrier must:
1. Make the area safe — evacuate per ERG distance
2. Call **CHEMTREC (1-800-424-9300)** or the carrier's emergency contact on shipping papers
3. Call **911** and **NRC**
4. File **DOT incident report (Form 5800.1)** within 30 days per `§ 171.16`
5. Some releases require **immediate telephone notification** to NRC per `§ 171.15` (death, hospitalization, evacuation, marine pollution, etc.)

## Terminal / workplace incidents
OSHA jurisdiction covers the terminal:
- Slip/fall, forklift injury, dock injuries
- **OSHA 300 log** required for recordable injuries
- **OSHA Form 301** detail for each
- Annual **300A summary** posted Feb 1 - April 30
- Fatality → notify OSHA within **8 hours**
- In-patient hospitalization, amputation, loss of eye → notify within **24 hours**

## Spill kits and PPE
For any operation that handles fuel transfers or hazmat:
- Absorbent pads, booms
- Drip pans for fueling
- Shovels, spill containment
- PPE: gloves, eye protection, respirators where indicated
- Eyewash stations near battery / chemical handling

## Used oil and waste
- Used oil from PM: handled per EPA used oil rules
- Antifreeze: separate disposal
- Filters: drained and recycled
- Batteries: returned for recycling
- Aerosol cans: hazardous waste in many states

## Documentation
- Spill response log
- Hazmat security plan and incident records per `§ 172.802`
- OSHA injury records
- Training records for spill response
- Contractor invoices and manifests

## Common errors
- Driver tries to clean a spill themselves and creates worse problem
- Carrier doesn't report a reportable spill — EPA citations + penalties
- OSHA logs not maintained at terminal
- Hazmat 5800.1 form not filed within 30 days
- No emergency contact on shipping papers — placard violation

name: Eld Mandate Compliance
q: Use this skill when the user asks about Electronic Logging Device (ELD) compliance under 49 CFR 395
body:
# ELD Mandate Compliance

The Electronic Logging Device (ELD) mandate requires most CMV drivers subject to Hours of Service rules to record duty status electronically rather than on paper. Governed by `Part 395` subpart B, with device technical specs in `§ 395.20` through `§ 395.38`.

## Who must use an ELD
- Interstate drivers required to keep RODS under `§ 395.8`
- Property and passenger CMVs (vehicles in interstate commerce meeting CMV thresholds)

## Who is exempt
- Drivers using the **short-haul exception** under `§ 395.1(e)(1)` (150 air-mile radius, return to work-reporting location within 14 hours)
- Driveaway-towaway operations where the vehicle is the commodity
- Vehicles with model-year engines older than **2000** (pre-2000 engine, not pre-2000 chassis)
- Drivers who keep RODS no more than **8 days in any 30-day period**

## Device requirements
1. Registered and self-certified on the **FMCSA ELD list**
2. Integrally synchronized with the engine
3. Records date, time, location, engine hours, vehicle miles, driver/carrier identity
4. Supports data transfer via web service, email, USB, or Bluetooth
5. Provides a printout or display on roadside request

## Carrier obligations
- Maintain user manual, instruction sheet for data transfer, malfunction guide, and **8 days of blank paper logs** in the truck (`§ 395.22(h)`)
- Train drivers on ELD operation and malfunction reporting
- Retain ELD records for **6 months** plus supporting documents under `§ 395.11`
- Address malfunctions within **8 days** of discovery (`§ 395.34`)

## Common errors
- Using an **AOBRD** (the pre-ELD device); the AOBRD grandfather period ended December 16, 2019
- Allowing unidentified driving time to accumulate without assignment or annotation
- Missing the 8 paper-log backup requirement
- Not certifying logs at the end of each 24-hour period

## What auditors look for
- Device on the FMCSA registered list
- Driver edits properly annotated with reason
- Unassigned driving cleared promptly
- Supporting documents (BOLs, fuel receipts, dispatch records) retained alongside ELD data

name: Electric Truck Readiness
q: Use when a carrier asks about electric trucks — Tesla Semi, Freightliner eCascadia, Volvo VNR Electr
body:
# Electric Truck Readiness

Battery-electric Class 7 and 8 tractors (Tesla Semi, Freightliner eCascadia, Volvo VNR Electric, Peterbilt 579EV, Kenworth T680E) are subject to the same FMCSA regulations as diesel CMVs under `Part 390` — DOT number, operating authority, driver qualification, HOS, inspection, and maintenance rules all apply. The differences are operational, not regulatory.

## What's the same as a diesel CMV
- USDOT number and MCS-150 obligations
- CDL requirements (Class A for >26,001 lb GCWR with trailer >10,001 lb)
- HOS rules under `Part 395` and ELD mandate
- DVIRs under `§ 396.11` and annual inspection under `§ 396.17`
- IFTA registration **does still apply** for interstate operations — electricity is not currently a taxable IFTA fuel, but the registration and mileage reporting structure remains for fleets that also run any diesel

## What's different
1. **Range and charging** — payload-loaded ranges are typically 150–500 miles depending on model. Route planning must include public DC fast charging or depot charging
2. **Weight** — battery weight reduces payload. Federal weight allowance under FAST Act gives EVs an extra **2,000 lb** on the gross vehicle weight (up to 82,000 lb)
3. **Maintenance** — fewer fluids, no diesel emissions systems, regenerative braking reduces brake wear, but high-voltage systems require trained technicians
4. **Driver training** — high-voltage safety, charging protocols, regenerative braking behavior

## Readiness checklist
- Confirm depot electrical capacity (Level 3 DC fast charging typically needs 350 kW per stall)
- Verify utility interconnection and demand-charge tariff
- Train technicians on high-voltage lockout (NFPA 70E)
- Update emergency response plan for battery thermal events
- Update driver training to cover charging, range management, and one-pedal driving

## What auditors look for
FMCSA does not audit charging or batteries — they audit the same compliance categories. Make sure DQF, HOS, maintenance, and inspection records reflect the EV the same way they would a diesel truck.

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

name: Emergency Equipment On Cmv
q: Use this skill when the user asks what emergency equipment a CMV must carry under 49 CFR 393
body:
# Emergency Equipment on CMVs

Every power-unit CMV operated in interstate commerce must carry specific emergency equipment at all times. Governed by `§ 393.95`.

## Required equipment
1. **Fire extinguisher** — properly filled and located so it is readily accessible:
   - Hazmat vehicles (placarded): **UL rating of 10 B:C or two extinguishers totaling 20 B:C**
   - All other CMVs: **UL rating of at least 5 B:C**
   - Must be securely mounted, labeled with UL rating, and have a visible pressure gauge
2. **Spare fuses** — one spare for each type and size of fuse needed, unless the vehicle uses circuit breakers
3. **Warning devices for stopped vehicles** — one of the following sets:
   - **Three bidirectional emergency reflective triangles** meeting FMVSS 125, or
   - **Six fusees** plus three liquid-burning flares (with restrictions), or
   - **Three liquid-burning flares** (with restrictions)

## Where warning devices are NOT required
- Buses transporting passengers (different rules under `§ 393.95(f)`)
- Vehicles transporting Class 1 explosives, hazmat that requires placards, or flammable liquid/gas in cargo tanks cannot use flares or fusees as warning devices

## How to deploy warning devices
Per `§ 392.22`, when a CMV is stopped on a highway or shoulder for any reason other than necessary traffic stops, the driver must place warning devices within **10 minutes**:
- **Two-lane road**: one triangle 100 ft behind, one 100 ft ahead, one 10 ft behind on the traffic side
- **Divided/one-way highway**: triangles 10 ft, 100 ft, and 200 ft behind, all on traffic side
- **Hill, curve, or obstruction**: extend the rear triangle up to **500 ft** to give approaching drivers warning

## Common errors
- Expired or discharged fire extinguisher (no pressure on gauge)
- Fire extinguisher not securely mounted (rolling loose in cab)
- Missing one of the three triangles
- Triangle reflective surface damaged or faded
- No spare fuses on a fuse-equipped vehicle

## What auditors and roadside inspectors look for
These are common Level I and Level II inspection findings. Missing or defective emergency equipment is an out-of-service condition under the **CVSA North American Standard** when the extinguisher is missing or fully discharged on a placarded hazmat load.

name: Ergonomics Of Cmv Operation
q: Use this skill when the user asks about driver ergonomics — back/neck/shoulder injury prevention, se
body:
# Ergonomics of CMV Operation

Driver ergonomics is not directly regulated by FMCSA, but the medical qualification rules in `§ 391.41` and `§ 391.43` make musculoskeletal fitness part of every DOT physical. Repetitive-strain injuries (back, neck, shoulders, knees) are a leading cause of driver workers' comp claims and early disqualification.

## What drives injury risk
- **Whole-body vibration** from the seat and chassis (worst on older suspensions, rougher roads)
- **Repeated entry/egress** from the cab (a Class 8 driver climbs in and out 8–12 times per shift; knees and shoulders take the worst of it)
- **Twisting while seated** to check mirrors or operate trailer connections
- **Manual cargo handling** — touch freight, tarping flatbeds, refrigerated unit operation
- **Static seated posture** for 10+ hours

## How to reduce risk
1. **Air-ride seat properly adjusted** — weight setting matched to driver, lumbar support engaged, seat height so knees are slightly below hips
2. **Three points of contact** every time in and out of the cab — face the truck, never jump
3. **Mirror and steering-wheel adjustment** before driving, not while moving
4. **Stretch breaks** every 2 hours during the 30-minute break or fuel stops
5. **Cargo handling training** — proper lift mechanics, mechanical aids, partner-lift heavy items
6. **Cab climate control** that lets the driver shed cold-weather layers when cab warms up

## What the DOT physical checks
The medical examiner evaluates:
- Range of motion in neck, shoulders, back, hips, knees, ankles
- Grip strength and upper-body strength
- Ability to climb in and out of the cab
- Cervical spine flexibility (to see mirrors)
- Any condition that interferes with safe vehicle control

## Carrier program elements
- Pre-employment functional capacity check (where allowed by state law and ADA)
- Wellness program with stretching, weight management, hydration
- Equipment specs that prioritize air-ride seat, automated transmission, easy-entry grab handles
- Modified-duty return-to-work for soft-tissue injuries

## What auditors look for
FMCSA does not audit ergonomics directly. OSHA and state workers' comp authorities do. If injury rates are high, expect scrutiny on training records, equipment maintenance, and accommodation processes.

name: Fatigue Management And Night Driving
q: Use this skill when the user asks about driver fatigue management — circadian rhythm impact on drivi
body:
# Fatigue Management and Night Driving

FMCSA addresses fatigue primarily through the Hours of Service rules in `Part 395`, but a **Fatigue Risk Management Program (FRMP)** goes beyond minimum HOS compliance to address circadian rhythm, sleep quality, and driver health. `§ 392.3` prohibits operating a CMV while ability is so impaired by fatigue that continued driving is unsafe.

## Circadian fundamentals
- Human alertness drops sharply between **02:00 and 06:00** and again in a smaller dip from **14:00 to 16:00**
- Most single-vehicle, run-off-road crashes happen during the early-morning low
- Sleep debt accumulates — losing 2 hours per night for a week produces impairment similar to a 0.05 BAC
- Drivers cannot reliably self-assess fatigue past a certain threshold

## What HOS gives you (the floor)
- 11-hour driving limit, 14-hour shift cap, 10-hour off-duty (`§ 395.3`)
- 30-minute break after 8 hours driving
- 60/70-hour weekly limits
- 34-hour restart

## What an FRMP adds (above the floor)
1. **Sleep apnea screening** for high-BMI drivers (no federal mandate but allowed under `§ 391.41` general fitness)
2. **Schedule design** that limits back-to-back nights
3. **Rest-quality coaching** (sleeper berth setup, blackout curtains, light exposure)
4. **Fatigue-detection technology** (Lytx DriveCam, Smart Drive, Guardian by Seeing Machines)
5. **Stand-down policy** that lets a fatigued driver shut down without penalty

## Night-driving safety
- Headlight aim verified at PM intervals
- Mirror and windshield cleanliness checked at start of shift
- Avoid sunrise/sunset glare windows for high-risk routes
- Increase following distance — reaction times are longer at night
- Plan fuel and rest stops in advance; circling for parking burns the clock and adds fatigue

## What auditors look for
FMCSA does not audit FRMP programs directly, but in a compliance review or post-crash investigation, evidence of fatigue management (training records, coaching logs, parking policies) helps establish the carrier's safety management posture.

## Pitfalls
- Treating the 30-minute break as a fueling stop only — the rule exists for fatigue mitigation
- Dispatching that forces drivers to switch night/day schedules week to week
- Ignoring driver complaints of inability to sleep

name: Fleet Financial Modeling And Budgeting
q: Use when a carrier owner, CFO, or controller asks how to build an annual budget, monthly P&L model,
body:
# Fleet Financial Modeling and Budgeting

There is no FMCSA rule that requires a carrier to build a budget, but the **BMC-91/BMC-91X** financial responsibility filings (`§ 387.7`) and the financial-fitness elements of the safety rating process create indirect pressure to know your numbers. A working financial model is also necessary to make rate, hiring, and equipment decisions.

## Core model structure
1. **Revenue** — loaded miles × rate per mile, plus accessorials (detention, layover, fuel surcharge, lumper reimbursement)
2. **Variable cost per mile** — fuel, tires, maintenance, tolls, driver pay (if mileage-based), IFTA fuel tax
3. **Fixed cost per truck per week** — truck payment, trailer payment, insurance, permits, base salaries, dispatcher and office overhead allocation
4. **Cost per total mile (CPM)** = (variable + fixed) ÷ total miles, including deadhead
5. **Breakeven rate** = CPM ÷ loaded-mile ratio

## Typical small-fleet benchmarks (informational, not regulatory)
- All-in CPM (1–10 truck dry van): **$1.80 to $2.30** depending on fuel and labor cost
- Loaded-mile ratio: aim for **88–92%** (deadhead 8–12%)
- Fuel as % of revenue: **20–28%** depending on rate and MPG
- Driver pay as % of revenue: **28–35%**
- Insurance per truck per year: **$10,000 to $18,000** for small interstate fleets (highly variable)

## Monthly P&L cadence
1. Close revenue from factoring/AR ledger
2. Reconcile fuel-card and ELD mileage
3. Allocate maintenance from work orders
4. Capture insurance, permits, and depreciation
5. Compute CPM, revenue per truck, profit per truck
6. Variance-analyze actual vs budget

## Annual budget elements
- Revenue plan by lane and customer
- Equipment plan (replacements, additions, disposals)
- Headcount plan
- Capex schedule
- Insurance renewal forecast (often the largest single fixed cost change year over year)
- Debt schedule

## What auditors look for
FMCSA financial-responsibility review is limited to verifying the BMC-91 filing and that liability coverage meets the minimums in `§ 387.9` ($750,000 to $5,000,000 depending on commodity). State authorities, lenders, and shippers will look deeper at the actual financial statements.

name: Fleet Fuel Card Programs
q: Use when a carrier asks about fuel-card vendor selection (Comdata, EFS, WEX, RTS, Pilot Flying J, Lo
body:
# Fleet Fuel Card Programs

Fuel cards are an operating tool, not a regulated one — but they are also the source of the mileage and gallon data that drives **IFTA quarterly returns** and the supporting documents that satisfy `§ 395.11` ELD record requirements.

## Major vendors
- **Comdata** — large independent fleet network, deep TMS integrations
- **EFS / WEX** — broad acceptance, strong reporting
- **RTS Carrier Services** — popular with small fleets, often bundled with factoring
- **Pilot Flying J / TCH** — best in-network discounts at Pilot/Flying J locations
- **Love's Express** — best in-network discounts at Love's
- **TCH (Transportation Clearing House)** — broad acceptance, common in small-fleet space
- **Major-oil cards** (Mobil, Shell) — narrower acceptance but sometimes better retail pricing

## What to compare
1. **Discount structure** — cents off retail vs cost-plus vs negotiated rack
2. **In-network vs out-of-network spread** — where will your drivers actually fuel?
3. **Transaction fees** — per-swipe, monthly card, statement
4. **Funding terms** — daily ACH vs weekly billing vs credit line
5. **Controls** — per-card limits, product restrictions, day/time windows, geofence, PIN+driver-ID
6. **Reporting** — gallons by state for IFTA, MPG by truck, exception alerts
7. **TMS / accounting integration** — direct feed into McLeod, ProTransport, QuickBooks, etc.

## IFTA support
A good fuel-card report gives you:
- Date, location (state), gallons, price per gallon
- Card number / driver ID / unit number
- Net cost including state fuel tax already paid at the pump

That is most of what you need for the IFTA return — the rest is jurisdictional miles from the ELD.

## Fraud controls
- Require PIN plus driver ID on every transaction
- Set per-transaction gallon caps slightly above tank capacity
- Restrict to diesel and DEF (block tobacco, lottery, cash advance)
- Set day/time windows that match operating hours
- Geofence to authorized states or corridors where possible
- Monitor exception reports weekly

## Common pitfalls
- Choosing the card with the lowest sticker discount and ignoring transaction fees
- Letting drivers share a card or PIN
- Not reconciling fuel-card gallons to ELD distance monthly (early warning for theft)
- Forgetting that retail fuel cards may not capture state fuel tax in the format IFTA needs

name: Fleet Safety Scorecard Design
q: Use this skill when the user asks how to design or improve a fleet safety scorecard — what KPIs to t
body:
# Fleet Safety Scorecard Design

A safety scorecard rolls up the inputs that the FMCSA's **Safety Measurement System (SMS)** uses for `Part 385` scoring, plus internal leading indicators, into a per-driver or per-truck rating used for coaching, pay, and termination decisions.

## Lagging indicators (outcomes)
- DOT-recordable crashes (`§ 390.5`)
- Preventable crashes (carrier determination)
- Roadside inspection violations by BASIC
- Workers' comp claims
- Cargo claims

## Leading indicators (behaviors)
- Telematics events: hard brake, hard accel, hard turn, speeding
- Camera events: following distance, lane drift, mobile phone use, seat belt
- HOS violations: form & manner, missing log, late certification
- DVIR defects per inspection
- On-time delivery and detention rates (proxy for schedule pressure)
- Training completion

## How to weight
A defensible scorecard:
1. Weights crashes the heaviest (e.g., 25–35% of total score)
2. Weights at-fault inspections second (15–25%)
3. Distributes the rest across leading indicators
4. Normalizes per mile or per duty hour so high-mileage drivers aren't punished
5. Uses rolling 12-month or 24-month windows so one bad week doesn't sink a tenured driver

## Scoring scale options
- **0–100 numeric** with thresholds (e.g., 90+ = Gold, 80–89 = Silver, etc.)
- **A through F** letter grade
- **Green / Yellow / Red** zones

## What to do with the score
- **Coaching** — green checks-in, yellow targeted coaching, red mandatory ride-along or remediation
- **Pay** — safety bonus tied to threshold (carefully — never financially penalize a driver for refusing an unsafe load under `§ 392.14` or sick under FMLA)
- **Termination** — only after documented coaching steps and progressive discipline

## Pitfalls
- Scoring drivers on outcomes they cannot control (e.g., a parked-and-struck crash)
- Letting the camera vendor's default scoring drive HR decisions without review
- Failing to keep coaching documentation that supports adverse actions
- Using the scorecard to retaliate for protected activity (sick leave, refusal of unsafe equipment under `§ 396.7`)

## What auditors look for
FMCSA does not audit internal scorecards, but during a compliance review they will check that coaching of high-risk drivers is documented and that driver discipline tracks behavior, not protected activity.

name: Fleet Vehicle Replacement Cycle Planning
q: Use when a fleet manager or owner asks when to replace tractors and trailers, optimal trade cycle ag
body:
# Fleet Vehicle Replacement Cycle Planning

FMCSA does not mandate a tractor or trailer replacement age. The trigger is whether the vehicle continues to meet `Part 393` equipment standards and pass the `§ 396.17` annual inspection. The economic question — when to replace — is driven by the curve where maintenance cost per mile rises faster than the depreciation savings of holding the truck longer.

## Common replacement targets
- **Linehaul tractors** (long-haul OTR): **500,000 to 700,000 miles** or **4 to 5 years**
- **Regional tractors**: **600,000 to 900,000 miles** or **5 to 7 years**
- **Local / day cab**: **750,000 to 1,000,000 miles** or **7 to 10 years**
- **Dry vans and reefers**: **7 to 10 years** (reefer trailers shorter due to refrigeration unit life)
- **Flatbeds and tankers**: **10 to 15 years**, sometimes longer

These are targets, not rules. The right number depends on duty cycle, terrain, driver care, and capital structure.

## Decision inputs
1. **Maintenance cost per mile trend** — when CPM rises 20%+ above fleet average, the truck is a candidate
2. **Aftertreatment cost** — DPF, SCR, EGR repairs after 500k miles can run $5,000–$15,000 per event
3. **Resale value curve** — the steepest depreciation is years 1–3; after year 5 the curve flattens
4. **Warranty coverage** — most OEM extended warranties end at 5 years or 500k–750k miles
5. **Driver retention** — newer trucks are a retention tool, especially for company drivers
6. **Fuel economy gap** — a 2026 truck may run 1.0–1.5 MPG better than a 2018, worth thousands per year
7. **Emissions trends** — California ACT/ACF and other state rules may force EV or near-zero adoption on certain duty cycles

## Build the replacement model
1. List every unit with year, miles, current book value, trailing 12-month maintenance
2. Project next 12 months of maintenance and downtime cost
3. Compare to monthly payment + insurance on a replacement unit
4. Calculate breakeven mileage where keep-vs-replace flips
5. Sequence replacements to smooth capex year over year

## Pitfalls
- Running trucks past warranty without budgeting for major aftertreatment events
- Replacing on a calendar without checking actual condition (newer can have more miles)
- Trading too early and losing the low-payment, paid-off years
- Ignoring trailer aging — a 12-year-old reefer trailer with a worn-out unit can cost more in claims than a new one in payments

- `49 CFR § 396.17` (annual inspection)
- `49 CFR § 396.3` (maintenance records)

name: Fmcsa Clearinghouse Workflow
q: Use this skill when the user asks about the FMCSA Drug & Alcohol Clearinghouse — full vs limited que
body:
# FMCSA Clearinghouse Workflow

The FMCSA Drug & Alcohol Clearinghouse is the federal database of CDL driver D&A violations, return-to-duty status, and follow-up testing. Required queries and reporting are set in `§ 382.701` and the surrounding subpart G. Effective January 6, 2023, state licensing agencies (SDLAs) must also query before issuing/renewing a CDL.

## Carrier registration
- Register at clearinghouse.fmcsa.dot.gov as the **employer** of CDL drivers operating CMVs in commerce
- Assign a Clearinghouse administrator and (optional) assistants
- Purchase a **query plan** sized to your hiring volume
- Designate or contract a **Consortium/Third-Party Administrator (C/TPA)** for testing program management

## Driver registration
- Drivers must register to consent to **full queries** and to challenge information
- Full-query consent is electronic; a driver who refuses consent cannot be hired/maintained in safety-sensitive duty

## Query types
1. **Pre-employment full query** — required for every new CDL driver before performing safety-sensitive functions (`§ 382.701(a)`). Must obtain specific electronic consent in the Clearinghouse.
2. **Annual limited query** — for each current driver, once per 12 months (`§ 382.701(b)`). General written consent on file is enough; only requires a follow-up full query if the limited query indicates records exist.

## What must be reported (by the employer)
Per `§ 382.705(b)`:
- Verified positive, adulterated, or substituted DOT drug test
- Confirmed alcohol test ≥ 0.04
- Refusal to test (including no-show, leaving the collection site, etc.)
- Actual knowledge of on-duty alcohol or controlled-substance use
- Negative return-to-duty test
- Successful completion of follow-up testing plan

Reports must be made by the close of the **third business day** after the event.

## What MROs and SAPs report
- **MRO** reports the verified positive/adulterated/substituted within two business days
- **SAP** reports successful initial evaluation, education/treatment, and follow-up plan

## Prohibited driver status
A driver in **prohibited** status cannot perform safety-sensitive functions until SAP completion and a negative return-to-duty test. Pre-employment full query catches this; SDLA query catches it at CDL renewal.

## Recordkeeping
- Query results: **3 years**
- Consent records: duration of employment + **3 years** after
- Reports of violations: **5 years** (consistent with `§ 382.401`)

## Common errors
- Skipping the pre-employment full query and only running the limited query
- Missing the 3-business-day reporting clock
- Not pulling annual limited queries on every driver in the rolling 12-month window
- Treating Clearinghouse as a substitute for the previous-employer inquiry under `§ 391.23` — it is additional, not replacement

## How Compass surfaces this

name: Fmcsa Driver Disqualification And Reinstatement
q: Use when a driver has been disqualified or is at risk of disqualification — major offense conviction
body:
# FMCSA Driver Disqualification and Reinstatement

A CDL driver becomes **disqualified** from operating a CMV when specific offenses, BAC results, or court orders occur. Federal disqualifications are set in `§ 383.51` (drivers) and `§ 391.15` (carrier-side rules). State actions on the underlying license follow `Part 384` requirements.

## Major offenses (first conviction — disqualifies for at least 1 year)
Under `§ 383.51(b)`:
- BAC of 0.04 or greater while operating a CMV
- Driving a CMV under the influence (alcohol or controlled substance)
- Refusing to test
- Leaving the scene of a crash involving the CMV
- Using a CMV to commit a felony
- Driving a CMV while CDL is suspended, revoked, or canceled
- Negligent operation resulting in a fatality

Second major offense = **lifetime disqualification** (reinstatement possible under `§ 383.51(b)(11)` after 10 years with rehab program)

## Hazmat felonies
Using a CMV to commit a felony involving controlled substances = **lifetime disqualification, no reinstatement**

## Serious traffic violations (second in 3 years = 60 days; third = 120 days)
Per `§ 383.51(c)`:
- Excessive speeding (15+ mph over)
- Reckless driving
- Improper or erratic lane change
- Following too closely
- Traffic violation arising from a fatal crash
- Driving CMV without a CDL or proper class/endorsement
- Texting while driving (`§ 392.80`)
- Using a hand-held mobile phone (`§ 392.82`)

## Railroad-crossing violations (`§ 383.51(d)`)
- 60 days first offense, 120 days second in 3 years, 1 year third in 3 years

## Out-of-service order violations (`§ 383.51(e)`)
- Operating after being placed OOS at roadside: 180 days to 2 years (longer for hazmat or passenger)

## Carrier-side disqualification (`§ 391.15`)
A carrier cannot permit a driver to operate a CMV if the driver:
- Has a suspended/revoked/canceled CDL
- Is disqualified under `§ 383.51`
- Lost privilege in any state

## Reinstatement process
1. Serve the disqualification period in full
2. For DUI/refusal: complete SAP evaluation, treatment, and return-to-duty test (`§ 382.503`)
3. Pay any state reinstatement fees and complete any required courses
4. Re-take CDL knowledge/skills test if state requires
5. Pre-employment full Clearinghouse query (`§ 382.701`) before returning to safety-sensitive duty
6. Document the entire chain in the DQF and personnel file

## What auditors look for
- Carrier checked MVR before allowing return to duty
- Clearinghouse status is **not prohibited**
- Annual review (`§ 391.25`) caught any state action between hires
- DQF reflects the certificate of violations under `§ 391.27`

## How Compass surfaces this

name: Fmcsa Grants And Funding
q: Use this skill when the user asks about FMCSA financial assistance + grants — Motor Carrier Safety A
body:
# FMCSA Grants and Funding

FMCSA administers several grant programs that flow through state agencies to support safety, enforcement, and driver training. These are not direct payments to private motor carriers, but carriers benefit indirectly through state programs, and CDL schools and training providers can access certain funds.

## Main FMCSA grant programs
1. **Motor Carrier Safety Assistance Program (MCSAP)** — funds state CMV enforcement (roadside inspections, traffic enforcement, compliance reviews). About $400M/year, distributed to states by formula
2. **High Priority Program (HP)** — competitive grants for state and non-profit projects that improve CMV safety beyond MCSAP baseline
3. **Commercial Driver's License Program Implementation (CDLPI)** — funds state CDL system improvements (SDLA infrastructure, ELDT registration, Clearinghouse integration)
4. **Commercial Motor Vehicle Operator's Safety Training (CMVOST)** — grants for veterans and refresher training programs
5. **Innovative Technology Deployment (ITD) / Performance and Registration Information Systems Management (PRISM)** — state IT and screening infrastructure
6. **Safety Data Improvement Program (SaDIP)** — state crash and inspection data quality

## What private carriers can actually get
Direct federal grants to a single private carrier are rare. Carriers can access:
- **State pass-through programs** funded by MCSAP/HP/CMVOST
- **CMVOST tuition reimbursement** for veterans entering CDL training
- **State workforce development boards** funding CDL school tuition
- **EPA SmartWay and DERA** funding for emissions reductions (separate from FMCSA)
- **Department of Energy / state utility incentives** for EV charging or alt-fuel adoption
- **USDA REAP grants** for rural carriers investing in efficiency

## How to find current opportunities
- grants.gov — federal-wide grant portal
- fmcsa.dot.gov/grants — current FMCSA NOFOs
- State DOT and DMV grant pages
- Trade associations (ATA, OOIDA, state associations) often track and circulate opportunities

## Pitfalls
- Treating FMCSA grants as a revenue source for routine operations — they are not
- Missing federal pass-through requirements (Davis-Bacon, Build America Buy America, reporting)
- Underestimating the administrative burden of a federal grant — most small carriers do better with state programs or commercial financing

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

- `49 U.S.C. § 31102` (MCSAP authority)
- `49 CFR Part 350` (MCSAP regulations)
- `49 CFR Part 355` (compatibility of state laws)

name: Fmcsa Portal Navigation
q: Use this skill when the user asks where to find specific information at fmcsa
body:
# FMCSA Portal Navigation

FMCSA spreads its data and tools across several public and authenticated systems. Knowing which site holds what saves real time during audits, MCS-150 updates, and Clearinghouse work.

## Public sites — no login
- **fmcsa.dot.gov** — regulations, guidance, news, FAQs
- **SAFER (safer.fmcsa.dot.gov)** — public carrier snapshot, look up by USDOT or MC number; shows operating authority, insurance on file, recent inspections, crashes, safety rating
- **SMS public site (ai.fmcsa.dot.gov/sms)** — Safety Measurement System BASIC percentiles for carriers, not driver-level
- **Licensing & Insurance (li-public.fmcsa.dot.gov)** — operating authority history, BOC-3 process agents, insurance filings (BMC-91/BMC-91X/BMC-34/BMC-32)
- **National Registry of Certified Medical Examiners** — verify examiner status
- **National Consumer Complaint Database (nccdb.fmcsa.dot.gov)** — consumer complaints, primarily for HHG/passenger carriers

## Authenticated portals — login required
- **FMCSA Portal (portal.fmcsa.dot.gov)** — the master account for carriers; from here:
  - File and update **MCS-150** (`§ 390.19` biennial update)
  - Access **A&I** crash and inspection detail (your data, not public)
  - Access **Pre-Employment Screening Program (PSP)** for new-hire records
  - Access **DataQs** (RDR) to challenge inspections or crashes
  - Manage user roles
- **Drug & Alcohol Clearinghouse (clearinghouse.fmcsa.dot.gov)** — pre-employment full and annual limited queries; employer violation reporting
- **Unified Registration System (URS)** — initial USDOT and operating authority registration
- **National Registry of CDL Skills Testers** — CDL examiners (state-administered, FMCSA-hosted)
- **ELDT Registry (tpr.fmcsa.dot.gov)** — Entry-Level Driver Training provider listing and certificate verification

## Where common docs live
- **MCS-150 / MCS-150B**: FMCSA Portal
- **MC/MX authority application**: URS
- **BOC-3 (process agent)**: filed by your designated process agent, viewable in L&I
- **BMC-91/91X insurance**: filed by your insurer, viewable in L&I and SAFER
- **PSP report**: PSP login (carrier-only access with driver consent)
- **Clearinghouse status**: Clearinghouse login

## Common pitfalls
- Confusing SAFER (public snapshot) with SMS (BASIC scoring)
- Updating MCS-150 by the legacy paper method instead of the Portal
- Letting Portal access roll over after a personnel change without updating roles
- Missing the biennial MCS-150 even when nothing has changed

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- `49 CFR § 390.19` (MCSL-150/MCS-150B updates)
- `49 CFR § 391.23` (PSP/MVR/Clearinghouse use in pre-employment)

name: Fmcsa Pre Employment Investigation Deep Dive
q: Use when a carrier asks about the full pre-employment investigation process for new CDL drivers unde
body:
# FMCSA Pre-Employment Investigation Deep Dive

The pre-employment investigation is the bundled set of inquiries a carrier must complete before a new CDL driver performs safety-sensitive functions. The core authority is `§ 391.23`, with supporting requirements at `§ 391.21`, `§ 391.25`, `§ 391.27`, `§ 382.701`, and the Privacy Act / FCRA overlay at 15 U.S.C. § 1681.

## What must be obtained before dispatch
1. **Driver's Application for Employment** (`§ 391.21`) — full 3-year address, employment, accident, and license history; 10 years for CDL employment
2. **MVR from every state** the driver held a license in the past 3 years (`§ 391.23(a)(1)`) — must be on file within 30 days of hire
3. **Safety performance history / Previous Employer Information Request** (`§ 391.23(d)`) — covers prior 3 years of DOT-regulated employment; sent to each prior DOT employer
4. **Drug & Alcohol Clearinghouse pre-employment full query** (`§ 382.701(a)`) — required before performing safety-sensitive function; specific electronic consent required
5. **Road test or equivalent** (`§ 391.31` and `§ 391.33`) — actual road test or accept CDL+endorsement as equivalent for some classes
6. **Medical certification** (`§ 391.43`) — current MEC from National Registry examiner
7. **Entry-Level Driver Training certificate** (`§ 380.609`) — for first-time CDL or upgrade applicants on or after February 7, 2022
8. **Pre-employment drug test** (`§ 382.301`) — verified negative before first safety-sensitive function (limited exceptions at `§ 382.301(b)`)

## Optional but strongly recommended
- **Pre-Employment Screening Program (PSP)** report — driver consent required; provides 5 years of crashes and 3 years of roadside inspections
- Criminal background check — handle under FCRA, with adverse-action protocol
- Functional capacity evaluation (where legal under state law and ADA)

## Sequence
1. Application + consent forms (Clearinghouse, PSP, MVR, drug test, prior-employer release)
2. Send PEIRs and MVR requests, pull PSP
3. Run Clearinghouse pre-employment full query
4. Schedule drug test and DOT physical (if no current MEC)
5. Verify ELDT in TPR if applicable
6. Road test or equivalent acceptance
7. Final qualification determination by the safety director, documented in DQF

## Recordkeeping
- All `§ 391.23` inquiries kept in the DQF for **duration of employment + 3 years**
- Drug test records kept under `§ 382.401`
- Clearinghouse query results: 3 years

## Common errors
- Letting the driver run a load before the Clearinghouse pre-employment full query result
- Pulling MVR from only one state when driver held licenses in others
- Treating PEIR responses (or no-response) as optional — `§ 391.23(d)` requires the carrier to make the request and document responses or non-responses
- Missing the ELDT TPR verification step for post-2/7/2022 hires

## What auditors look for
- All `§ 391.23` items present with timely dates
- Application complete with no gaps in 3-year employment history
- Negative pre-employment drug test before dispatch
- Clearinghouse query before safety-sensitive duty
- Adverse action documentation under FCRA when used
