name: Med Vision Standards Monocular
q: Use this skill when a driver has vision in only one eye or significantly reduced vision in one eye
body:
# Vision Standards & Monocular Driver Certification

Federal vision standards under § 391.41(b)(10) require distance visual acuity of at least 20/40 in each eye with or without correction, and field of vision of at least 70 degrees in horizontal meridian in each eye. Drivers not meeting these standards may apply for the FMCSA Vision Exemption Program.

## Federal vision baseline
- **20/40 distance acuity** in each eye, with or without corrective lenses
- **70 degrees horizontal field of vision** in each eye
- **Ability to recognize colors** of traffic signals + devices showing standard red, green, amber

## Monocular driver eligibility
A driver with vision loss in one eye may continue commercial driving if:
- Acuity in the better eye meets 20/40 distance + 70-degree field
- Has been monocular for at least 1 year
- No degenerative condition affecting the better eye
- Demonstrates good driving record with current vision status

## Vision Exemption Program
For drivers below the 20/40 standard:
- Apply to FMCSA Vision Exemption Program
- Provide medical history + current ophthalmologist's report
- Demonstrate 3 years of safe CMV driving with current vision status
- Annual renewal of exemption
- Annual ophthalmologist exam confirms continued ability

## How Compass tracks
- Driver's current vision exemption status
- Next required ophthalmologist visit
- Field of vision documentation
- Annual exemption renewal due dates

## Common compliance concerns
- Driver claims monocular qualification but vision in remaining eye has degraded
- Vision exemption renewal lapses
- New examination required after eye surgery (LASIK, cataract removal)

## Pitfall
A driver with a vision exemption who is hired by a new carrier — the exemption is portable but must be re-documented in the new DQF. New employer must file new exemption with FMCSA showing continued employer awareness.

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 391.41(b)(10)**
- **FMCSA Vision Exemption Program**

name: Medical Certification
q: Use this skill when the user asks about CDL driver medical certification — 49 CFR 391
body:
# Medical Certification

CDL drivers operating CMVs in interstate commerce must hold a current **Medical Examiner's Certificate (MEC, MCSA-5876)** issued by an examiner on the **National Registry of Certified Medical Examiners**. Governed by `§ 391.41` (physical qualifications), `§ 391.43` (examination), `§ 391.45` (when required), and `§ 391.51(b)(7)` (DQF retention).

## Who needs it
Any driver operating a CMV in interstate commerce that:
- Has GVWR or GCWR of 10,001 lb or more, OR
- Is designed/used to transport 9+ passengers (including driver) for compensation, or 16+ not for compensation, OR
- Transports hazmat requiring placards

Intrastate drivers follow state requirements, which are often similar.

## Validity period
- Standard certification: **up to 24 months** (`§ 391.43(b)(2)`)
- Conditional certifications for monitored conditions: shorter periods (3, 6, 12 months) at examiner's discretion
- A medical variance, exemption, or skill performance evaluation (SPE) may overlay

## Physical qualifications (`§ 391.41`)
Key thresholds:
- **Vision** — at least 20/40 distance in each eye and both, with or without correction; 70° peripheral; recognize traffic-signal colors (`§ 391.41(b)(10)`); FMCSA's alternative vision standard (effective 2022) applies for monocular vision
- **Hearing** — must perceive forced whisper at not less than 5 ft, or 40 dB or less average hearing loss in better ear (`§ 391.41(b)(11)`)
- **Blood pressure** — Stage 1 (140–159 / 90–99) certified for 1 year; Stage 2 (160–179 / 100–109) certified for 3 months one time; Stage 3 (180+/110+) disqualifying until controlled
- **Diabetes** — insulin-using drivers qualify under `§ 391.46` provided exemption form and treating-clinician evaluation
- **Seizure** — disqualifying unless `§ 391.41(b)(8)` exemption
- **Heart, respiratory, neurologic, musculoskeletal, mental** — examiner judgment under the rule

## Sleep apnea
Not a separate disqualifying condition, but examiners may require evaluation under the general respiratory and cardiovascular standards. Many examiners use BMI > 40, neck circumference, and Epworth scale as screening triggers.

## State licensing notification
Under `§ 383.71(h)`, CDL drivers must provide a current MEC to the state DMV (SDLA), which posts the medical status to the CDLIS record. This eliminated the paper med-card-in-the-wallet for most CDL drivers — the MVR is the proof.

## DQF requirements
- Original or copy of MEC kept in DQF (`§ 391.51(b)(7)`)
- **National Registry number** of the examiner must be verified and documented
- Retention: duration of employment + 3 years

## Common errors
- Examiner not on the National Registry at time of exam
- MEC expires while driver continues to operate
- Driver fails to provide MEC to state DMV, resulting in CDL downgrade
- Conditional certificate's shorter expiration not tracked
- Skill Performance Evaluation (SPE) or medical variance not in DQF

## What auditors look for
- Current MEC for every active CDL driver
- National Registry number verified
- CDLIS shows current medical status (no "not certified" or "expired")
- Diabetes and vision exemptions documented with FMCSA letter

name: Mexico Cross Border Operations
q: Use this skill when the user asks about US-Mexico cross-border CMV operations — long-haul cross-bord
body:
# Mexico Cross-Border Operations

Three distinct authority categories cover Mexico-domiciled motor carriers operating in the United States. The framework is in `49 CFR Part 365` (operating authority) and the FMCSA's Mexico Cross-Border Long-Haul rules, with NAFTA/USMCA underpinnings.

## Three authority levels for Mexico-domiciled carriers
1. **Commercial zone authority** — operates within the U.S. commercial border zone (typically 20–25 miles, varies by city). Most cross-border drayage today.
2. **Enterprise (long-haul) authority** — full U.S. interstate operation beyond the commercial zone. Issued only after USMCA dispute settlement. Subject to enhanced FMCSA monitoring and inspection.
3. **Mexico-domiciled carriers transporting hazmat or passengers** — additional restrictions; passenger long-haul has separate rules

U.S. and Canadian carriers operating into Mexico need Mexican SCT/SICT authority, separate from FMCSA.

## Pre-Authorization Safety Audit (PASA)
For Mexico-domiciled applicants seeking enterprise authority — FMCSA-conducted at carrier's place of business in Mexico before any U.S. operation:
- DQF review
- HOS and ELD records
- Maintenance program review
- Drug & alcohol testing program
- Insurance verification (US-licensed, US claims-paying)

## Operational requirements
- US insurance (US-licensed insurer) at `§ 387.9` minimums
- ELD required for crossings beyond short-haul radius
- Mexican CDL (Licencia Federal) treated as equivalent to U.S. CDL **only for the specific authority granted** — driver still subject to U.S. drug & alcohol testing and Clearinghouse if performing covered operations
- **Drug & alcohol** — Mexico-domiciled carriers must follow `Part 382` and report to the Clearinghouse for drivers operating in the U.S.
- **CMV must display USDOT number** and operating authority numbers

## Customs and border processes
- C-TPAT/FAST for trusted-trader expedited crossings
- ACE manifest filing electronically before crossing northbound
- Pedimento documentation southbound
- Live or in-bond movements

## U.S.-domiciled carriers operating into Mexico
- Mexican SCT/SICT permit
- Mexican insurance — U.S. insurance does not cover claims in Mexico
- Driver does not need a Mexican license for U.S. authority drayage near border, but extended Mexican operation requires SCT-recognized credentials

## Common pitfalls
- Mexico-domiciled carrier operating beyond commercial zone without enterprise authority
- U.S. carrier operating in Mexico on U.S. insurance only (claims won't pay)
- Missing Clearinghouse pre-employment query for Mexican drivers on U.S. authority operations
- Hours-of-service issues at the border crossing — wait time can be drive vs on-duty depending on circumstances
- Falling out of compliance with the carrier's own MCS-150 if cross-border operating status changes

## What auditors look for
FMCSA targets enterprise-authority Mexico carriers for enhanced reviews. Items include DQF completeness with Mexican-license verification, ELD records consistent with crossing data, U.S. insurance currency, Clearinghouse compliance, and PASA follow-through.

name: Mvr And Monitoring
q: Use this skill when the user asks about Motor Vehicle Records (MVRs), 49 CFR 391
body:
# MVR and Monitoring

The Motor Vehicle Record (MVR) is the state driver-licensing agency's official driving-history report. FMCSA requires carriers to obtain and review MVRs at hire and annually for every CDL driver. Governed by `§ 391.23` (initial), `§ 391.25` (annual), and `§ 391.27` (driver's own certificate of violations).

## Initial MVR (`§ 391.23(a)(1)`)
- Obtain from every state in which the driver held a license in the **preceding 3 years**
- Must be in the DQF within **30 days** of employment
- Review for disqualifying offenses and serious violations under `§ 383.51` and `§ 391.15`

## Annual MVR (`§ 391.25`)
- Once every **12 months** for each driver
- Carrier prepares a **written review** documenting whether the driver remains qualified
- The written review signed/dated by the safety official is the document auditors look for, not just the MVR
- Retain MVR + review in DQF for duration of employment + 3 years

## Driver's Certificate of Violations (`§ 391.27`)
- Driver self-reports all moving violations during the prior 12 months (other than parking) on a form signed by the driver
- Cross-checked against the MVR for discrepancies
- Kept in the DQF

## Continuous MVR monitoring (recommended but not federally required)
Services (Samba Safety, HireRight, Sterling, Foley) that auto-flag MVR changes (new violations, license suspension, downgrade) between annual reviews. Not mandated by FMCSA, but:
- Reduces window of unknown disqualification
- Speeds detection of CDL medical downgrade
- Supports insurance loss-control credits

## What to flag during review
- Major offenses (`§ 383.51(b)`) — DUI, refusal, hit-and-run, etc.
- Serious violations (`§ 383.51(c)`) — excessive speeding, reckless, texting, etc., especially second/third in 3 years
- Out-of-service orders
- License downgrade (medical, ELDT, payment of fines)
- License suspension or revocation
- Class or endorsement changes affecting current job
- CSMS/PSP inspection record discrepancies

## State naming differences
The MVR is also called the **3-year MVR, abstract, driving history, or H6** depending on state. Some states issue a separate **CDLIS MVR** showing federal CDL history; pulling both is best practice.

## Common errors
- Pulling MVR from only the current state when driver had license in another in past 3 years
- Forgetting the written annual review (just having the MVR is not enough)
- Not catching license downgrade between annual pulls — continuous monitoring closes this gap
- Driver's Certificate of Violations missing or unsigned
- Treating PSP as equivalent to MVR — they are different reports

## What auditors look for
- MVR from every state for past 3 years on file at hire
- Annual MVR + written review for each year of service
- Driver's certificate of violations annually
- DQF retention period observed
- Documented disqualification process when MVR shows a triggering event

name: Mvr Continuous Monitoring Vs Annual
q: Use this skill to evaluate whether to switch from annual MVR pulls to continuous monitoring
body:
# Continuous MVR Monitoring vs Annual Pull

Annual MVR pulls under § 391.25 satisfy regulation. Continuous monitoring goes further — surfacing violations within hours of conviction. Worth the cost? Depends on fleet size + risk profile.

## Annual MVR (regulatory minimum)
- Pull MVR within 12 months of hire/last review
- Cost: $3-25 per pull (state-dependent)
- Annual driver's certificate of violations + MVR review documents compliance

## Continuous monitoring
- Daily check against state MVR database
- Alert sent within hours of conviction posting
- Cost: $4.95-9/driver/month (SambaSafety, Foley, others)
- Annual cost: ~$60-108/driver

## When continuous monitoring pays off
- Fleets with safety incentives (driver-of-the-year, performance bonuses)
- High-CSA carrier — need violation alerts to be reactive
- Hazmat or high-risk operations
- Insurance carrier discount for continuous monitoring (some insurers offer)
- Driver shortage market — quick intervention prevents losses

## When annual is sufficient
- Smaller fleets where personal knowledge of drivers
- Strong driver-of-the-year discipline (drivers self-report)
- Low-margin operations where the monthly cost doesn't pay off

## Major continuous monitoring providers
- **SambaSafety** — largest, full state coverage, real-time alerts
- **Foley Carrier Services** — bundled MVR + DQF management
- **Driver iQ** — fleet-focused
- **HireRight DAC** — also handles employment + criminal

## How to implement
1. Get driver consent for continuous monitoring (form)
2. Subscribe to provider service
3. Provider monitors state DMV records
4. Alert workflow: SMS/email to safety director
5. Investigation + driver coaching/correction action

## Compass integration
Compass MVR module connects to SambaSafety, Foley, and Driver iQ. Alerts flow directly into the carrier's notification system. Compass can also pull annual MVRs from state portals for carriers staying on the annual model.

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 391.25**
- **FMCSA Driving Record Monitoring**

name: Mvr Conviction Reporting Driver Side
q: Use this skill to clarify when a driver must report a conviction to the carrier, and what records th
body:
# Driver-Side Conviction Reporting Requirements

Drivers have legal obligations to report convictions to their employer per § 391.27. Carriers should ensure drivers understand this.

## Annual driver's certificate of violations (§ 391.27)
- Filed annually in the DQF
- Driver certifies all CMV-related convictions in the past 12 months
- Includes federal violations + state CDL violations
- Driver signature + date
- Carrier retains for 3 years

## Mid-year conviction reporting (§ 383.31)
Drivers must notify their CDL issuing state AND their employer within:
- **30 days** of conviction for a moving violation in any state (federal or state CDL)
- Notification includes the date, jurisdiction, charge, and disposition

## What counts as a conviction
- Pleading guilty
- Pleading no contest (nolo contendere)
- Forfeiting bail/collateral
- Finding of guilt by court
- Adjustment under deferred adjudication
- Administrative finding of violation

## What does NOT count (for federal CDL reporting)
- Pending charges (not yet adjudicated)
- Civil infractions (some states classify minor traffic this way)
- Dismissed charges

## Carrier obligation
- Receive driver's mid-year notification
- Document receipt in driver's file
- Investigate impact on driver's CDL status
- Update annual driver's certificate of violations at next renewal

## State-issued notifications
States with CDL conviction reporting to FMCSA:
- All US states have agreement to report
- Reported to CDLIS within 10 days of conviction
- Available to continuous MVR monitoring services

## Compass automation
Compass tracks:
- Annual driver's certificate of violations due dates
- Mid-year notifications received from drivers
- Cross-reference with continuous MVR data (any conviction the driver hasn't self-reported is a red flag)
- Carrier reminder if driver fails to provide annual certificate

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 391.27**
- **49 CFR § 383.31**

name: Mvr Disqualifying Offenses
q: Use this skill to understand which MVR violations disqualify a driver under federal rules
body:
# MVR Disqualifying Offenses

Per § 391.15, certain offenses disqualify a person from driving a CMV in interstate commerce. These are federal — state DQ rules may be stricter.

## Federally disqualifying offenses
- **DUI/DWI**: 1-year minimum disqualification (3-year for hazmat)
- **DUI involving fatality**: lifetime disqualification (10-year minimum)
- **Felony involving CMV**: 1-year minimum
- **Two serious traffic offenses in 3 years**: 60-day disqualification
- **Three serious traffic offenses in 3 years**: 120-day disqualification
- **Leaving the scene of an accident involving a CMV**: 1-year minimum
- **Drug-related offense**: 1-year minimum (lifetime if second)

## What's a "serious traffic offense"
- Excessive speeding (15+ mph over)
- Reckless driving
- Improper lane change
- Following too closely
- Drug-related offense (any)
- Driving CMV without CDL
- Driving CMV with suspended/revoked CDL
- Causing injury or death in a CMV-related incident

## Disqualification triggers (cumulative)
- Two serious in 3 years → 60-day DQ
- Three serious in 3 years → 120-day DQ
- This is per the driver — runs across all employers

## Reinstatement
- After DQ period, driver may apply to reinstate CDL
- Some states require road test or written exam
- Driver must self-certify the disqualification ended

## What carriers must do
- Check MVR for disqualifying convictions at pre-employment
- Annual review of MVR for new convictions
- Investigate driver's prior 3-year history for cumulative offenses
- Disqualified driver cannot operate CMV during DQ period

## Compass tracking
Compass MVR module:
- Pulls historical convictions from state MVR
- Flags any disqualifying offense within DQ period
- Calculates cumulative serious-offense count
- Alerts on new convictions if continuous monitoring is enabled
- Generates required reporting documentation

## Common pitfall
Driver moves between states; convictions in former state are not automatically transferred. Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration maintains the federal record (CDLIS — Commercial Driver License Information System), which is what continuous monitoring services query.

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 391.15**
- **49 CFR § 383.51**

name: Mvr Multi State Cdl Driver
q: Use this skill when a driver holds CDLs in multiple states or has resided in multiple states
body:
# MVR for Multi-State CDL Drivers

Per § 391.23(a)(1), a carrier must inquire to every state where the driver was licensed to drive in the past 3 years. The driver's primary CDL state holds the most current record.

## Required MVR pulls
- **State of current CDL issuance** — annual review per § 391.25
- **Every state where driver was licensed in past 3 years** — pre-employment + within DQF

## Multi-state scenario
A driver who lived/worked in 3 states in past 3 years:
- Pull MVR from each state at pre-employment
- Annual review uses current state of CDL issuance
- Driver self-certification at the state level resolves which state is "current"

## States with continuous MVR monitoring services
- All US states allow individual MVR pulls
- Continuous monitoring services (SambaSafety, Foley, Driver iQ) cover all states
- Pricing varies by state (some states charge $3, others $25)

## Driver moving between states
Driver moves from TX to CA:
1. Driver surrenders TX CDL
2. Driver applies for CA CDL (typically 30-day transfer)
3. Carrier should pull both TX and CA MVRs for the transition period
4. Driver self-certifies in CA
5. After CA CDL issued, annual review uses CA MVR

## What to look for across states
- Suspensions or revocations in any state
- Reciprocal-state convictions
- Habitual offender designations in any state
- DUI/DWI history (states differ on retention periods)

## Compass automation
Compass MVR module:
- Tracks driver's CDL state(s)
- Auto-pulls MVR from primary state annually
- Alerts on state changes (via SambaSafety or carrier upload)
- Flags multi-state inconsistencies

## CFR citations

name: New Entrant Safety Audit Prep
q: Use this skill when the user asks specifically about preparing for the New Entrant Safety Audit (NES
body:
# New Entrant Safety Audit Prep

Every new motor carrier that obtains a USDOT number for interstate operation enters an **18-month new entrant monitoring period** governed by `Part 385` subpart D. During that window, FMCSA conducts a **New Entrant Safety Audit (NESA)** to verify the carrier has basic safety management controls. Failure leads to a Notice of Failure and possible revocation of new entrant registration.

## When the audit happens
- Typically scheduled within **12 months** of registration
- FMCSA or a contracted state agency conducts it
- Most are now **offsite/remote audits** using electronic document submission, though onsite is still possible
- Carrier receives advance notice with a document request list

## Documents commonly requested
1. **MCS-150** verification — accurate VMT, power units, drivers
2. **Operating authority and insurance filings** (BMC-91)
3. **DQF** for each driver — full `§ 391.51(b)` contents
4. **Drug & alcohol program** — written policy, consortium agreement, test records, supervisor training, Clearinghouse registration
5. **HOS records** — 6 months of ELD/RODS plus supporting documents
6. **Vehicle list, annual inspections** (`§ 396.17`), DVIR samples (`§ 396.11`), maintenance records (`§ 396.3`)
7. **Accident register** (`§ 390.15`)
8. **Roadside inspection reports** received
9. **CDL verifications** and MVRs

## Automatic failures (`§ 385.321(b)`)
A single instance of any of these fails the audit on the spot:
- Failing to implement a drug & alcohol program
- Using a driver without a valid CDL
- Failing to require a driver to have a current MEC
- Operating without required insurance
- Operating a vehicle declared OOS
- Using a disqualified driver
- Operating without the required USDOT number

## Other failure triggers
- Violations in 4 or more of the audit areas
- Substantial pattern of HOS violations
- Crash rate above the threshold during the new entrant period

## Preparation timeline (90 days before audit)
1. **MCS-150 update** — verify VMT, drivers, units, classification
2. **DQF audit** — every active driver, every required document
3. **D&A program audit** — written policy, consortium, supervisor training certificates, current Clearinghouse queries, test records
4. **HOS audit** — ELD enrollment for required drivers, edits annotated, supporting documents organized
5. **Maintenance audit** — annual inspection on every unit, DVIRs reviewed, maintenance records by VIN
6. **Accident register** — `§ 390.15` items captured
7. **Roadside inspection review** — DataQs challenges filed where appropriate
8. **Mock audit** — internal or outside compliance consultant runs the same document checklist

## After the audit
- **Pass** — moves to full operating authority
- **Pass with corrective action** — must submit Corrective Action Plan within timeframe specified
- **Fail** — Notice of Failure; carrier must submit CAP and may be subject to expedited revocation; new entrant registration revocation means cessation of interstate operation

name: Oilfield Operations
q: Use this skill when the user asks about CMV oilfield operations — the 24-hour restart exemption (49
body:
# Oilfield Operations

FMCSA provides a limited Hours-of-Service exception for drivers operating CMVs supporting oilfield operations, recognizing the unique waiting and standby patterns of well-site work. The provisions are in `§ 395.1(d)` and `§ 395.1(o)`, with the **24-hour restart** as the centerpiece.

## Who qualifies
Drivers operating CMVs that are **specially constructed for oil-well servicing** OR drivers transporting supplies, equipment, or materials to/from oil/gas drilling and producing wells. The exception is operation-specific, not driver-specific — a driver hauling a load to a Walmart does not qualify even if he/she is normally an oilfield driver.

## The 24-hour restart (`§ 395.1(o)`)
- Drivers may restart their 60/70-hour clock with **24 consecutive hours off duty**, instead of 34
- This is the most-used oilfield provision
- Applies only to drivers of CMVs servicing oilfield operations

## Waiting-time provision (`§ 395.1(d)`)
For a driver of a **CMV specially constructed for oil-well servicing**:
- Waiting time at a natural gas or oil well site, and time spent traveling between the carrier terminal and the well site, may be recorded as **off-duty or sleeper berth (if a sleeper is provided)** even when the driver is required to be on the well site
- Time spent away from the work site is on-duty/driving as normal
- Carrier must keep detailed records of the waiting time

## What does NOT change
- 11-hour driving limit
- 14-hour shift limit
- 30-minute break
- Other parts of `Part 395`
- Drug & alcohol testing, CDL, medical, maintenance — all standard

## Tanker, hazmat, and HMSP overlays
Many oilfield loads are placarded hazmat (crude, condensate, fracking chemicals). Carriers commonly need:
- Tanker endorsement (N) and Hazmat endorsement (H) → combined X
- HMSP (`§ 385.403`) for certain materials
- `Part 173` and `Part 177` hazmat compliance
- Cargo tank specification compliance (`§ 178` for the tank itself)

## Common pitfalls
- Using the 24-hour restart on a trip that did not service an oilfield
- Treating well-site standby as off-duty when the driver is NOT operating a vehicle specially constructed for oil-well servicing — the relaxed waiting-time rule is narrower than many assume
- Forgetting that the 11/14 rules still apply during well-site work — the off-duty waiting time does not extend the 14-hour drive window
- Hazmat training (`§ 172.704`) lapse on tank truck drivers

## What auditors look for
- Verification that the operation actually qualifies as oilfield servicing
- ELD edits/annotations supporting the 24-hour restart and waiting-time entries
- HMSP currency where required
- Cargo tank inspection and pressure-test records

name: Operating Authority And Registration
q: Use this skill when the user asks about getting/maintaining motor carrier operating authority — USDO
body:
# Operating Authority and Registration

Operating authority is the FMCSA grant of permission to operate as a **for-hire** motor carrier in interstate commerce. Private carriers (hauling their own goods) need a USDOT number but not operating authority. Property authority comes through the Unified Registration System (URS) under `Part 365`, with insurance and process-agent filings under `Parts 387` and `366`.

## Numbers and what they mean
- **USDOT number** — issued to every interstate carrier (and many intrastate); the FMCSA identification number
- **MC number** — Motor Carrier authority number for for-hire interstate property and passenger carriers
- **MX number** — Mexico-domiciled carriers
- **FF number** — Freight forwarder authority
- **BR number** — Broker authority

Most trucking companies need **USDOT + MC** if they haul for hire interstate.

## URS application steps
1. **Apply at URS** (urs.fmcsa.dot.gov) — Form OP-1 for property authority, MCS-150 for safety info
2. **Pay the $300 application fee** (per authority type)
3. **Designate process agents** — BOC-3 filed by a national process agent service for all 50 states + DC (`§ 366.4`)
4. **File insurance** — BMC-91 or BMC-91X for liability; BMC-34 (some HHG); BMC-32 (passenger)
5. **Insurance minimums** (`§ 387.9`): $750,000 general freight; $1,000,000 oil; $5,000,000 hazardous; passenger varies by capacity
6. **Publication and wait period** — 21-day protest period; if no protest, authority is **granted**
7. **Authority becomes active** approximately 21–45 days after complete filing

## Required after grant
- **MCS-150 biennial update** (`§ 390.19`) — every 24 months based on last two digits of USDOT
- **Unified Carrier Registration (UCR)** — annual fee, based on fleet size; managed at ucr.gov
- **State authority** if running intrastate or with state-specific permits
- **IRP (apportioned plate)** if running interstate qualified vehicle
- **IFTA license** if running interstate qualified vehicle
- **State permits** as needed (oversize, hazmat, agricultural)

## Common registration pitfalls
- Confusing USDOT with MC — they are different and most for-hire carriers need both
- Letting insurance lapse — FMCSA receives notice from insurer; authority is revoked after 30 days unless replacement filed
- Missing the MCS-150 biennial update — risks deactivation
- Operating before authority is officially granted (the 21-day wait is the rule)
- BOC-3 process agent service expires without renewal

## Maintenance and renewal
- **MCS-150**: biennial
- **UCR**: annual
- **BMC-91**: continuous as long as insurance is filed
- **BOC-3**: tied to your process agent service; verify annually
- **IRP plate**: annual renewal in base state
- **IFTA license**: annual renewal in base state

## What auditors look for
- USDOT and MC active and accurate
- BMC-91 on file with correct limits for commodity
- MCS-150 current and accurate (VMT, units, drivers)
- UCR paid for current year
- BOC-3 active

name: Operational Kpis And Dashboards
q: Use when a carrier asks which KPIs to track, how to build a fleet dashboard, what targets to set, ca
body:
# Operational KPIs and Dashboards

A carrier dashboard turns the raw data the FMCSA already requires you to keep (DQF, ELD, maintenance, accident register) plus your TMS/accounting data into the metrics that drive decisions. FMCSA does not mandate KPIs, but its SMS BASIC categories shape the safety side of the dashboard.

## Safety KPIs
- **DOT-recordable crash rate** per million miles (industry benchmark roughly 0.6–1.0)
- **Preventable crash rate** (carrier determination)
- **Roadside inspection violations per inspection**
- **Out-of-service rate** — vehicle and driver, vs national averages (5.4% vehicle, 3.5% driver in recent FMCSA data)
- **CSA BASIC percentile rank** (Unsafe Driving, Crash Indicator, HOS Compliance, Vehicle Maintenance, Controlled Substances, HM, Driver Fitness)
- **HOS violations** — form & manner, driving without certifying, no record
- **Camera/telematics events** per 1,000 miles
- **DQF and MEC expiration counts** — overdue annual review, expiring MEC, overdue MVR

## Operational KPIs
- **Revenue per truck per week** and **revenue per total mile**
- **Loaded ratio** (loaded miles / total miles), target 88–92%
- **Deadhead %**
- **Utilization** (loaded hours / available hours)
- **On-time pickup and delivery %**
- **Detention hours per pickup and per delivery**
- **Out-of-service days per truck per year** (target single digits)
- **MPG by truck and driver**
- **Cost per mile** all-in, plus components (fuel, maintenance, payroll, insurance)

## Financial KPIs
- **Operating ratio** = operating expenses / operating revenue (target 90–95% for healthy small carriers)
- **DSO** (days sales outstanding) — target ≤ 40 days; factoring resets this to 0–1 day at a cost
- **Cash burn / runway** for any month
- **Insurance loss ratio**

## People KPIs
- **Driver turnover** annualized (industry average for OTR is high, 70–90%)
- **Average tenure**
- **Recruiting cost per hire**
- **Training completion %**

## Dashboard structure
1. **Daily** — fleet board, available drivers, available trucks, unplanned OOS, overdue DVIRs, HOS at-risk drivers
2. **Weekly** — revenue, miles, loaded ratio, MPG, safety events, DQF/MEC expirations next 30 days
3. **Monthly** — full P&L, OR, KPI scorecard vs target, CSA percentile movement
4. **Quarterly** — IFTA, IRP, insurance review, strategic review

## Sources
- ELD/telematics: HOS, miles, events, MPG
- TMS: revenue, loaded ratio, detention, on-time
- Camera: behavior events
- Maintenance system: DVIR defects, OOS days, PM compliance
- Accounting: P&L, OR, cash, DSO
- FMCSA Portal / SMS: BASIC percentiles, A&I reports

## Pitfalls
- Tracking 50 metrics — pick the 8–12 that actually drive decisions and review the rest quarterly
- Vanity metrics (gross revenue without OR)
- Lagging only — pair lagging outcomes with leading behaviors
- Targets without thresholds — define green/yellow/red

name: Oversize Overweight Permits
q: Use this skill when the user asks about oversize / overweight load permits — state-by-state permitti
body:
# Oversize/Overweight Permits

Federal weight on the Interstate Highway System is capped at **80,000 lb gross** with axle limits per the Federal Bridge Formula. Anything heavier or with dimensions beyond federal/state limits requires a permit from each state the load will travel through. Permits are state-issued and state-specific.

## Federal baseline (Interstate)
- **Gross**: 80,000 lb
- **Single axle**: 20,000 lb
- **Tandem axle**: 34,000 lb
- **Federal Bridge Formula** governs axle group weights
- Width: typically **8 ft 6 in**
- Height: typically **13 ft 6 in** (eastern US) or **14 ft** (western US) — state-specific
- Length: trailer 53 ft typical, with state variation; double/triple combinations restricted by state

## What requires a permit
- Any dimension or weight beyond the state's legal limit
- Loads that are **non-divisible** (cannot be broken down without compromising the load) typically qualify for permitting; divisible loads usually do not
- Routing may be restricted to specific roads, daylight hours, and weekday-only travel

## Permit types
1. **Single trip** — one origin to one destination, dated
2. **Annual** — for repeated movements within set dimension/weight limits
3. **Superload** — extreme dimensions/weight requiring engineering review and bridge analysis
4. **Continuous travel** — by-the-mile or by-the-route for ongoing project

## Typical state requirements
- Carrier USDOT and MC
- Insurance proof (often higher than federal minimums for heavy loads)
- Detailed dimensions and weight by axle
- Route plan submitted in advance
- Escort/pilot car requirements (state-specific by dimension)
- Bridge clearance verification
- Time-of-day and day-of-week restrictions
- Holiday no-move dates

## Pilot/escort cars
Rules vary by state, but common triggers:
- **Width > 12 ft** — front escort
- **Width > 14–15 ft** — front and rear escort
- **Length > 100 ft** — escorts required
- **Height > 14 ft 6 in** — pole car for height check
- Some states require certified escort drivers (training and credential)

## Securement and equipment
- Trailer must be rated for the load (lowboys, RGNs, multi-axle trailers)
- Standard `§ 393.100` securement rules apply
- Oversize signage and flags per state spec
- Lights for nighttime moves where permitted

## Common pitfalls
- Buying a single-trip permit for one state and being out of compliance the moment the truck crosses the next state line
- Missing the route restriction — running a permitted load on a non-permitted road voids the permit
- Holiday no-move dates ignored
- Pilot car shortage on day of move
- Bridge formula math wrong — gross may be legal but an axle group illegal
- Weather restrictions ignored (some states prohibit moves above certain wind speeds)

## What auditors look for
FMCSA does not directly audit state permits, but state DOT/DMV roadside enforcement does. Violations include fines, OOS, and can drive insurance and bonding consequences.

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- `49 CFR § 393.100` (securement standards apply)
- `23 CFR § 658` (federal weight and dimensions on Interstate)
- State permitting regulations (state-specific)

name: Owner Operator Tax And Deductions
q: Use when an owner-operator (1099 or LLC/S-corp) asks how to lower their tax bill, what they can dedu
body:
# Owner-Operator Tax and Deductions

Tax treatment for an owner-operator depends on the legal structure (sole prop, single-member LLC, multi-member LLC, S-corp, C-corp). FMCSA does not regulate tax — IRS and state revenue departments do — but the recordkeeping required by `Part 396` (maintenance), `§ 395.11` (HOS supporting docs), and the IFTA mileage/fuel logs already covers most of what you need.

## Entity structures
- **Sole proprietor / single-member LLC** — Schedule C, self-employment tax (15.3%) on net profit
- **S-corp** — reasonable salary subject to payroll taxes, remainder as distribution (no SE tax). Requires W-2 wages to the owner-driver
- **Multi-member LLC** — partnership return (Form 1065), K-1 to each member
- **C-corp** — separate entity tax, double taxation on dividends; rarely used by single owner-operators

Most single-truck operators stay sole-prop or single-member LLC until net profit consistently exceeds **$70,000–$90,000**, at which point S-corp typically becomes worth the added complexity.

## Common deductions
1. **Truck and trailer depreciation** — Section 179 immediate expensing for qualifying equipment up to annual limits; bonus depreciation phasing down (80% in 2023, 60% in 2024, 40% in 2025, 20% in 2026)
2. **Truck loan interest** (the principal is recovered through depreciation, not deduction)
3. **Fuel** (less the part covered by FSC if you're billing it separately on your books)
4. **Maintenance and repairs**
5. **Tires**
6. **Insurance** — liability, cargo, occ-acc, physical damage
7. **Permits, licenses, IFTA, IRP, UCR, BOC-3**
8. **Tolls, parking, scale fees**
9. **Cell phone** (business use portion)
10. **ELD and software subscriptions** (TMS, accounting, route tools)
11. **Per diem meal allowance** — IRS Special Transportation Industry rate (verify current year rate; **80% deductible** for transportation workers under DOT HOS, vs 50% for other industries)
12. **Home-office** — limited; usually small for owner-operators
13. **Health insurance** premiums (self-employed health insurance deduction)
14. **SEP-IRA / Solo 401(k) contributions**

## Records to keep (3+ years; 7 years preferred)
- Profit & Loss
- Bank and credit card statements
- Fuel receipts and IFTA returns
- Maintenance invoices
- Truck purchase, finance, lease documents
- 1099-NEC received
- IRS Form 2290 (Heavy Highway Vehicle Use Tax)

## Federal taxes specific to trucking
- **Form 2290 (Heavy Highway Vehicle Use Tax)** — for vehicles 55,000 lb GVW or more, $100 + $22/1,000 lb over 55,000 (max ~$550); due **August 31** for prior tax year (July–June)
- **Federal Excise Tax** — 12% on first-purchase of new heavy trucks
- **Quarterly estimated tax payments** — April 15, June 15, September 15, January 15

## State tax
- State income tax in residence state
- IFTA quarterly fuel tax (compliance, not income)
- IRP apportioned plate fees
- State unemployment if you have employees

## Pitfalls
- Mixing personal and business expenses on one card or account
- Missing the **per diem 80% rate** specific to DOT-regulated transportation workers
- Late Form 2290
- Underpayment of estimated tax
- S-corp without a reasonable salary (IRS audit target)
- Personal-use mileage on a company-titled truck

## What auditors look for
IRS audit triggers for owner-operators: high deductions relative to revenue, unreasonably low S-corp salary, missing 1099s reported, large per diem without supporting trip logs.

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- This topic is IRS-governed; FMCSA rules referenced for supporting records: `49 CFR § 396.3`, `§ 395.11`
- IRS Publication 463 (Travel)
- IRS Form 2290 (Heavy Vehicle Use Tax)

name: Owner Operator Vs Company Driver Economics
q: Use this skill when the user asks about the financial differences between being an owner-operator vs
body:
# Owner-Operator vs Company Driver Economics

The decision between operating as an **owner-operator** (independent contractor with own authority or leased to a carrier) and a **company driver** (W-2 employee of a carrier) is primarily financial, but FMCSA rules at `Part 376` (leasing) and the IRS/DOL classification standards shape the trade-offs.

## Company driver (W-2)
- Paid hourly, salary, mileage, or percentage; W-2 employment
- Employer covers truck, insurance, fuel, maintenance, permits, tolls
- Employer handles HOS compliance, ELD, IFTA, IRP, MCS-150
- Eligible for workers' comp, unemployment, group health, 401(k)
- Predictable take-home, no equipment risk
- Typical OTR pay: **$0.50–$0.80/mile** plus accessorials; experienced drivers $80,000–$110,000/yr

## Owner-operator with own authority
- Has own USDOT, MC, insurance, BMC-91
- Hauls direct for shippers or through brokers
- Full revenue, full cost, full risk
- Self-employment tax + income tax
- No employer benefits
- Gross revenue often $200,000–$300,000/year for one truck OTR; net after all costs **typically $60,000–$120,000** depending on lanes, MPG, freight market

## Owner-operator leased to a carrier (`Part 376`)
- Operates under carrier's authority
- Carrier handles authority, insurance (some types), broker relationships
- Owner-operator provides truck and (often) trailer
- Paid by **percentage of revenue (typically 65–75%)** or by mileage (typically $1.20–$1.50/mile)
- Pays own fuel (sometimes via carrier fuel-card discount)
- Lease must comply with `§ 376.12` requirements
- Must receive copies of rated freight bill or documents showing percentage basis

## Cost comparison (typical single-truck OTR, illustrative)
- Truck payment: $1,800–$2,800/month
- Insurance (with own authority): $850–$1,500/month
- Fuel (110,000 mi @ 7 MPG @ $4.00/gal): ~$5,200/month
- Maintenance and tires: $800–$1,500/month
- Permits, IFTA, IRP, UCR: $200/month average
- ELD, TMS, accounting: $150–$300/month
- Total fixed + variable typically $9,000–$12,000/month
- Revenue 110,000 mi × $2.20/mi = ~$20,000/month; net ~$8,000–$11,000

## Misclassification risk
The DOL's economic-realities test and IRS factors (behavioral control, financial control, relationship type) determine whether a "contractor" is really an employee. Misclassified owner-operators trigger back wages, payroll taxes, penalties, and may invalidate the carrier's authority structure. `Part 376` leasing alone does not establish independent-contractor status.

## When owner-operator makes sense
- Disciplined operator who manages cost and books carefully
- Direct shipper relationships or premium freight
- Paid-off or low-payment truck
- Stable lane and rate base
- Comfortable with variable income and self-employment overhead

## When company driver makes sense
- Predictable income preference
- No interest in owning equipment
- Need group health, workers' comp, unemployment
- Less tolerance for the administrative load

## Pitfalls
- Owner-operator without a fuel-price hedge or surcharge structure — diesel volatility wipes out margin
- Lease-purchase programs that look like ownership but actually transfer all risk to the driver without real equity
- Treating gross revenue as income — net after costs is the comparable number
- Misclassification challenges (AB-5 in California, federal DOL rulemaking)

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- `49 CFR Part 376` (leasing of equipment)
- `49 CFR § 387.7` (financial responsibility — applies to authority holder)
- IRS Publication 1779 (Independent Contractor or Employee)

name: Passenger Carrier Specifics
q: Use this skill when the user asks about passenger-carrying CMVs — buses, motorcoaches, charter opera
body:
# Passenger Carrier Specifics

Motor carriers transporting passengers — buses, motorcoaches, charter and tour, intercity scheduled, transit — operate under FMCSRs with passenger-specific overlays. Key differences from property carriage live in `§ 395.5` (HOS), `§ 393.92` (buses), and `Part 374` (passenger transportation rules).

## Who is a passenger carrier under FMCSA
- Vehicle designed or used to transport **9 or more passengers (including driver) for compensation**, OR
- Vehicle designed or used to transport **16 or more passengers (including driver) not for compensation**
- Operating in interstate commerce → triggers FMCSA jurisdiction

Smaller-passenger operations (limos under 9, etc.) may still be subject to FMCSA if commercial and crossing state lines; verify against `§ 390.5` CMV definition.

## Authority
- USDOT number
- MC number with **passenger authority** (different filing from property)
- BMC-32 (passenger insurance form) instead of BMC-91
- Insurance minimums under `§ 387.33`:
  - 16+ passenger seating capacity: **$5,000,000**
  - 15 or fewer passengers: **$1,500,000**
- BOC-3 process agents

## Hours of Service (`§ 395.5`)
Differs from property:
- **10-hour driving** within 15-hour shift
- **15-hour on-duty** (off-duty inside the shift can extend the window — different from the 14-hour property rule)
- **8 consecutive hours off duty** to reset
- 60/70-hour rule same as property
- Different sleeper-berth split provisions for passenger

## Equipment (`§ 393.92`)
- Standees not permitted forward of standee line
- Aisle clearance
- Emergency exits and markings
- Pushout windows, roof escape hatches per standards
- Fire extinguisher, warning devices same general rule as property CMV under `§ 393.95`
- Seat belts for driver and (for newer buses) passengers under federal standards

## CDL
Drivers need CDL with **Passenger (P) endorsement** and, if school bus, **School Bus (S) endorsement**, under `Part 383`. Skills/knowledge test and TSA-style check for some endorsements; all medical and DQF rules apply.

## Drug & alcohol testing
`Part 382` fully applies to CDL passenger drivers in safety-sensitive function (driving a CMV). Pre-employment, random, post-accident, reasonable suspicion, return-to-duty, follow-up. Clearinghouse queries required.

## Maintenance and inspection
- Annual inspection under `§ 396.17`
- Pre-trip and post-trip DVIR (`§ 396.11`)
- Charter and motorcoach industry typically uses enhanced pre-trip standards

## Passenger-carrying tariff and operating rules
- Charter passenger carriers may need to file tariff/operating regulations with state PUC depending on state
- HHG, household goods — different category, not passenger

## Common pitfalls
- Mistaking HOS — many drivers know the property 11/14 rule and apply it to passenger ops
- Insurance below the `§ 387.33` minimum for the seating capacity
- Forgetting the P (and S, if school bus) endorsement
- Random testing rates — same as property in current year (verify FMCSA annual rate notice)
- Missing the school bus operating rules under state DOE in addition to FMCSA

## What auditors look for
- DQF complete for every driver with P endorsement
- HOS compliance under `§ 395.5`
- Annual inspection on every bus
- Insurance per `§ 387.33`
- D&A testing program with Clearinghouse

Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- `49 CFR Part 374`
- `49 CFR § 387.33`
- `49 CFR § 391.41`
- `49 CFR § 393.92`
- `49 CFR § 395.5`
- `49 CFR Part 382`

name: Post Crash Driver Care And Return To Work
q: Use when a driver has been involved in a crash — regardless of preventability or injury — and the ca
body:
# Post-Crash Driver Care and Return-to-Work

A crash sequence triggers FMCSA-mandated steps (`§ 382.303` post-accident testing, `§ 390.15` accident register, `Part 391` requalification) and a parallel workers' comp/HR track. Coordinating both keeps the driver supported and the carrier compliant.

## Immediate scene (driver and carrier)
1. Driver ensures safety, calls 911, secures the scene
2. Driver contacts dispatch and reports to safety per carrier policy
3. Carrier dispatches accident response if available (DriverFacts, USFleetTracking, internal team)
4. Driver does NOT discuss fault or sign statements except to law enforcement
5. Driver gathers required information per `§ 392.6` and carrier policy

## Post-accident testing (`§ 382.303`)
Required when:
- **Human fatality** — drug + alcohol test for **all surviving drivers** of CMVs involved, regardless of citation
- **Injury treated immediately away from scene + driver receives citation** — test required
- **Disabling tow-away + driver receives citation** — test required

Timeframes:
- **Alcohol test within 8 hours** of crash
- **Drug test within 32 hours** of crash
- Document inability to test in writing

## Accident register and recordkeeping
- `§ 390.15` entry within reasonable time
- 1-year active + 2 additional years archive (3 years total)
- Police report, photos, statements, telematics/camera data, ELD pull
- Preservation letter to driver and carrier (litigation hold)

## Workers' comp track
- File the workers' comp claim per state requirement (typically within 1–7 days)
- Provide driver with treating physician network info
- Document medical authorizations and HIPAA releases
- Track medical-only vs lost-time status
- Coordinate with EAP if available

## Driver care steps
1. **Same day**: in-person or phone contact with driver after release from scene; ensure transportation home/lodging; basic emotional check-in
2. **24–72 hours**: confirm medical follow-up; offer EAP/mental health referral; debrief
3. **Week 1**: stand-down from driving until cleared; light duty or paid time off depending on policy and state law
4. **Ongoing**: regular check-ins until cleared for return to safety-sensitive duty

## Return-to-duty (RTD) sequence
If the post-accident test is positive or driver is medically removed:
- **SAP evaluation and treatment** (`§ 40.281`)
- **Return-to-duty test** (negative required) — `§ 40.305`
- **Follow-up testing plan** — minimum 6 tests in 12 months, can extend to 5 years (`§ 40.307`)
- **Clearinghouse reporting** of completion (`§ 382.705`)
- DQF updates: any new medical certificate, MVR pull, statement of compliance

If the driver was not tested positive but was injured:
- Treating-physician release to full duty
- New DOT physical if MEC expired or condition changed
- Possibly skills assessment if extended absence
- Documented return-to-duty meeting and re-orientation

## Preventability determination
Carrier's internal determination of preventable vs non-preventable, separate from law enforcement fault. FMCSA's Crash Preventability Determination Program lets carriers request review of certain crash types in `§ 385.305` context.

## Pitfalls
- Missing the 8-hour alcohol / 32-hour drug test window
- Treating post-accident testing as discretionary — it is mandatory when criteria are met
- Putting driver back to safety-sensitive duty without negative RTD test after a positive
- Failing to coordinate carrier safety with workers' comp adjuster
- Skipping driver emotional/mental health follow-up — leading cause of post-crash attrition

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- `49 CFR § 382.303`
- `49 CFR § 382.503`
- `49 CFR § 382.705`
- `49 CFR § 390.15`
- `49 CFR § 391.45`
- `49 CFR § 392.6`
- `49 CFR Part 40`

name: Preventive Maintenance Program Design
q: Use this skill when the user asks how to design or improve a Preventive Maintenance (PM) program for
body:
# Preventive Maintenance Program Design

`§ 396.3` requires every motor carrier to systematically inspect, repair, and maintain (or cause to be maintained) all motor vehicles subject to its control. The annual inspection under `§ 396.17` and DVIR under `§ 396.11` are floor-level requirements; a real PM program goes beyond.

## Program elements
1. **Vehicle list** by VIN, year, make, model, GVWR, current mileage, in-service date
2. **PM schedule** per OEM recommendations and operating conditions:
   - **A-service** (routine, every 15k–25k miles): chassis lube, oil/filter, visual brake check, tire rotation
   - **B-service** (every 50k miles or so): A items + fuel filter, air dryer cartridge, brake adjustment, alignment check
   - **C-service** (every 100k–150k miles): B items + transmission fluid, differential, brake hardware, kingpins/U-joints, full brake reline check
   - **D-service** (250k+ miles or major component): full powertrain inspection, aftertreatment (DPF clean, sensor swap), suspension overhaul
3. **Annual inspection** (`§ 396.17`) — by qualified inspector (`§ 396.19`), documented with the FMCSA-prescribed annual inspection report
4. **DVIR review and repair** — driver post-trip DVIR review, defect repair, certification before next dispatch
5. **Roadside inspection follow-up** — every Level I-III inspection reviewed; OOS items corrected and re-certified; DataQs filed when appropriate
6. **PM records** (`§ 396.3`) — kept for life of vehicle plus 6 months after disposition (current rule: maintenance records 1 year while in service plus 6 months after)

## Records to keep (`§ 396.3`)
- Identification of vehicle (make, model, year, VIN, company unit number, tire size)
- Schedule of inspections, lubrications, repairs
- Records of inspections, repairs, maintenance showing date and nature of service
- Records of tests on push-out windows, emergency doors, marking lights (where applicable to buses)

## Annual inspection (`§ 396.17` and Appendix G)
- Performed by a qualified inspector meeting `§ 396.19` standards
- Documented on FMCSA-prescribed report
- Sticker or decal on the vehicle with month, year, carrier, and inspector
- Retained for 14 months
- Must cover all items in Appendix G: brakes, coupling, exhaust, fuel system, lighting, safe loading, steering, suspension, frame, tires, wheels, windshield wipers, emergency equipment

## Brake and tire programs
- Brake adjustment check at A-service
- Brake reline thresholds per OEM and operating duty
- Tire wear/inflation per `§ 393.75` (minimum tread 4/32 steer, 2/32 other)
- Air pressure monitoring (manual weekly or auto inflation)

## Aftertreatment
- DPF regen monitoring (active and parked regen tracking)
- DEF level monitoring
- DOC/SCR sensor monitoring
- Forced regen and DPF cleaning at OEM intervals (typically 200k–400k miles)

## Outsourced vs in-house
- **In-house** — best for 20+ trucks with predictable maintenance volume; control of quality, faster turnaround
- **OEM dealer** — best for warranty work and complex aftertreatment
- **National network** (Speedco, Love's, TA-Petro) — best for on-road PM and tires
- **Mobile vendor** — best for fleet that runs hub-and-spoke and PM can happen overnight at yard

## Pitfalls
- DVIR with "defect noted" but no corresponding repair record
- Annual inspection performed by an unqualified inspector
- Brake reline pushed past safety margin to save short-term cost
- Aftertreatment ignored — DPF replacement at $5k–$10k cheaper than failure on the road
- PM schedule based on calendar without checking mileage — short cycles or long cycles depending on duty

## What auditors look for
- `§ 396.3` recordkeeping consistency
- Annual inspection currency on every unit
- DVIR defects repaired and re-certified
- Roadside OOS items repaired
- Maintenance records retained per timing rule

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- `49 CFR § 396.3`
- `49 CFR § 396.11`
- `49 CFR § 396.17`
- `49 CFR § 396.19`
- `49 CFR § 396.21`
- `49 CFR Part 393`

name: Pricing And Rate Negotiation
q: Use this skill when the user asks about trucking rate negotiation — cost-plus pricing, market rate b
body:
# Pricing and Rate Negotiation

FMCSA does not regulate freight rates (deregulated under the Motor Carrier Act of 1980), but rate decisions drive whether the carrier can fund the compliance program required under `Part 385` and the rest of the FMCSRs. Rate-making is also constrained by financial responsibility filings (`§ 387.7`) and by contract law.

## Cost-plus pricing baseline
Know your **total cost per mile (CPM)** before quoting:
- Variable: fuel, tires, maintenance, driver pay (if mileage), tolls, IFTA
- Fixed: truck payment, insurance, permits, base salaries, overhead
- All-in CPM = (variable + fixed) ÷ total miles
- **Breakeven rate per loaded mile** = total CPM ÷ loaded ratio (e.g., 92%)
- Add **target margin** (10–20% for healthy operating ratio)

## Market rate benchmarks
- **DAT RateView** — historical and current spot rates by lane
- **Truckstop.com** — load board with rate data
- **Greenscreens.ai, Sonar** — predictive rate intelligence
- **NMFC** for LTL freight class
- **Customer's historical paid rates** — track every load by lane

## Spot vs contract
- **Spot** — load-by-load, brokered, exposed to weekly volatility; higher rate but no commitment
- **Contract / dedicated** — 6 to 18 month commitment with shipper, lower rate but steady volume, often with MCQ (minimum committed quantity)
- **Mixed book** — most healthy small carriers run 60–80% contract, 20–40% spot

## Accessorials to bill
- **Detention** — typically free first 2 hours, then $50–$75/hr after
- **Layover** — $250–$400 per night when a driver is held over
- **Driver assist / lumper** — pass-through plus markup
- **TONU (truck order not used)** — $150–$250 when load cancels after dispatch
- **Multiple stops** — $50–$100 per extra stop
- **Reconsign / re-route** — $150–$300
- **Permits / oversize escort** — at cost plus markup
- **Tarp / strap charges** — flatbed
- **Fuel surcharge** — indexed to EIA weekly retail diesel; $0.05 per $0.05 over baseline is common

## Negotiation tactics
1. **Open with the lane data** — what other carriers are billing on the lane this quarter
2. **Anchor with the cost** — what the lane costs you, not what you wish it paid
3. **Pair head-haul and back-haul** as a round-trip rate to monetize the empty leg
4. **Bundle volume** — multi-week or multi-month commitment in exchange for a $0.10–$0.20 rate increase
5. **Get accessorials in writing in the rate confirmation**
6. **Avoid "all-in" rates** unless you have priced the detention and FSC explicitly
7. **Walk away** from below-breakeven lanes — taking unprofitable freight to keep a truck moving is a slow bleed

## Contract terms
- **Rates** with effective and expiration dates
- **Fuel surcharge index** explicitly defined
- **Accessorial schedule** as exhibit
- **Payment terms** (Net 30 standard; factor adjusts effective)
- **Limitation of liability** for cargo (Carmack Amendment is the default; contract may modify)
- **Insurance requirements** matching your filed coverage
- **Indemnification** scoped narrowly
- **Lien rights** under `§ 49 USC 13707`
- **Termination** for convenience and for cause

## Pitfalls
- Pricing on revenue per loaded mile without accounting for deadhead
- Accepting customer's rate confirmation that strips your accessorials
- Not adjusting rates when fuel moves 30+ cents
- Letting customer dictate "all-in" rate with no FSC pass-through
- Signing a contract with detention provisions that don't track real-world cycle time

name: Records Active Driver Retention
q: Use this skill to understand record retention requirements for currently-employed drivers
body:
# Active Driver Record Retention

Different record types have different retention periods. Federal rules are minimums; state law may extend.

## Driver Qualification File
- **Retention**: duration of employment + 3 years after termination
- **What's in DQF**: 12 specific documents per § 391.51

## Hours of Service Records (RODS)
- **Retention**: 6 months from the date of the record
- **Format**: paper or ELD-generated
- **Per § 395.8(k)**

## Vehicle Maintenance + Inspection Records
- **Retention**: 1 year + 6 months after vehicle leaves the carrier's control
- **What's covered**: annual inspections, maintenance logs, DVIRs
- **Per § 396.3(c)**

## Drug & Alcohol Records
- **Negative test results**: 1 year
- **Positive test results, refusals**: 5 years
- **Random selection records**: 2 years
- **Annual MIS reports**: 5 years
- **Per § 382.401**

## Accident Register
- **Retention**: 1 year + 3 years archive (4 years total)
- **What's recorded**: DOT-recordable crashes only
- **Per § 390.15**

## Driver Investigation History (§ 391.23)
- **Retention**: 3 years
- **What's recorded**: prior employer responses, attempts, MVRs

## Other records
- Operating authority documents (MC/DOT): permanent
- Insurance (BMC-91): until replaced
- Process agents (BOC-3): until replaced
- Tax records: 7 years (IRS)
- Payroll records: 7 years (DOL)

## What to keep beyond minimum
- Vehicle maintenance for longer than 1+6 months (insurance, sales)
- Accident records (claim history, subrogation)
- Performance reviews + safety records (HR retention)

name: Records Electronic Records Acceptance
q: Use this skill to understand when electronic records are acceptable to FMCSA inspectors
body:
# Electronic Records Acceptance by FMCSA

FMCSA accepts electronic records under most circumstances. Specific format requirements per § 390.30.

## Acceptable electronic formats
- PDF (most common)
- Original digital format (Word, Excel, etc.)
- Image scans (TIFF, JPG, PNG)
- Database extracts
- ELD-generated (specific format per § 395.20)

## Required characteristics
- **Legible**: clearly readable
- **Searchable**: organized so inspectors can find specific records
- **Available**: producible within reasonable time
- **Complete**: no missing pages or partial documents
- **Unaltered**: same content as the original

## ELD-specific requirements
- ELD records in the eRODS XML format per § 395.20
- Driver edit history retained
- Original entry retained
- Annotation reasons retained

## When paper is required (or preferred)
- Some inspectors prefer paper
- Some state DMVs request paper
- Driver's medical card original may be required
- Annual physical exam reports often paper-based

## Electronic record systems
- **Cloud-based**: SaaS document management (Compass, Foley, JJ Keller, etc.)
- **On-premise**: local server-based document management
- **Hybrid**: cloud + local backup

## Backup + redundancy
- Maintain backups (recommended weekly)
- Test restore procedures
- Have offline copies of critical documents
- Cloud-based systems typically include backup

## Access during audit
- Compass + similar systems: web interface, instant search
- File-share systems: organized folder structure
- Email + email attachments: searchable but slow

## What auditors don't like
- Disorganized file systems (folders without naming convention)
- Scanned documents missing pages
- Records that can't be produced quickly
- Records in non-standard formats

## Compass records module
- Per-record indexing
- Search across all records
- Audit-quality production from one screen
- Standardized formatting

body:
# Terminated Driver Record Retention Schedule

When a driver terminates, retention periods become explicit. Failing to maintain proper retention = potential audit + legal exposure.

## DQF for terminated drivers
- **Active employment + 3 years after termination**
- After 3 years post-termination: can be destroyed
- Some carriers retain longer for liability purposes
- Backup copies (electronic) may extend retention practically

## D&A records (terminated drivers)
- **5 years for positive/refusal records**
- **1 year for negative records**
- Annual MIS records: 5 years
- Driver D&A history follows them through Clearinghouse anyway

## Vehicle records
- Driver's specific vehicle assignments + ELD records: per HOS retention (6 months)
- Vehicle maintenance: per vehicle retention (1 + 6 months)

## Other records
- Personnel file: per HR retention (typically 3-7 years)
- Payroll: 7 years (DOL)
- Workers comp: per state law

## Liability considerations
- Carrier may want longer retention than federal minimum for:
  - Pending litigation (insurance claims, accidents)
  - Subrogation actions
  - Driver-related complaints
  - Future hiring inquiries

## How long to keep beyond minimum
- 5-7 years typical for terminated driver records
- Some carriers go 10 years
- Driver who left badly (firing, accident) may warrant longer

## What to destroy
- Personal information beyond what's required
- Documents superseded by newer versions
- Documents past retention period (with audit trail)

## What to retain forever
- DOT-recordable accident records (life-of-carrier interest)
- Hazmat shipment records (security concerns)
- Settlements + legal documents (life of legal interest)

name: Recruiting And Driver Acquisition
q: Use this skill when the user asks how to recruit CDL drivers — sourcing channels (CDL schools, job b
body:
# Recruiting and Driver Acquisition

Driver recruiting is not regulated by FMCSA, but the qualification standards in `Part 391`, the Clearinghouse query rules in `§ 382.701`, and the FCRA background-check overlay shape every part of the process.

## Sourcing channels
1. **CDL schools and ELDT training providers** (`Part 380`) — partnerships for new-CDL hires; sometimes tuition reimbursement programs
2. **Driver job boards** — Indeed, ZipRecruiter, Driver.com, TruckersReport, AllTruckJobs, Trucker Path
3. **Social media** — Facebook driver groups, TikTok, YouTube (recruiting content)
4. **Referral programs** — current drivers, $1,000–$3,000 per successful hire with retention vesting
5. **Owner-operator lease-on** — direct sourcing from O/O community, freight commitments as recruiting tool
6. **Veterans** — Veteran Hiring Initiative, Hiring Our Heroes, GI Bill ELDT funding
7. **Apprenticeship programs** — Safe Driver Apprenticeship Pilot Program (for 18–20 year-olds in interstate) — limited slots, federal pilot

## Compensation structures
- **Cents per mile (CPM)** — most common OTR; $0.50–$0.80/mile for experienced drivers, accessorials extra
- **Hourly** — local and regional; $22–$32/hr in most markets, OT after 40
- **Salary** — dedicated routes
- **Percentage of revenue** — typically owner-operator lease-on (65–75%)
- **Hybrid** — base + per-mile or base + safety bonus
- **Per diem** — partition of pay paid as per diem (with substantiated travel) — 80% deductible to driver, payroll-tax-free; reduces W-2 wages and 401(k) base

## Sign-on and retention
- **Sign-on bonus** — $2,000–$10,000, vested over 6–12 months
- **Retention bonus** — paid at 90 days, 6 months, 1 year
- **Safety bonus** — quarterly or annual
- **Per-mile bonus** for clean inspections, on-time service
- **Home time guarantees** — competitive lever especially OTR
- **Equipment** — late-model, automatic, APU, refrigerator, inverter

## Disqualifying screens before you spend time
MVR and PSP red flags to define up front:
- Any major `§ 383.51(b)` offense in the past X years
- More than N serious `§ 383.51(c)` offenses in past 3 years
- DOT-recordable crash within past 12–24 months (carrier policy)
- Insurance carrier limits (most underwriters set their own MVR rules)
- Clearinghouse "prohibited" status — automatic disqualifier until SAP completion

## The legal process for using consumer reports
When using MVR, PSP, or criminal background reports as part of hiring:
1. Disclosure on standalone form
2. Written consent
3. Pre-adverse action notice with copy of report and FCRA summary of rights
4. Reasonable waiting period (typically 5 business days)
5. Final adverse action notice if not hired

## Funnel metrics to manage
- Applications per channel
- Cost per qualified application
- Interview-to-orientation rate
- Orientation no-show rate (often 15–30%)
- 90-day retention (industry-typical OTR: 50–70%; key inflection point)
- 1-year retention
- All-in cost per hire

## Pitfalls
- Marketing a sign-on bonus you can't fund consistently
- Using PSP without driver consent
- Skipping FCRA pre-adverse action notice
- Promising home time that the operational pattern can't deliver
- Lease-purchase programs that drive churn instead of retention
- Treating Clearinghouse query as a courtesy step instead of a hard gate

name: Refrigerated Cargo Specifics
q: Use this skill when the user asks about refrigerated (reefer) trucking — cold chain compliance, FDA
body:
# Refrigerated Cargo Specifics

Reefer freight is subject to FMCSA's standard `Part 393` cargo securement and `Part 395` HOS rules, plus FDA's **Sanitary Transportation of Human and Animal Food** rule under `21 CFR Part 1, Subpart O` (often called the FSMA STF rule).

## FSMA Sanitary Transport rule
Applies to shippers, loaders, carriers, and receivers transporting human or animal food **except** fully packaged shelf-stable food, live animals, raw agricultural commodities transported by farms, and limited other exclusions. Effective for non-small businesses since April 6, 2017.

### Carrier obligations
1. **Vehicle and equipment** — designed, constructed, and maintained to prevent contamination; cleaning when carrier learns previous cargo could contaminate next load
2. **Operations** — temperature control during transport, separation of food from non-food, hand-washing where required
3. **Written agreements** — when the shipper assigns responsibility (e.g., supplies pulping thermometer, sets temperature, requires inspection), the carrier follows shipper specs
4. **Training** — carrier personnel performing transportation operations trained in sanitary practices when carrier is responsible for sanitary conditions
5. **Records** — written procedures, agreements, training records retained for **12 months**

## Temperature management
- Pre-cool trailer before loading
- Verify pulp temperature at loading (record it on BOL)
- Set unit to product temperature, not air temperature
- Continuous vs cycle-sentry depending on product (cycle-sentry can drift)
- Reefer download / temperature record at delivery (most modern units record continuously)
- Common claim cause: gap between pulp temp at load and the BOL spec

## Equipment
- Carrier responsibility under FSMA includes equipment design and cleaning
- Common reefer specs: TK Whisper Edge, Carrier Vector, Thermo King Precedent
- 6–10 year useful life on reefer unit; tractor with idle-protect for reefer fuel
- Trailer floor drains, return-air bulkhead, curtains, e-tracks for produce

## Common commodities and quirks
- **Fresh produce** — strict temp tolerance; floor-loaded, air-circulation critical
- **Meat/poultry** — USDA-inspected; 28–34°F typical; chain-of-custody documentation
- **Frozen foods** — -10°F to 0°F; trailer pre-cool critical
- **Pharmaceuticals** — 2–8°C cold chain; often white-glove with continuous monitoring, qualification, validation
- **Floral** — 33–35°F; high turnover; specific air-flow needs

## Hazmat overlap
Some refrigerated chemicals/biologicals carry hazmat placarding. UN3473, UN1845 (dry ice), UN2814 (Category A infectious substances), UN3091 lithium-battery temperature-sensitive products — all hazmat overlay.

## Common pitfalls
- Pulling a load without verified pre-cool
- Trusting the air-temperature display when product temp is what matters
- Skipping the pulp-temp note on BOL — leaves carrier exposed to claims
- FSMA training records missing
- Reefer fuel running out at the dock or in transit
- Mixing chemical/produce or meat/non-meat without prior cleaning

## What auditors look for
FMCSA — standard FMCSR compliance. FDA — sanitary transport written procedures, training records, cleaning records, written agreements with shippers, response to feedback when a load is rejected for contamination concerns.

name: Roadside Inspection Levels
q: Use this skill when the user asks about CMV roadside inspection levels (Level I through Level VIII),
body:
# Roadside Inspection Levels

The **Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance (CVSA)** defines eight roadside inspection levels used by FMCSA and state enforcement. The results feed into the carrier's **CSA SMS** scores under `Part 385`.

## Level I — North American Standard Inspection
Most comprehensive. **37-step examination** covering:
- Driver credentials (CDL, MEC, RODS, Clearinghouse, hazmat)
- Vehicle: brakes, coupling, exhaust, fuel system, frame, lighting, securement, steering, suspension, tires, wheels, windshield, wipers, emergency equipment
- Hazmat compliance if applicable
Takes 45–60 minutes. CVSA decal issued for passing vehicles.

## Level II — Walk-Around Driver/Vehicle Inspection
Driver portion same as Level I; vehicle portion is **walk-around** only — items not requiring the inspector to go under the vehicle. Takes 30–40 minutes.

## Level III — Driver/Credential Inspection
Driver-only — CDL, MEC, RODS/ELD, Clearinghouse, hazmat endorsements, seatbelt, drug & alcohol indicators. No vehicle inspection. 15–20 minutes.

## Level IV — Special Inspection
One-time examination for a specific item (e.g., emission test for a research study, special law enforcement focus).

## Level V — Vehicle-Only Inspection
Level I vehicle items, no driver present. Often at carrier yard during a compliance review.

## Level VI — Enhanced NAS Inspection for Radioactive Shipments
For highway-route-controlled-quantity (HRCQ) radioactive shipments. Includes Level I + radiation surveys, enhanced criteria. CVSA Level VI decal required.

## Level VII — Jurisdictional Mandated Inspection
State-specific inspection (school bus, intrastate, terminal inspection). Not under standard CVSA.

## Level VIII — Electronic Inspection
Driver/vehicle data transferred and reviewed electronically while the vehicle is in motion (e.g., wireless inspection via DSRC or smart roadside). Limited current deployment.

## Out-of-service criteria
Each inspection level can result in driver and/or vehicle OOS based on the **CVSA Out-of-Service Criteria** handbook. Common OOS items:
- Brakes — defective beyond OOS thresholds
- Tires — flat, exposed cord, below 2/32 (4/32 on steers)
- Lights — required lamps not working
- Steering, suspension, frame defects
- Driver — no CDL, no MEC, HOS violation in current shift, BAC ≥ 0.04, under influence, OOS prior order in effect, no ELD
- Cargo securement — load shift, broken tiedown, inadequate restraint

## Inspection-to-CSA flow
- Each violation is weighted in the relevant **BASIC** category
- Time-weighted (recent violations count more)
- Severity-weighted by FMCSA's published severity tables
- Roll up to BASIC percentile vs peers in the carrier's safety event group
- Carriers above intervention threshold get warning letters, A&I scrutiny, or investigations

## DataQs
Carriers can challenge inspection results that are factually wrong via the **DataQs (Request for Data Review)** system. Common successful challenges: wrong USDOT on report, violation later found inapplicable, citation dismissed in court.

## Common errors
- Driver not having required documents accessible (CDL, MEC if applicable, ELD instruction manual)
- ELD data transfer not working (must work via web service, email, USB, or Bluetooth)
- Missing supporting documents (BOL, fuel receipts)
- DVIR not on the truck or incomplete
- Annual inspection decal expired or missing

name: Safety Culture And Management
q: Use this skill when the user asks how to build, measure, or improve safety culture in a motor carrie
body:
# Safety Culture and Management

FMCSA expects every motor carrier to have **safety management controls** — the programs, policies, training, and practices that produce regulatory compliance. This is the explicit standard for the New Entrant audit (`§ 385.321`) and the basis for the safety rating process (`§ 385.5`). The phrase "safety culture" is the human side of those controls.

## What FMCSA actually measures
- DQF completeness
- Drug & alcohol program execution
- HOS compliance via ELD
- Vehicle maintenance and inspection
- Hazmat compliance if applicable
- Insurance and authority
- Accident register and crash rate
- Roadside inspection BASIC percentiles

A Satisfactory safety rating requires acceptable performance across these areas.

## Elements of a working safety culture
1. **Leadership commitment** — owner and senior management publicly prioritize safety over revenue when they conflict
2. **Written policy** — a safety manual with the carrier's specific procedures, signed by the responsible officer
3. **Designated safety officer** with authority — not a side job for someone without standing
4. **Hiring standards** that include safety, not just MVR minimums
5. **Onboarding and ongoing training** — defensive driving, HOS, fatigue, cargo, hazmat where applicable
6. **Coaching loop** — telematics/camera events reviewed and discussed with drivers, not used solely punitively
7. **Open reporting** — drivers report concerns without fear of retaliation (protected under `§ 405` STAA whistleblower)
8. **Equipment investment** — newer tractors, ABS/ESC/AEB where available, cameras
9. **Pay structure that doesn't punish compliance** — drivers don't lose money for taking required breaks or refusing unsafe loads (`§ 392.14`)
10. **Post-incident review** — every crash and serious near-miss has a written root-cause review
11. **Continuous improvement** — KPIs tracked, trend-reviewed monthly, targets adjusted

## Common cultural failure modes
- Dispatch pressure to skip the 30-minute break or push past the 14-hour shift
- "Don't tell me how, just get it done" management
- Treating ELD edits as a workaround for HOS violations
- Punishing drivers for refusing to operate unsafe equipment
- Ignoring DVIR defects to save shop time
- Rewarding only on-time delivery without a safety check

## Measuring culture
- Anonymous driver surveys (annual)
- Coaching-to-incident ratio (coaching events without incidents → good)
- Driver tenure and turnover
- Voluntary near-miss reporting volume
- Time from defect noted to repair completed
- Refusal-of-load events and how they're resolved

## What auditors look for
At a compliance review, beyond the document checklists, auditors form an impression of whether the carrier has actual safety management or just paper compliance. Patterns of HOS edits, repeat OOS, repeat violations on the same units, and high crash rate all point to weak controls regardless of paperwork.

## Pitfalls
- Buying a safety manual template and never using it
- Hiring a safety officer with no authority over dispatch
- Treating safety as a cost center rather than the foundation of insurability and rate-ability
- Failing to investigate "minor" crashes — patterns hide in those
- Letting safety bonuses become a reason to under-report
