name: Safety Meeting Agenda Templates
q: Use when a safety director, operations manager, or fleet owner asks for templates, topics, or struct
body:
# Safety Meeting Agenda Templates

Safety meetings are a core element of an effective compliance program. While `§ 390.5` defines the carrier as responsible for driver safety, the meetings themselves are recommended practice rather than a hard CFR mandate. Treat them as documented evidence of an ongoing safety culture — useful at FMCSA audits, insurance underwriting, and CSA defense.

## Recommended cadence
- **Monthly** safety meeting (30–60 min) for most fleets
- **Quarterly** for very small carriers (1–5 trucks)
- **Immediately after** any DOT-recordable crash or roadside out-of-service

## Standard agenda template
1. Roll call and sign-in sheet (proof of attendance)
2. Review of last meeting's action items
3. CSA scorecard snapshot — current BASIC percentiles
4. Recent inspections — wins and violations
5. Crashes and near-misses since last meeting
6. Topic of the month (rotating — see list below)
7. Open driver Q&A
8. Action items and next meeting date

## Rotating monthly topics
- January: Winter driving, chains, black ice
- February: HOS refresher and ELD malfunction procedure
- March: DVIR completion and air-brake checks
- April: Pre-trip inspection deep dive
- May: Cargo securement (`Part 393` Subpart I)
- June: Distracted driving and hands-free rules
- July: Heat illness, hydration, tire blowouts
- August: Speed management and following distance
- September: Drug & alcohol awareness (`Part 382`)
- October: Backing, blind spots, intersections
- November: Holiday traffic and fatigue
- December: Year-end review and goals

## What to document
- Sign-in sheet with driver signatures
- Agenda used
- Handouts distributed
- Action items and owners
- Photos of any demonstrations

## Common errors
- No sign-in sheet (no proof of attendance)
- Same topic repeated quarterly without varying content
- No follow-through on action items
- Meetings cancelled and not rescheduled

## What auditors look for
At an FMCSA review, safety meeting records strengthen a carrier's defense on driver-management questions and on CSA Unsafe Driving BASIC scores. Missing meetings are not a per-se violation but suggest weak oversight.

name: Samsara Vs Motive Vs Geotab Comparison
q: Use when a carrier is evaluating ELD / telematics / dashcam platforms and needs an objective compari
body:
# Samsara vs Motive vs Geotab Comparison

All three platforms produce FMCSA-registered ELDs that satisfy `Part 395` Subpart B. The differences are in user experience, dashcam integration, pricing, and add-on telematics — not in core HOS compliance. This skill covers selection criteria for a small-to-mid carrier.

## ELD compliance baseline
All three are on the FMCSA Registered ELDs list and meet `§ 395.20`–`§ 395.38` technical requirements:
- Automatic recording of driving time
- ELD malfunction and data-diagnostic indicators
- Unidentified driving capture
- Driver edit and annotation logging
- Roadside data transfer (web services or USB)

## Samsara
- Strong dashcam (AI-driven event detection)
- Polished driver app and dispatcher dashboard
- Premium pricing — typically the highest of the three
- Strong API for integration
- Best fit: fleets prioritizing safety analytics and willing to pay

## Motive (formerly KeepTruckin)
- Mid-tier pricing
- AI Dashcam with driver coaching
- Built-in fuel cards, factoring, load board (vertically integrated)
- Driver app is widely adopted, low training friction
- Best fit: small-to-mid carriers wanting all-in-one

## Geotab
- Telematics-first; ELD added later via Geotab Drive app
- Hardware-agnostic (works with many third-party devices)
- Lower base price; complex feature surface
- Strong reporting and rules engine
- Best fit: mixed fleets, enterprise integrations, custom reporting

## Selection checklist
1. Verify the model is on the **FMCSA Registered ELDs list** at the time of purchase (not the Revoked list)
2. Confirm hardware works with each truck's ECM (model year ≥ 2000)
3. Check dashcam policy — required by insurer? front-only or driver-facing?
4. Pull a sample malfunction report — how does the vendor flag and resolve issues?
5. Run a 30-day pilot on 1–2 trucks before fleet rollout

## Common errors
- Choosing on price alone; cheapest ELD often has weak support during a roadside data transfer issue
- Skipping the driver-facing camera question (privacy pushback after install)
- Not budgeting for cellular/data plan on top of hardware

name: Seasonal Operations Winter Summer
q: Use when a carrier or driver asks about winter trucking, snow chain requirements, hot-weather precau
body:
# Seasonal Operations: Winter and Summer

The CMV maintenance and inspection rules in `Part 396` do not change by season, but operational practice does. This skill covers seasonal preparation that supports `§ 396.3` (systematic inspection, repair, and maintenance) and reduces roadside out-of-service exposure.

## Winter preparation
- **Tire chains**: required on many western mountain passes. States with chain laws include CA, OR, WA, CO, NV, ID, MT, UT, WY. Carry sets sized for the drive and trailer axles.
- **Block heater**: confirm plug condition; brief drivers on shore-power protocol
- **Antifreeze**: test concentration before October; replace coolant on schedule
- **Air dryer**: drain tanks; verify desiccant cartridge service interval
- **Fuel additive / anti-gel**: use winter-blend diesel; carry anti-gel for emergencies
- **Wipers and washer fluid**: stock winter-rated washer fluid (rated to -25°F or lower)
- **Emergency kit**: blanket, food, water, road flares (`§ 393.95`), extra layers

## Winter driving topics for driver briefing
- Black ice recognition (bridges, shaded curves, dawn/dusk)
- Brake-in-a-straight-line rule
- Increased following distance (8+ seconds)
- When to shut down — driver authority under `§ 392.14` (hazardous conditions)

## Summer preparation
- **Tire pressure**: heat raises PSI; check cold pressure each morning
- **Cooling system**: verify hose condition, radiator clean, fans engaging
- **A/C**: driver comfort directly affects fatigue management
- **Brake adjustment**: heat accelerates wear on long grades
- **DEF**: monitor consumption; summer dosing rates increase

## Summer driver topics
- Heat illness recognition (cramps → exhaustion → stroke)
- Hydration protocol — water, not energy drinks
- Tire blowout response (steer straight, off throttle, no hard brake)
- Construction zones (highest seasonal crash risk)

## Seasonal documentation
- Pre-season inspection checklist signed by mechanic
- Driver briefing sign-in sheet
- Photos of winter kit in each truck

## Common errors
- No documented chain training for drivers
- Summer tire pressure set at delivery PSI (overinflated by 10–15 PSI when cold-checked)
- Idling rules ignored — many states cap idle at 5 minutes

name: Shipper Relationship Management
q: Use this skill when the user asks how to build + manage direct shipper relationships — moving from s
body:
# Direct Shipper Relationship Management

Moving from broker-only freight to direct shipper relationships changes a carrier's margin, predictability, and operational compliance posture. While `49 CFR Part 390` governs general motor carrier responsibilities, the direct-shipper relationship adds contractual and insurance considerations beyond core compliance.

## Why go direct
- **Margin**: brokers take 10–25%; direct freight captures that spread
- **Predictability**: contracted lanes vs spot market volatility
- **Driver retention**: known routes, known docks
- **Cash flow**: net-30 or net-15 with established shippers vs broker QuickPay fees

## What shippers require
1. Active MC and DOT authority (`Part 390`)
2. **Certificate of Insurance (COI)** typically: $1M auto liability, $100K cargo, $1M general liability
3. Additional insured endorsement naming the shipper
4. Satisfactory or Unrated CSA status (no Conditional)
5. Safer.fmcsa.gov clean report
6. Sometimes: SmartWay registration, drug & alcohol program proof, W-9

## Building the pipeline
- Cold outreach to traffic managers (LinkedIn, ThomasNet, industry directories)
- Trade shows (your shipper's industry, not trucking shows)
- Backhaul conversations with current consignees
- Referrals from existing shippers

## Contract terms to negotiate
- Rate per mile or per load, fuel surcharge formula
- Detention pay (after 2 hours typically)
- Layover, TONU, and accessorial schedule
- Payment terms (target net-15 to net-30)
- Cancellation and force-majeure clauses
- Insurance and indemnification scope

## Compliance considerations
- Cargo claims process — document with photos at pickup and delivery
- Hazmat shippers add `Part 172` and `Part 177` obligations (training, placarding, registration)
- Food-grade shippers require **Sanitary Transportation Rule** compliance (`21 CFR Part 1.900`)

## Common errors
- Signing shipper contracts without legal review (broad indemnification clauses)
- Underinsuring (shipper's COI requirement higher than your policy)
- No backup plan when a direct shipper's volume drops 30%

- **49 CFR Part 387** (minimum financial responsibility)

- **21 CFR Part 1.900** (Sanitary Transportation, for food)

name: State Mvr Fee Lookup
q: Use this skill when the user asks the cost of pulling a Motor Vehicle Record (MVR) in a specific sta
body:
# State MVR Fee Lookup

Motor Vehicle Records (MVRs) are required at hire and annually thereafter under `§ 391.23` and `§ 391.25`. Each state's Department of Motor Vehicles (or equivalent) sets its own fee for an MVR. This skill helps carriers budget annual MVR costs across their driver roster.

## Why this matters
- A 30-driver carrier with drivers licensed in 10 states pays 30 MVR fees per year at hire-state rates
- Fees range from **$2 to $25+** per record depending on state
- Most carriers pull MVRs through a third-party service (HireRight, DriverFacts, Foley) which adds $3–8 vendor markup

## Approximate state MVR fees (verify current rates — fees change)
- **Low (under $5)**: AL, GA, MS, NM, TN
- **Mid ($5–$15)**: most states, including TX, FL, IL, OH, PA, NC
- **High ($15–$25+)**: CA, NY, NJ, IL (3-year), WA, OR
- **Special**: Some states require additional driver authorization forms (CA — DL 14, MA — RMV release)

## How to verify current fee
1. Search "[State] DMV motor vehicle record fee" on the state DMV site
2. Confirm the fee for **3-year commercial MVR** (not standard)
3. Note any extra processing or expedite fees
4. Verify required release form (DOT-compliant driver authorization, signed)

## Vendor pricing typical structure
- Per-MVR cost (state fee + vendor fee)
- Monitoring subscription (continuous MVR — flags new violations between annual pulls)
- Bulk discounts at 50+ drivers/year

## Compliance reminder
- Annual MVR per `§ 391.25` is required regardless of fee
- Driver Information Resource (DIR) / Clearinghouse query is **separate** from MVR
- States with verified DL-history APIs (CDLIS) are required for CDL drivers

name: State Trucking Taxes
q: Use this skill when the user asks about state-specific trucking taxes BEYOND IFTA — NY Highway Use T
body:
# State Trucking Taxes (Beyond IFTA)

IFTA covers state fuel-tax reciprocity, but several states impose additional carrier-specific taxes. This skill covers the four most common ones beyond IFTA. These are state tax obligations, not FMCSA rules under `49 CFR Part 390`, but they directly affect carrier cost and operations.

## New York Highway Use Tax (NY HUT)
- Required for vehicles over **18,000 lbs** operating on NY public highways
- Quarterly returns; rate based on gross weight and miles driven
- Apply for credentials at NY Department of Taxation and Finance
- **HUT Decal** required on each truck; renew every 3 years
- Penalty for missing decal: up to $1,000 per violation

## Kentucky Weight Distance Tax (KYU)
- Required for vehicles over **59,999 lbs** operating in KY
- Quarterly returns; rate per mile
- KYU number required on truck
- Audited separately from IFTA

## New Mexico Weight Distance Tax
- Required for vehicles over **26,000 lbs** in NM
- Quarterly tax based on weight and miles
- Permit issued by NM Taxation and Revenue Department

## Oregon Weight-Mile Tax
- All trucks over **26,000 lbs** operating in OR
- Monthly or quarterly returns depending on volume
- Oregon does NOT participate in IFTA for these vehicles
- Permit issued by Oregon DOT Motor Carrier Division
- Rates vary by weight class

## Other state taxes to watch
- **Highway use permits** in some states for oversize/overweight
- **Unified Carrier Registration (UCR)** — federal-state cooperative; annual fee based on fleet size
- **State income/franchise tax** apportionment where the carrier has nexus

## Common errors
- Missing the NY HUT decal — visible violation at any NY weigh station
- Running OR without weight-mile credentials
- Filing KYU returns late (penalty + interest)
- Forgetting UCR renewal (Dec 31 deadline annually)

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- **IFTA Articles of Agreement** (interstate fuel)
- **49 CFR Part 367** (Unified Carrier Registration)
- State tax codes vary by jurisdiction — see each state's department of revenue

name: Team Driving Operations
q: Use this skill when the user asks about team driving — two-driver OTR operations, how teams maximize
body:
# Team Driving Operations

Team driving — two qualified CDL drivers in one tractor — allows near-continuous movement under `Part 395`. Each driver maintains a separate ELD record. This skill covers how teams stack on-duty/off-duty time, sleeper-berth use, and compliance traps.

## How teams stack hours
Under `§ 395.3`, each driver has their own:
- **11-hour driving** limit
- **14-hour duty window**
- **70-hour / 8-day** (or 60/7) cycle
- **30-minute break** requirement

With two drivers, the truck moves up to **22 hours** in a 24-hour period (theoretical max, less in practice).

## Sleeper-berth provision (`§ 395.1(g)`)
The split-sleeper provisions apply to each driver individually. A team driver in the sleeper while their partner drives is **off-duty** for HOS accounting, provided the berth is FMCSA-compliant (`§ 393.76`).

## ELD setup for teams
- Each driver logs in to the ELD with their own credentials
- The driving driver's log records driving time
- The non-driving driver logs off-duty or sleeper-berth
- Both drivers must verify their daily log before submitting

## Pre-trip and DVIR
- The driver in control at the time of pre-trip signs the DVIR
- Both drivers should walk around at shift changes
- Post-trip DVIR (`§ 396.11`) signed at end of duty by the driver responsible

## Pay structure considerations
- Split mileage (each gets ~50% of total miles)
- Or single rate per truck split by agreement
- W-2 vs 1099 carries normal IRS and state rules
- Detention and accessorials usually split equally

## Common compliance errors
- Both drivers logging on-duty simultaneously when only one is driving (inflates duty time)
- Sleeper berth not meeting `§ 393.76` dimensions or construction
- Sleeper-berth time recorded but driver wasn't actually in the berth (ELD GPS data exposes this)
- One driver doing all the work while logged in as the other (fraud)

## Roadside inspection notes
- Inspectors will request both drivers' logs
- Mismatched on-duty times between drivers raise flags
- Both drivers must produce CDL, medical card, and ELD records

- **49 CFR § 395.3** (driving limits)
- **49 CFR § 395.1(g)** (sleeper berth)
- **49 CFR § 393.76** (sleeper-berth construction)
- **49 CFR § 396.11** (DVIR)

name: Tire Management Program
q: Use when a carrier asks about tire program design, when to retread vs replace, position management (
body:
# Tire Management Program

Tires are the single largest variable cost after fuel for most fleets, and they account for a meaningful share of out-of-service violations under `Part 396`. A documented tire program supports both cost control and compliance.

## Regulatory minimums (`§ 393.75`)
- **Steer tire tread depth**: minimum **4/32 inch** in any major groove
- **Drive and trailer tire tread depth**: minimum **2/32 inch** in any major groove
- No regrooved, recapped, or retread tires on the **steer position** of a CMV (other than power units used in driveaway-towaway)
- No fabric exposed through tread or sidewall
- No tire marked "Not for Highway Use"
- Tire must not be flat or have audible leak

## Program elements
1. **Spec'd brands and sizes** per position (steer, drive, trailer)
2. **Pressure checks**: weekly minimum; daily during temperature swings
3. **Tread depth measurement**: every PM inspection
4. **Rotation schedule**: drives every 30–50K mi; trailers as needed
5. **Retread policy**: drive and trailer only; never steer
6. **Disposal log**: track scrap tires for environmental compliance

## When to retread vs replace
- Retread candidate: casing in good shape, 1 retread maximum on drives, 2 max on trailers
- Replace: sidewall damage, casing breaches, age over 6 years, casing temperature events
- Retread cost: 30–40% of new tire; saves significant cost at fleet scale

## Position management
- **Steer**: highest-quality new tire, rib tread, replace at 4/32 or sooner
- **Drive**: lug or hybrid tread, rotate inside/outside duals to even wear
- **Trailer**: rib tread, low rolling resistance to save fuel

## DVIR considerations
- Driver checks pressure and visible damage at pre-trip (`§ 396.11` / `§ 392.7`)
- Audible air leaks must be repaired before dispatch
- Tread depth below CFR minimum is out-of-service

## Common errors
- Retreads on steer axle (out-of-service violation, automatic)
- Mixed sizes on duals
- Tread depth measured only in shallowest groove without checking major grooves
- Sidewall damage missed at pre-trip

## What auditors look for
CSA Vehicle Maintenance BASIC: tire-related violations heavily weighted. Severity multiplier on flat tires and out-of-service tread depth.

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 393.75** (tires)
- **49 CFR § 396.11** (DVIR)
- **49 CFR § 396.17** (periodic inspection)

name: Towing And Recovery
q: Use this skill when the user asks about towing + recovery operations — separate FMCSA authority clas
body:
# Towing and Recovery Operations

Towing and recovery carriers operate under FMCSA authority just like other motor carriers but face unique CSA scoring quirks under `Part 385`. Many towing-related crashes appear on the towed vehicle's carrier record, not the tow company's. This skill covers the operational and reporting nuances.

## FMCSA authority for tow carriers
- **Motor Carrier of Property (MC)** authority required for interstate non-consensual tows beyond a commercial zone
- Some intrastate-only tow operators may be exempt from federal authority but still need DOT number
- **Cargo insurance** required for property tows (`Part 387`)
- **MCS-90 endorsement** required

## Vehicle classification
- **Light-duty wrecker**: under 10,001 lbs GVWR — typically not CMV
- **Medium-duty wrecker**: 10,001–26,000 lbs — CMV under federal rules
- **Heavy-duty wrecker / rotator**: over 26,000 lbs — full CMV compliance

## CSA reporting quirks
- A crash involving a towed vehicle (the disabled vehicle being recovered) generally lists on the **tow carrier's** record while the truck is under tow
- Pre-tow crashes (the crash that caused the disablement) remain on the **disabled vehicle's** carrier
- DataQ challenges are the appeal channel when crashes appear on the wrong carrier

## HOS for tow operators
- Standard `Part 395` rules apply
- "Property-carrying" provisions
- Some emergency-response exemptions (`§ 390.23`) for declared emergencies — narrow scope, time-limited

## Insurance considerations
- **On-hook coverage** for the towed vehicle
- **Garage liability** for shop operations
- **Garage keepers legal liability** for vehicles in custody
- **Auto liability** at federal minimum (`§ 387.9`) or higher

## Common compliance traps
- Operating a heavy wrecker over 26K without DQF on the operator
- Towing across state lines without interstate authority
- Failing to placard if the towed vehicle was carrying hazmat
- Missing DataQ deadlines on misattributed crashes (typically 60 days from posting)

name: Tractor Spec Options
q: Use when a carrier asks how to spec a new tractor — engine choice (X15 vs DD16 vs PACCAR MX), transm
body:
# Tractor Spec Options for a New Order

Spec'ing a new tractor affects HOS compliance (driver fatigue management under `Part 395`), maintenance cost under `Part 396`, and inspection performance. This skill covers the spec decisions that have compliance and cost consequences for a small-to-mid carrier.

## Engine choice
- **Cummins X15**: most common for OTR; broad parts and service network
- **Detroit DD15 / DD16**: strong for fleets running Freightliner / Western Star
- **PACCAR MX-13**: standard in Kenworth / Peterbilt; good fuel economy
- **Volvo D13**: integrated with I-Shift; long service intervals

Spec choice affects: torque/power for terrain, MPG, parts availability, resale.

## Transmission
- **Automated Manual (AMT)** — Eaton UltraShift, Volvo I-Shift, Detroit DT12: now over 90% of new OTR orders; better MPG, lower driver fatigue, easier for newer drivers
- **Manual** — fading; some specialty applications
- **Automatic torque-converter** — vocational only

## Rear axle ratio
- **2.47–2.79**: highway fuel-economy spec, low RPM at cruise
- **3.08–3.42**: mixed application
- **3.55+**: vocational, heavy-haul, frequent grades

## Sleeper size
- **Day cab**: regional, no sleeper
- **48-inch sleeper**: short OTR, drop-and-hook
- **72–86 inch sleeper**: long OTR; must meet `§ 393.76` for sleeper-berth HOS credit

## Safety options affecting compliance
- **Collision mitigation** (radar + camera): reduces Unsafe Driving CSA exposure
- **Lane departure warning**
- **Adaptive cruise control**
- **Dashcam integration** with the ELD
- **Tire pressure monitoring**: avoids `§ 393.75` violations
- **Air-disc brakes**: shorter stopping distance vs drum

## Compliance-relevant standard items
- Speed limiter (carrier policy)
- Idle shutdown (5–10 minutes typical)
- ELD-ready ECM (model year 2000+ required for ELD mandate)

## Common errors
- Ordering too aggressive a rear-axle ratio for the application (kills fuel economy)
- Skipping collision mitigation to save up-front cost (insurance discount usually pays it back)
- Buying a sleeper that does not meet `§ 393.76` dimensions when sleeper-berth HOS credit is needed

name: Trailer Types And Specifications
q: Use when a carrier asks about trailer types — dry van, reefer, flatbed, step-deck, conestoga, tanker
body:
# Trailer Types and Specifications

Trailer selection drives revenue per mile, regulatory exposure, and compliance under `Part 393` (parts and accessories) and `Part 396` (inspection and maintenance). This skill summarizes the common trailer types in US OTR freight and the compliance considerations for each.

## Dry van (53 ft most common)
- General freight, pallet count typically 26–30
- Cargo securement (`Part 393` Subpart I): straps, e-track, load bars
- DVIR checks: doors, floor, lights, ABS
- Cleanest CSA exposure of the trailer types

## Refrigerated (reefer)
- 53 ft most common; Carrier or Thermo King reefer unit
- **FSMA Sanitary Transportation Rule** (`21 CFR Part 1.900`) applies for food
- Temperature logs typically retained 12 months
- Reefer fuel and DEF separate from tractor
- DVIR adds reefer unit checks (refrigerant, belts, defrost cycle)

## Flatbed (48–53 ft)
- Open deck; cargo exposed
- Cargo securement is the dominant compliance area:
  - Working Load Limit (WLL) calculation per `§ 393.106`
  - Tie-down count based on cargo length (`§ 393.110`)
  - Edge protection for chains
  - Tarping for weather-sensitive loads
- Higher injury risk for drivers (falls from deck)

## Step-deck / Drop-deck
- Lower deck height for taller cargo
- Same securement rules as flatbed
- Often paired with oversize permits

## Conestoga
- Flatbed with rolling tarp system
- Easier loading, weather protection
- Higher trailer cost; reduces tarp labor

## Tanker (liquid bulk)
- DOT 406/407/412 specs (`§ 178.345`)
- Hazmat endorsement on CDL (`§ 383.93`) if carrying hazmat
- Periodic tank tests (V, K, P, I per cargo)
- Surge management training for drivers
- Smoothbore vs baffled

## Lowboy / RGN
- Heavy haul, equipment moves
- Oversize/overweight permits per state
- Pilot car requirements vary by state and load

## Common compliance issues by trailer type
- Flatbeds: securement violations are #1 OOS category
- Reefers: temperature recordkeeping under FSMA
- Tankers: failed periodic tests, missing endorsement
- Dry vans: ABS lights, brake adjustment

name: Train Annual Refresher Requirements
q: Use this skill to design an annual driver refresher training program
body:
# Annual Refresher Training Recommendations

Annual refresher training isn't federally mandated for general CMV drivers, but it's strong industry practice and required for some specialized operations.

## What to cover in annual refresher
- HOS rule updates (any changes since last training)
- Drug & alcohol rule reminders
- Hazmat-specific (if applicable): security awareness annually
- Driver safety topics (carrier-selected based on incident pattern)
- ELD usage refresher
- CSA scoring impact

## Frequency
- **Minimum recommended**: 1-2 hours per year
- **Best practice**: 4-8 hours per year (varies by carrier risk profile)
- **Hazmat-required**: 1 hour security awareness annually + 3 hours general DOT safety every 3 years

## Format options
- Online LMS modules (most efficient, $10-15/driver/month)
- In-person classroom (for new hires, group sessions)
- Toolbox talks (informal, in fleet operations)
- One-on-one (post-accident, post-violation)

## Documentation
- Course completion record (date, hours, content, instructor)
- Driver acknowledgment signature
- Test results (where applicable)
- Retention: 3 years minimum

## What gets the best ROI
- HOS scenario training (reduces violations)
- Defensive driving (reduces crashes)
- Hazmat-specific (for hazmat carriers)
- Vehicle inspection (reduces equipment-related violations)

## What's often wasteful
- Generic "safety meeting" content
- One-size-fits-all training
- Topics drivers already know cold
- Training without follow-up coaching

## Compass training plan
Compass Training module:
- Tracks per-driver annual training hours
- Recommends curriculum based on driver's CSA + accident history
- Imports completion data from LMS vendors
- Generates compliance reports

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR Part 380**
- **49 CFR § 391.11**

name: Train Defensive Driving Course Requirements
q: Use this skill to understand defensive driving course expectations for CMV drivers
body:
# Defensive Driving Course Requirements

Federal law does NOT mandate defensive driving training for CMV drivers (except for entry-level ELDT requirements). State and carrier requirements vary widely.

## What federal law requires (§ 391.11)
Driver must "possess the necessary skills to safely operate a CMV." This is a general qualification, not a course requirement. ELDT (49 CFR Part 380) requires 31 theory + 19 behind-the-wheel topics for first-time CDL applicants — but no recurring federal training.

## State-level requirements
- Some states (CA, OH, others) mandate defensive driving for renewal of certain CDL endorsements
- Some states mandate accident-history-triggered training (driver had X+ accidents → required course)
- Hazmat endorsement renewal may require security awareness training

## Carrier-level requirements (most common)
- New-hire orientation: typically 2-8 hours
- Annual refresher: 1-4 hours (recommended, not required)
- Post-accident review (if accidents occur)
- Roadside-inspection-triggered: if BASIC alerts, supplemental training

## Programs commonly used
- **Smith System** — defensive driving methodology (5 keys to safety)
- **CarriersEdge** — DOT-focused online courses
- **JJ Keller Encompass** — full LMS with hundreds of DOT courses
- **Smith System certified instructor** — at carrier or vendor
- **Various TPR-registered providers** for ELDT

## What auditors look for
- Training records in employee file (not DQF)
- Date completed, hours, instructor/vendor
- Specific course/topic covered
- Driver acknowledgment of completion

## How Compass tracks
Compass Training module:
- Course library imported from LMS vendors (Infinit-i, JJ Keller, etc.)
- Per-driver completion tracking
- Renewal alerts for required training
- Audit-ready report exports

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 391.11**
- **49 CFR Part 380**

name: Train Eldt Btw Vendor Vetting
q: Use this skill when selecting a TPR-registered Training Provider for behind-the-wheel ELDT training
body:
# ELDT Behind-The-Wheel Vendor Vetting

Per § 380.609, entry-level driver training (ELDT) for first-time CDL applicants requires both theory (31 topics) and behind-the-wheel (BTW, 19 topics). BTW must be conducted by a TPR-registered provider.

## TPR registry verification
- Go to tpr.fmcsa.dot.gov
- Verify provider's TPR number is active
- Check effective + expiration dates
- Confirm provider has training delivery capability (instructor + vehicles)

## Provider evaluation criteria
- TPR registration current
- Instructor qualifications (some states require additional licensing)
- Training vehicle equipment (proper safety equipment, instructor controls)
- Course materials (FMCSA-approved curriculum)
- Audit history (any FMCSA findings against the provider)
- Reputation (industry references)

## Cost considerations

# Reasonable Suspicion 2-Hour Supervisor Course Documentation

Per § 382.603, every supervisor must complete 60 minutes of training on each of alcohol misuse and controlled substance use indicators. The "2-hour" reference is the combined total.

## Course content (per FMCSA)
- Physical, behavioral, speech, performance indicators of probable drug/alcohol use
- The reasonable-suspicion testing requirement
- The supervisor's role in observation
- Documentation of observed behavior

## Required documentation
- Training certificate (instructor or vendor-issued)
- Training date
- Hours: 60+ minutes alcohol + 60+ minutes drug = 2 hours minimum
- Instructor name or vendor
- Topics covered (list)
- Supervisor name + position

## Where to retain
- Supervisor's personnel file (NOT the DQF)
- HR/training records section
- Retention: per § 382.401(b)(1)(iii) — 2 years

## Frequency
- **Initial**: before supervisor can make reasonable-suspicion calls
- **Refresher**: not federally mandated, but best practice every 2-3 years (FMCSA expects supervisors to remain "knowledgeable")

- **JJ Keller Reasonable Suspicion** — online + self-paced

# Smith System vs Other Defensive Driving Programs

Defensive driving programs differ in methodology, content, delivery, and cost. The right choice depends on fleet size, operational profile, and learning preferences.

## Smith System
- 5 keys to safety methodology
- Industry standard for many large fleets
- In-person classroom + on-road instruction
- Certified instructor (Smith-certified or in-house)
- Cost: ~$50-100/driver one-time training; certification typically $500-1500
- Pros: proven methodology, recognized credentials
- Cons: requires Smith-certified instructor, classroom logistics

## CarriersEdge
- Online courses with video + interactive

- Self-paced delivery
- Cost: ~$10-15/driver/month for subscription
- Pros: scalable, low logistic burden, fleet-wide rollout
- Cons: less interactive than instructor-led

## JJ Keller Training (Encompass)
- Comprehensive LMS (200+ courses)
- DOT specifics + general safety
- Self-paced or instructor-led
- Cost: ~$15-25/driver/month
- Pros: largest course library, integrated with JJ Keller compliance tools

name: Train Workplace Accident Investigation Training
q: Use this skill to develop the capability to investigate crashes internally
body:
# Workplace Accident Investigation Training

When a crash occurs, the carrier's investigation matters for: insurance claim, FMCSA Crash Preventability Determination Program, lessons learned, regulatory response. Train someone in your fleet to do this.

## Investigation steps
1. **Within 24 hours**: secure documentation (police report, photos, dashcam footage, ELD data, driver statement)
2. **Within 7 days**: interview driver + witnesses
3. **Within 14 days**: technical analysis (vehicle condition, equipment failure investigation)
4. **Within 30 days**: written summary (preventability assessment, lessons learned)

## What to look for
- Police report details
- Citations issued (if any)
- ELD data leading up to crash
- Dashcam footage
- Vehicle inspection of involved unit
- Weather + road conditions
- Driver's HOS status
- Driver's history (prior crashes, violations)
- Mechanical condition of vehicle

## Preventability assessment
- Driver had reasonable opportunity to avoid crash → Preventable
- Driver had limited reasonable opportunity → Possibly preventable
- Driver had no reasonable opportunity → Not preventable

This determination supports the FMCSA Crash Preventability Determination Program filing.

## When to escalate
- Fatal crash → outside expert immediately (insurance, attorney, expert witness)
- Multi-vehicle pile-up → outside expert
- Hazmat release → outside expert + regulatory notification
- Conflicting accounts → outside expert
- Significant property damage → outside expert

## Internal investigator qualification
- Experience handling crashes (not first investigation)
- Understanding of CMV operations
- Familiarity with FMCSA regulations
- Photography + documentation skills
- Interview skills
- Written report writing

## Documentation retention
- All investigation materials retained per FMCSA 1-year + 6 months rule (vehicles + accidents)
- Insurance claim copies retained as long as insurer requires
- Settlement records retained per state statute of limitations

## Compass support
Compass Accidents module:
- Investigation checklist by crash type
- Document upload (photos, statements, reports)
- Preventability determination filing
- Lessons-learned distribution to other drivers

name: Truck Financing And Leasing
q: Use this skill when the user asks about truck purchase financing, leasing options, factoring, fuel s
body:
# Truck Financing and Leasing

Financing decisions affect cash flow, balance-sheet treatment, and ultimately the carrier's ability to maintain compliance under `Part 390`. This skill covers the common financing structures for small-to-mid motor carriers.

## Cash purchase
- No interest cost
- Highest depreciation tax deduction (`Section 179`, bonus depreciation)
- Ties up working capital
- Best when carrier has $200K+ idle cash and an existing tax position

## Bank or credit-union loan
- Typical term: 4–6 years for new tractor, 3–4 for used
- Down payment: 10–25% depending on credit and operating history
- Title held by lender until payoff
- Interest deductible as a business expense
- Best for: established carriers with 2+ years of operating history and bank relationship

## Dealer/captive financing (PACCAR Financial, Daimler, Volvo)
- Promotional rates on new tractors
- Fast underwriting
- Sometimes higher rates than independent banks for credit-challenged buyers

## Equipment finance lease (capital lease)
- Lease with $1 buyout or fair-market-value buyout
- On balance sheet (ASC 842)
- Depreciation claimed by lessee
- Common in trucking; effectively a loan with different accounting

## TRAC lease (Terminal Rental Adjustment Clause)
- Common for commercial trucks
- Lower monthly than purchase
- Residual risk to lessee at end of term
- Useful for fleets cycling trucks every 3–4 years

## Operating lease / full-service lease (Penske, Ryder, NationaLease)
- Truck not on balance sheet (small lessees)
- Includes maintenance, often roadside, sometimes substitute trucks
- Highest per-month cost but predictable
- Useful for carriers that lack in-house shop or want hands-off equipment management

## Factoring (not financing, but cash-flow related)
- Sell invoices for 1.5–4% to access cash in 24–48 hours
- Useful when broker pays net-30+ and carrier needs faster cash cycle
- Recourse vs non-recourse factoring affects risk

## Fuel cards
- WEX, Comdata, EFS, RTS, Pilot/Flying J
- Negotiated discounts at fuel stops
- Reporting integration with accounting

## Common errors
- Stretching loan term beyond the truck's useful life
- Lease-purchase programs marketed to owner-operators with predatory residuals
- Not modeling total cost (including DEF, maintenance, insurance) when comparing purchase vs full-service lease

name: Trucker Mental Health Resources
q: Use when a driver or carrier asks about trucker mental health — depression, isolation, stress, fatig
body:
# Trucker Mental Health Resources

Driver mental health is a documented safety factor. While `Part 379` covers driver records broadly and there is no specific CFR mental-health mandate, fatigue, isolation, and stress affect HOS compliance, crash risk, and turnover. This skill catalogs available resources.

## Why this matters operationally
- Fatigue-related crashes correlate with depression and sleep disorders
- Driver turnover (typically 70–90% industry-wide) is partially driven by isolation and burnout
- A driver in crisis is a Hours-of-Service risk and a CSA risk
- Some insurance carriers offer premium credits for documented wellness programs

## National crisis resources
- **988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline** — call or text 988
- **SAMHSA National Helpline** — 1-800-662-4357 (substance abuse and mental health)
- **Crisis Text Line** — text HOME to 741741
- **Veterans Crisis Line** — call 988, press 1

## Trucking-specific organizations
- **Trucker Buddy International** — driver community connection
- **St. Christopher Truckers Relief Fund** — financial aid for medical hardships
- **Truckers Final Mile** — assistance for families after driver fatalities
- **Truckers Against Trafficking** — anti-trafficking training (related but separate)

## What carriers can do
1. Include EAP (Employee Assistance Program) in driver benefits — many EAPs cost $2–5 per employee per month
2. Train dispatchers to recognize warning signs (mood changes, missed check-ins, increased HOS violations)
3. Build a peer-support network — senior drivers as mentors
4. Encourage sleep apnea screening (separate from FMCSA medical exam but related to fatigue)
5. Plan home-time policies that fit family life
6. Provide healthy lifestyle resources (Rolling Strong, Trucking Solutions Group)

## Sleep apnea — the related medical issue
- Estimated 28–30% of CDL drivers have moderate-to-severe sleep apnea
- FMCSA does not currently mandate screening but medical examiners can require evaluation under `§ 391.41`
- Treated apnea (CPAP compliance documented) keeps the medical card valid

## Common errors
- Treating wellness as a poster on the wall, not a program
- Punishing drivers who report mental health struggles
- No anonymous reporting channel

name: Trucking Insurance 101
q: Use this skill when the user asks about trucking insurance — types of coverage (commercial auto, car
body:
# Trucking Insurance 101

Trucking insurance has multiple coverage layers and a unique federal endorsement (MCS-90) required for interstate motor carriers under `Part 387`. This skill covers the standard policies a small-to-mid carrier needs.

## Required by federal law
- **Commercial auto liability** — federal minimums per `§ 387.9`:
  - General freight: **$750,000**
  - Oil cargo (private/for-hire): **$1,000,000**
  - Other hazmat: **$5,000,000**
  - Passenger carriers: varies
- Most shippers and brokers require **$1,000,000** regardless of cargo
- **MCS-90 endorsement** — attaches to the auto liability policy; ensures public protection if standard coverage is denied for the loss

## Cargo insurance
- Not federally required for most general freight
- Typical limit: **$100,000**
- Required by brokers and most shippers
- Covers freight in the carrier's care, custody, and control
- Exclusions to watch: theft (often sub-limited), hazmat, high-value commodities

## General liability
- $1M typical limit
- Covers premises and operations not involving the vehicle
- Required by most shippers as additional insured

## Physical damage (collision + comprehensive)
- Optional for owned equipment but required by lender
- Insures the truck and trailer
- Deductibles typically $1,000–$5,000

## Trailer interchange / non-owned trailer
- Covers liability and physical damage when the carrier pulls trailers it does not own
- Required for drop-and-hook operations

## Workers compensation
- Required by state law in most states (varies by state — see Workers Comp For Trucking)
- Some states allow owner-operator opt-out under specific structures

## Bobtail / non-trucking liability
- For owner-operators leased to a carrier — covers liability when truck is operated without a load (off-dispatch)

## Occupational accident
- Alternative to workers comp for 1099 owner-operators in states that allow it
- Not equivalent to workers comp in all respects

## How premiums are set
- Loss runs (5-year claim history)
- CSA scores
- Driver MVR quality
- Radius of operations
- Cargo type
- Years in business
- Fleet age and equipment

## Common errors
- Buying minimum coverage when shipper contracts require higher limits
- Lapsing MCS-90 — leads to FMCSA out-of-service of operating authority
- Not adding additional insured for shipper contracts
- Misclassifying drivers (1099 vs W-2) — affects workers comp exposure

- **49 CFR § 387.7** (financial responsibility for motor carriers)

name: Veh Brake System Compliance Checks
q: Use this skill for vehicle brake system inspection requirements
body:
# Brake System Compliance Checks

Brake system is the #1 cited area in roadside inspections. § 393.40 sets construction standards; § 396.3 and § 396.17 set maintenance and inspection.

## What brake checks must occur
1. **Pre-trip** (§ 392.7) — every trip
2. **Post-trip (DVIR)** (§ 396.11) — every duty day
3. **Annual inspection** (§ 396.17) — comprehensive
4. **Periodic inspection** between annuals — carrier's program (typically every 30-90 days)

## Pre-trip brake check
- Air pressure builds + holds (governor cuts off ~120 psi)
- Brakes work in service position
- Brakes work in spring (parking) position
- Brake light functioning
- Air drained from tanks weekly

## DVIR triggers for brakes
- Reduced braking distance
- Pulling to one side
- Squealing or grinding
- Air loss
- Brake light malfunction

## Annual inspection brake requirements
- Each axle brake performance test
- Slack adjuster check (within tolerance per FMCSA Appendix G)
- Brake hose and tubing integrity
- Brake shoe + drum measurements
- Wheel-end inspection for leaks

## Out-of-adjustment rule
A brake is considered "out of service" if more than 20% of brakes on a vehicle are out of adjustment. Compass + maintenance log should track this.

## Common brake violations
- Slack adjuster out of tolerance
- Brake hose contact with another component
- Brake shoe excessive wear
- Air pressure cutoff issues
- Anti-lock brake malfunction lamp on

## Compass tracking
Compass Vehicles module:
- Tracks annual inspection completion + next due
- Flags vehicles with documented brake issues
- Calculates carrier's brake-violation rate vs peer group

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 396.3**
- **49 CFR § 396.17**
- **49 CFR § 393.40**

name: Veh Pmi Schedule Trigger Mileage
q: Use this skill to design a vehicle preventive maintenance schedule
body:
# Setting Your PM Schedule by Trigger Mileage

Per § 396.3, carriers must have a written PM program. Manufacturers recommend specific intervals; carriers decide their actual schedule.

## Manufacturer recommendations (typical Class 8)
- **Engine oil/filter change**: every 25,000-35,000 miles (synthetic) or 10,000-15,000 miles (mineral)
- **Air filter**: every 50,000-75,000 miles
- **Fuel filter**: every 50,000 miles
- **Coolant**: every 100,000-200,000 miles
- **Transmission oil**: every 100,000-150,000 miles
- **Differential lube**: every 100,000-200,000 miles
- **Brake adjustment**: every 50,000 miles or monthly
- **Tire rotation**: every 25,000-50,000 miles

## Carrier customization
- More frequent if:
  - Severe duty (construction, off-road, heavy idling)
  - High annual mileage (>120K)
  - High-heat operating environment
  - Vehicle-specific issues (driver complaints, prior failures)
- Less frequent if:
  - Light highway-only duty
  - Lower mileage (<60K/year)
  - Well-maintained fleet with good driver care

## Required PM program elements
- Written PM schedule
- Triggers (mileage AND/OR time)
- Approval process for skipping PM
- Documentation (PM completed event)
- Driver pre-trip role

## How Compass automates this
Compass Vehicles module:
- Defines PM schedule per vehicle (or per fleet)
- Tracks current mileage from ELD or manual input
- Calculates next-due dates based on triggers
- Generates work orders for PM events
- Logs completed PMs in maintenance history

## What auditors look for
- Written PM schedule exists
- PM events recorded chronologically
- Driver pre-trip notes referenced (driver-identified issues addressed)
- Maintenance staff or vendor signatures
- Receipts/invoices for major PM work

## Common errors
- PM schedule written but not followed
- Mileage tracking missed (ELD not connected to PM system)
- PM events not documented (just done verbally)
- Same template PM regardless of operating conditions

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 396.3**

name: Veh Pre Trip Inspection Coaching
q: Use this skill for training drivers on effective pre-trip inspection technique
body:
# Pre-Trip Inspection Coaching

A proper pre-trip inspection per § 392.7 + § 396.13 takes 15-20 minutes done right. Driver compliance varies; coaching improves both safety and CSA scores.

## What § 392.7 requires
Driver must inspect, examine, and verify:
- Service brakes (operation)
- Parking brake (operation)
- Steering mechanism (operation)
- Lighting devices + reflectors
- Tires (visible damage, inflation, tread)
- Horn
- Windshield wipers
- Rear-vision mirrors
- Coupling devices
- Wheels + rims
- Emergency equipment

## What § 396.13 requires
Driver must be satisfied that:
- Service brakes can stop the vehicle within 60 ft from 20 mph
- Parking brake holds against the engine
- Steering wheel turns vehicle without binding
- All lighting works
- Tires are sound
- All required emergency equipment is on the vehicle

## Driver training approach
- **15-minute physical inspection** of vehicle systems
- **Step-by-step checklist** (use a printed or app-based card)
- **Visual + manual inspection** (look + touch + activate)
- **Driver-completed sign-off**

## Common driver shortcuts (and how to coach)
- Skip wheel-end / hub inspection → coach to check oil + visible leaks
- Skip undercarriage check → coach to look under for hanging components
- Skip brake adjustment by hand → coach to check at next chance during the day
- Skip emergency equipment check → coach to verify each item present

## Pre-trip + post-trip documentation
- Driver signs off the pre-trip on RODS or paper log
- Post-trip is the DVIR if defects exist (no-defect post-trip not required)
- Inspector at roadside may ask "did you do a pre-trip?" — driver must say yes
- Inspector may verify by reviewing vehicle condition

## Compass support
Compass HOS + Vehicles modules:
- Pre-trip checklist available on driver app
- Pre-trip completion logged automatically
- Defect-found triggers DVIR
- Carrier review of common driver shortcuts (pattern detection)

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 392.7**
- **49 CFR § 396.13**

name: Veh Tire Tread Depth Requirements
q: Use this skill to understand FMCSA tire tread depth requirements
body:
# Tire Tread Depth Federal Requirements

Per § 393.75, tire tread must meet minimum depth standards. Specific differences by axle position.

## Minimum depths
- **Steer tires**: 4/32 of an inch
- **Other axles** (drive, trailer): 2/32 of an inch
- **Hazmat-placarded vehicles**: special requirements (5/32 + on steer)

## How to measure
- Use a tire tread gauge or coin test
- Measure in two adjacent grooves
- Measure at multiple points around the tire
- Take the lowest depth reading

## When measurement matters
- DVIR pre-trip inspection
- Annual DOT inspection
- Roadside inspection
- Pre-departure trip check

## What inspectors look for
- Tread depth in adjacent grooves
- Cuts, punctures, or sidewall damage
- Ply separation (visible)
- Mismatched tire sizes
- Excessive wear pattern (indicating misalignment)

## Tire age vs tread depth
- New tires: typically 22/32-32/32 tread
- Replace tires when:
  - Steer at or below 4/32 (federal minimum + safety margin)
  - Other at or below 2/32 (federal minimum)
  - Damage requires replacement
  - Excessive wear pattern (typically 4+ years for steer)

## Cost-benefit
- A typical Class 8 steer tire = $400-700; lasts 80-100K miles
- Premature replacement adds $$$; late replacement risks OOS

## Common tire violations
- Tread depth below minimum
- Sidewall damage
- Bead/cap separation
- Mismatched tires on dual position
- Improper inflation

## Compass tracking
Compass Vehicles module:
- Tracks tire age by VIN
- Logs replacement events
- Flags vehicles approaching tread minimums based on usage

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 393.75**

name: Veh Trailer Only Inspection

body:
# Trailer-Only Inspection (Standalone Trailer)

A standalone trailer (not coupled to a tractor) still requires periodic inspection. The carrier owns the inspection responsibility.

## Annual inspection (same as tractor)
- Required every 12 months
- Conducted by a qualified inspector
- Covers brakes, lights, hubs, structure, body, suspension
- Certificate retained in trailer file

## Pre-trip inspection of trailer
- Driver coupling to a trailer inspects the trailer at coupling
- Brake hose connections, lights, glass, mirrors
- Body integrity, latches, doors

## When trailer is parked
- Not subject to daily DVIR (only when in operation)
- Annual inspection still required regardless of parking time
- Lights, tires, structure visible from outside should be checked weekly

## Trailer ownership scenarios
- **Owned trailer** — carrier is responsible for inspection
- **Leased trailer** — depending on lease, lessor may be responsible (read the lease)
- **Hired trailer (drayage, intermodal)** — operator/owner responsible

## Trailer maintenance records
Required per § 396.3:
- Last annual inspection
- Last preventive maintenance event
- Last repairs
- Hub lubrication
- Lighting and electrical work

## Inspection at non-traditional times
- Before long-term storage (180+ days inactive)
- After unusual wear pattern noticed
- Following accident or impact event
- When carrier identifies trailer in trouble pool

## Compass Vehicles tracking
- Trailer fleet visible in main vehicle inventory
- Annual inspection due tracked per VIN
- Coupling event auto-logs pre-trip
- Inactivity flag for trailers inactive 180+ days

## CFR citations

name: Veh Used Vehicle Compliance Verification

body:
# Used Vehicle Compliance Verification at Purchase

A used vehicle should be inspected and verified compliant before integrating into the fleet. Hidden issues become carrier liability immediately.

## Pre-purchase inspection
- Annual DOT inspection on file (within 12 months)
- Recent service records
- Title clean (no salvage, no flood)
- Mileage verification
- Inspection report from independent mechanic

## Documents to obtain
- Annual inspection certificate
- Service history (oil changes, brake work, major repairs)
- Title (clean)
- VIN check (CARFAX or equivalent for commercial vehicles)
- Prior carrier's DOT number history (to check for major incidents)

## Hidden issues to look for
- Frame damage hidden by paint
- Engine block welding or shoddy repairs
- Brake friction surface excessive wear
- Tire age (DOT date code) regardless of tread
- Suspension wear (especially leaf springs)
- Wheel-end leaks not addressed
- Lighting fixtures recently swapped

## Post-purchase actions
1. Full DOT inspection by your mechanic
2. Brake adjustment check
3. Tire age verification (consider re-tiring soon)
4. Maintenance file setup (start fresh with PM schedule)
5. Lighting + reflector verification
6. ELD installation (if needed)
7. Annual inspection if more than 12 months old

## What NOT to skip
- Verify VIN matches title and registration
- Verify accident history (police record, insurance claim history)
- Verify any FMCSA violations against the vehicle
- Verify previous carrier had no compliance issues

Compass Vehicles module:
- New-vehicle wizard for purchase + integration
- PM schedule starts fresh
- Annual inspection due date set

- Inspection record + DataQ flags pre-loaded for prior incidents

name: Veh Wheel End Lubricant Inspection
q: Use this skill for wheel-end maintenance and lubrication
body:
# Wheel-End / Lubricant Inspection

Wheel-ends are a high-risk component. A wheel-off-axle event can be fatal. Inspection and maintenance per § 396.3.

## Types of wheel-end design
- **Oil bath** — wheel hub filled with oil, sealed with O-ring
- **Grease packed** — hub packed with grease, sealed with bearing dust shield
- **Oil-bath with breather** — slight ventilation to prevent pressure buildup

## What to inspect
- **Oil level** (oil-bath designs) — usually visible through fill hole or sight glass
- **Visible leaks** — oil running down rim or onto tire
- **Bearing temperature** — excessive heat indicates failure
- **Wheel play** — should be minimal
- **Wheel run-out** — wobble indicates imbalance or bearing wear

## Lubricant interval
- Manufacturer recommendation typically every 50,000-100,000 miles
- Different oils have different lifespans
- Driver should check oil level at every weekly fuel-and-inspection

## Wheel-off cases
A wheel-off-axle event is investigated as:
- Manufacturer defect
- Maintenance shortfall (bearing failure)
- Operator error (overtorque, under-torque on lug nuts)
- Overloading

## Carrier responsibilities
- Maintenance log per § 396.3
- Track wheel-end lubricant changes
- Lug nut re-torque schedule (typically 50, 200, 500 miles after wheel-off-then-on)
- Annual inspection includes wheel-end check (§ 396.17)

## Compass tracking
Compass Vehicles module:
- Tracks wheel-end maintenance events
- Lubricant change scheduling
- Bearing inspection records

name: Vehicle Inspection Dvir

body:
# Vehicle Inspection and DVIR

Driver Vehicle Inspection Reports (DVIRs) and pre-trip inspections are core requirements under `Part 396`. They are the single most common roadside-inspection topic and a frequent CSA scoring driver in the Vehicle Maintenance BASIC.

## Pre-trip inspection (`§ 392.7`)
Before driving, the driver must be **satisfied** that the following are in good working order:
- Service brakes (including trailer brake connections)
- Parking brake
- Steering mechanism
- Lighting devices and reflectors
- Tires
- Horn
- Windshield wipers
- Rear-vision mirrors
- Coupling devices
- Wheels and rims
- Emergency equipment (`§ 393.95`)

## Post-trip DVIR (`§ 396.11`)
At the end of each driving day, the driver must prepare a written report covering the same items checked at pre-trip, plus any defects that affect safety or are likely to cause a breakdown:
- Report identifies the truck and trailer(s)
- Notes defects or "no defects" affirmative
- Driver signs and dates
- Submitted to motor carrier

## Carrier action on defects (`§ 396.11(b)`)
- Repair defects that affect safety before next dispatch
- Sign certification of repair (or no repair needed)
- Retain DVIR + repair certification **3 months** from date received

## In-cab inspection
Driver must also confirm shipping documents, last DVIR (and signed certification of repair if defects were noted), and required ELD malfunction materials are present.

## What "DVIR-required" means in practice
- Required at the END of each day driven
- Required even if no defects ("no defects" affirmative report)
- Trailer DVIRs also required if defects noted; "no defects" trailer DVIRs are optional under the post-2014 rule (`§ 396.11(a)(2)`)

## Common errors
- No-defect DVIRs missing (driver didn't submit anything)
- Defect noted but no repair certification
- Repair certification signed by someone unauthorized
- Pre-trip done after the truck moves (ELD shows driving before pre-trip)
- Brake adjustment slack outside tolerance not caught

## What auditors look for
- 3-month retention period met
- Defect-to-repair chain documented end-to-end
- DVIR signed by driver
- Repair certification signed by qualified personnel
- Trailer DVIRs present when defects existed

name: Weigh Station Bypass Services
q: Use this skill when the user asks about weigh-station bypass services — Drivewyze, PrePass, BestPass
body:
# Weigh Station Bypass Services

Weigh station bypass services let qualifying carriers skip open weigh stations, saving fuel and time. They are not regulatory exemptions — the carrier still meets all CSA, weight, and HOS rules under `Part 385`. This skill compares the three main services.

## How bypass works
- Transponder in the cab communicates with state weigh-station systems
- State system checks the carrier's CSA scores, IFTA status, registration, and weight
- Green light: bypass; red light: must enter the scale
- Most state systems require a CSA scorecard better than a threshold (typically ISS score below 75)

## Drivewyze
- App-based (no hardware required) and ELD-integrated options
- Largest state network (40+ states)
- Monthly subscription model
- Free service for some safety alerts
- Strong integration with major ELD providers

## PrePass
- Older, hardware-based service
- Strong in California and western states
- Weight pre-clearance at some scales
- INFORM electronic credentialing

## BestPass
- Toll-management focus (also tolls in addition to bypass)
- Bundles tolls, bypass, and reporting
- Useful for fleets with heavy toll exposure (Northeast US)

## Eligibility criteria carriers should know
- Up-to-date IRP and IFTA
- Insurance current
- CSA scores below state-specific thresholds
- No federal out-of-service order
- Vehicle weight under registered weight

## What bypass does NOT do
- It does not exempt from random roadside inspections
- It does not change CSA scoring
- A red light means enter — drivers who pass it commit a violation
- It does not relieve weight or oversize/overweight permit requirements

## ROI math (rule of thumb)
- Time saved per bypass: 5–15 minutes
- Fuel saved per bypass: 0.3–0.5 gallons
- A driver hitting 100 scales per month, 80% bypass rate, saves substantial annual hours and fuel

## Common errors
- Subscribing without verifying CSA scores meet bypass thresholds
- Ignoring a red light (citation + possible CSA inspection)
- Multiple devices in one cab causing conflicts

name: Workers Comp For Trucking
q: Use this skill when the user asks about workers compensation for trucking — required by state law, c
body:
# Workers Compensation for Trucking

Workers compensation is governed by **state law**, not by 49 CFR. Each state requires employers (in most cases) to carry workers comp insurance for employees. This skill covers the trucking-specific considerations.

## State requirements vary widely
- **Most states**: workers comp required when the carrier has 1+ employees
- **Texas**: non-subscriber option (employer can opt out but loses tort defenses)
- **Some states**: corporate officers and owner-operators have election options
- Penalties for going without coverage can include criminal charges, fines, and stop-work orders

## Why trucking premiums are high
- High injury rates (lifting, falls from deck, crashes)
- Long claim duration when injuries occur
- Class code typically 7228 (long-haul) or 7219 (short-haul) — high rates
- Premiums based on payroll × class rate × experience modifier (EMR)

## How to control premium
1. **Safety program documented** — handbooks, training, meetings
2. **Return-to-work program** — light-duty assignments speed recovery and reduce claim cost
3. **Strong claims management** — report immediately, manage medical providers
4. **Driver hiring** — MVR, PSP, drug screen quality reduces injury risk
5. **DOT compliance** — clean CSA, clean inspection record helps premium
6. **Loss-sensitive plans** — deductible plans or captives for larger fleets

## Independent contractor (1099) vs employee (W-2)
- W-2 drivers: workers comp required
- 1099 owner-operators: usually carry their own occupational accident coverage
- **Misclassification is a major liability area** — state agencies and the IRS have aggressive enforcement
- Owner-operators leased to a carrier under `§ 376` still raise misclassification questions

## Occupational accident vs workers comp
- Occ Acc is a private policy, not state-mandated workers comp
- Lower premium
- More limited benefits (caps on lost wages, medical, death)
- Some states do not consider Occ Acc equivalent to workers comp
- Owner-operators often rely on Occ Acc; carrier should verify and document

## What to do when an injury occurs
1. Get the driver medical attention
2. Report to the carrier within 24 hours
3. File the first report of injury (FROI) per state deadline (usually 7–14 days)
4. Drug and alcohol test if post-accident criteria met (`§ 382.303`)
5. Document the scene and witnesses
6. Coordinate with carrier safety + insurance adjuster

## Common errors
- Misclassifying drivers as 1099 when they meet IRS / state employee tests
- Letting WC policy lapse (state-by-state penalty cascade)
- Not reporting injuries promptly (denial risk)
- No return-to-work program (longer claims = higher EMR)

- **State workers compensation statutes** (not in 49 CFR)
- **49 CFR Part 382** (D&A program; post-accident testing intersects with WC)
- **49 CFR Part 376** (leased equipment) — context for owner-operator classification

name: Class 1 Explosives Divisions
body:
# Hazmat Class 1 — Explosives Divisions

Class 1 (explosives) under the Hazardous Materials Regulations covers six divisions ranked by mass-explosion and fire hazard. Transport is regulated by `49 CFR Parts 172–180`. Most for-hire motor carriers do not move Division 1.1 or 1.2 without specialized hazmat authority.

## The six divisions
- **Division 1.1** — substances with a **mass-explosion hazard** (almost the entire load can detonate together). Examples: TNT, dynamite
- **Division 1.2** — projection hazard but not mass-explosion. Examples: certain detonators, some ammunition
- **Division 1.3** — fire hazard with minor blast or projection. Examples: certain propellants, display fireworks
- **Division 1.4** — minor explosion hazard, effects confined to package. Examples: consumer fireworks (1.4G), small-arms ammo (1.4S)
- **Division 1.5** — very insensitive substances with mass-explosion hazard. Examples: blasting agents
- **Division 1.6** — extremely insensitive articles with no mass-explosion hazard

## Authority required
- **Hazardous Materials Safety Permit (HMSP)** required under `Part 385` Subpart E for Division 1.1, 1.2, certain 1.3, and some other extreme hazards
- HMSP applicants must hold a Satisfactory safety rating

## Driver requirements
- CDL with **Hazardous Materials (H)** endorsement (`§ 383.93`)
- TSA background check
- Hazmat training under `§ 172.704` (general awareness, function-specific, safety, security awareness, in-depth security plan)
- Recurrent training every 3 years

## Placarding and marking
- **EXPLOSIVES 1.x** placards on all four sides of the vehicle
- Compatibility groups (letters A–S) determine what can be loaded together (`§ 177.848`)
- UN identification numbers on placards or orange panels

## Documentation
- Shipping papers with proper shipping name, hazard class, UN number, packing group
- **Emergency response information** per `§ 172.602` (ERG entry or equivalent)
- 24-hour emergency response phone number
- Driver carries documents within reach

## Routing
- **Designated routes** required (`§ 397.67`); avoid tunnels and certain bridges
- Pre-trip route plan filed and retained
- Attendance and surveillance rules under `§ 397.5`

## Common errors
- Loading incompatible compatibility groups in the same vehicle
- Missing HMSP for required loads
- Driver leaves vehicle unattended in violation of `§ 397.5`
- Outdated H endorsement

name: Class 2 1 Flammable Gas
body:
# Hazmat Division 2.1 — Flammable Gas

Division 2.1 covers gases that are flammable in air. Common examples include propane (UN1075), hydrogen, methane, acetylene, butane, and refrigerants in flammable form. Transport rules are in `49 CFR Parts 172–180`.

## Definition (`§ 173.115`)
A gas is Division 2.1 if at 20°C and 101.3 kPa it is:
- Ignitable in a mixture of 13% or less by volume with air, OR
- Has a flammable range with air of at least 12 percentage points

## Common UN numbers
- **UN1075** Petroleum gases, liquefied (LPG, propane)
- **UN1978** Propane
- **UN1971** Methane
- **UN1049** Hydrogen
- **UN1011** Butane
- **UN1001** Acetylene, dissolved

## Placarding
- **FLAMMABLE GAS** placard (red, flame symbol)
- 1,001 lbs aggregate gross weight rule for Table 2
- UN number on placard or orange panel

## Authorized packagings
- **DOT cylinders** per `Part 178` Subpart C (3A, 3AA, 3AL, 4BA, etc.)
- **DOT cargo tanks** — MC 331 most common for propane in bulk
- **Portable tanks** — DOT Specification or UN portable

## Cargo tank specifics for LPG
- **MC 331** specification cargo tanks
- Periodic external visual annually
- Internal visual every 5 years (or per service requirements)
- Pressure tests as required
- Emergency discharge controls (`§ 173.315`)

## Driver and training
- CDL with **H** endorsement (`§ 383.93`)
- **N (tank)** endorsement if cargo tank over 1,000 gallons
- **X (combined)** if both
- Hazmat training (`§ 172.704`)
- Cargo tank-specific training for cargo tank operations

## Emergency response
- ERG Guide 115 for most flammable gases
- Eliminate ignition sources
- 1-mile evacuation downwind for large fires
- Cylinder BLEVE risk in fire

## Common errors
- Cylinders not secured to prevent rolling and falling
- Improperly fitted regulators on cylinders in transit
- Missing N endorsement when cargo tank requires it
- Cargo tank emergency discharge not tested

name: Class 2 3 Poison Inhalation Hazard
body:
# Hazmat Division 2.3 — Poison Inhalation Hazard Gases

Division 2.3 covers gases known to be toxic or corrosive to humans (gas form). These materials carry the **Poison Inhalation Hazard (PIH)** designation and the strictest hazmat transport rules under `49 CFR Parts 172–180`.

## Definition (`§ 173.115(c)`)
A gas is Division 2.3 if:
- Known to be toxic enough to humans to pose a health hazard during transport, OR
- In the absence of adequate human data, presumed toxic based on animal LC50 data

## Hazard Zones (`§ 173.116`)
Division 2.3 gases are assigned to **Hazard Zones A through D** based on LC50:
- **Zone A**: most toxic (LC50 ≤ 200 ppm)
- **Zone B**: LC50 > 200 to ≤ 1,000 ppm
- **Zone C**: LC50 > 1,000 to ≤ 3,000 ppm
- **Zone D**: LC50 > 3,000 to ≤ 5,000 ppm

## Common UN numbers
- **UN1005** Anhydrous ammonia (Zone D in many cases; Zone C in others)
- **UN1017** Chlorine (Zone B)
- **UN1076** Phosgene (Zone A)
- **UN1067** Dinitrogen tetroxide (Zone A)

## Placarding
- **POISON GAS** or **TOXIC GAS** placard on all four sides
- UN number displayed on placard or orange panel
- White square-on-point background for **PIH** in some configurations

## Authority and permits
- **Hazardous Materials Safety Permit (HMSP)** required under `Part 385` Subpart E for PIH materials in quantities exceeding 3,500 gallons or specific thresholds
- Carrier must hold Satisfactory safety rating

## Driver and training
- CDL with **H** endorsement
- TSA security threat assessment
- Hazmat training (`§ 172.704`) including security plan elements
- PIH-specific function training

## Routing and security
- Designated routes per `§ 397.71`
- **Security plan** required under `§ 172.802` for PIH
- Attendance and surveillance per `§ 397.5`
- Emergency response information accessible

## Documentation
- Shipping papers with PIH designation and Hazard Zone
- 24-hour emergency response phone number
- Driver acknowledges PIH on the document
- ERG cross-reference

## Common errors
- Not declaring Hazard Zone on the shipping paper
- Missing HMSP for required quantities
- Driver lacking TSA security threat assessment
- Vehicle unattended in violation of `§ 397.5`

name: Class 2 Propane Lpg Tanker
body:
# Class 2 Propane / LPG Tanker Operations

LPG and propane (UN1075, UN1978) are Division 2.1 flammable gases. Bulk transport uses **MC 331 cargo tanks** under `49 CFR Parts 172–180`. This skill covers the operational and compliance specifics for LPG tankers.

## Cargo tank specification — MC 331
- High-pressure cargo tank (working pressures 250–315 psi typical)
- Construction per `§ 178.337`
- Required equipment: pressure relief, emergency discharge valves, gauging device, thermometer well
- Internal and external piping per spec

## Required tests and inspections
- **External visual**: every 1 year
- **Internal visual**: every 5 years
- **Hydrostatic test or alternative**: every 5 years (V test)
- **Lining inspection**: not typical for LPG (lined for other commodities)
- **Pressure relief valve**: every 5 years
- **Emergency discharge control test**: per `§ 180.405`
- All test reports retained while tank is in service plus 2 years

## Driver endorsements
- CDL with **N (Tanker)** endorsement
- **H (Hazmat)** endorsement with TSA background check
- Combined **X** endorsement covers both
- Hazmat training (`§ 172.704`) plus cargo tank function-specific training

## Loading and unloading
- Bonding and grounding before transfer
- Driver **attendance required** during loading/unloading (`§ 177.834`)
- Wheel chocks set
- Emergency discharge controls operable
- No unauthorized ignition sources within the area
- Posted emergency shutoff procedures

## Placarding
- **FLAMMABLE GAS** placard on all four sides
- **UN1075** or **UN1978** displayed
- Markings per `Part 172` Subpart D

## Emergency response
- ERG Guide 115
- Initial evacuation: 100 m (330 ft) all directions for small leaks
- Large fire: 1-mile downwind evacuation
- BLEVE risk if tank exposed to fire

## Routing
- **No tunnel** restrictions where posted
- Limited access to certain bridges and structures
- Many states require designated hazmat routes

## Common errors
- Loading without grounding/bonding
- Emergency discharge valves not tested per schedule
- Driver leaves the tank unattended during transfer
- Periodic test expired (MC 331 tanks have visible test markings)

name: Class 3 Flammable Liquid Cargo Tank Loading
body:
# Class 3 Flammable Liquid Cargo Tank Loading

Loading and unloading flammable liquid (Class 3) cargo tanks is among the highest-risk hazmat operations. Rules in `49 CFR Parts 172–180` cover personnel attendance, bonding/grounding, vapor control, and emergency procedures.

## Tank specifications for flammable liquid
- **DOT 406** — most common for gasoline, diesel, ethanol
- **DOT 407** — chemical liquid (lower pressure)
- **MC 306** — predecessor, still in service
- Tank must show current test markings

## Required tests on DOT 406 / MC 306
- **External visual**: every year
- **Internal visual**: every 5 years
- **Lining inspection** (if lined): annually
- **Hydrostatic / pressure test (P)**: every 5 years
- **Leakage test (K)**: every year
- **Pressure relief valves**: every year

## Loading procedures
1. **Position vehicle** away from ignition sources; engine off (with limited exceptions)
2. **Chock wheels** before leaving the cab
3. **Bonding and grounding** to the loading rack — verify continuity (`§ 177.837`)
4. **Driver attendance required** at all times during loading (`§ 177.834`)
5. **Vapor recovery** connected where required (EPA + state)
6. **Top-loading vs bottom-loading**: bottom-loading preferred for static control
7. **Outage / ullage**: leave required outage per `§ 173.24a`
8. **Verify compartment levels** before disconnecting
9. **Disconnect grounding** only after loading complete and vapor lines closed

## Documentation at loading
- Shipping paper prepared by shipper, accepted by driver
- Driver checks: proper shipping name, hazard class, UN number, quantity, ERG reference, 24-hour emergency phone
- Driver confirms quantity matches

## Placarding before leaving
- **FLAMMABLE 3** placard on all four sides
- UN number on placard or orange panel
- Subsidiary placards if applicable

## Unloading
- Same attendance, bonding, and grounding rules apply
- Vehicle positioned away from buildings, ignition
- No smoking within 25 feet
- Hose connections inspected before flow starts
- Driver remains within 25 feet and has unobstructed view

## Common errors
- Bonding clip attached to painted surface (no electrical continuity)
- Driver leaves cab during loading without setting chocks
- Driver away from vehicle during unloading
- Outage not verified — overfill risk
- Engine left running during transfer

name: Class 3 Flammable Liquid Specifics
body:
# Class 3 Flammable Liquid Specifics

Class 3 (flammable liquid) covers liquids with a flash point of not more than 60°C (140°F) under standard test methods. Rules are in `49 CFR Parts 172–180`. This skill covers identification, packing groups, and transport requirements.

## Definition (`§ 173.120`)
- **Flammable liquid**: flash point at or below 60°C (140°F)
- **Combustible liquid**: flash point above 60°C and below 93°C (200°F) — domestic transportation only by motor carrier may be classified as combustible if not otherwise hazardous

## Packing groups
- **PG I**: high danger (initial boiling point ≤ 35°C)
- **PG II**: medium danger (flash point < 23°C and initial boiling point > 35°C)
- **PG III**: low danger (flash point 23°C to 60°C and IBP > 35°C)

## Common UN numbers
- **UN1203** Gasoline
- **UN1202** Diesel fuel / fuel oil (often regulated as combustible domestically)
- **UN1170** Ethanol
- **UN1090** Acetone
- **UN1230** Methanol
- **UN1133** Adhesives, flammable
- **UN1263** Paint, flammable

## Placarding
- **FLAMMABLE 3** placard required
- Some PG III combustible liquids in non-bulk packaging may have reduced placarding requirements
- Bulk packaging always requires placard

## Authorized packagings
- **Non-bulk**: drums (1A1, 1A2), jerricans, IBCs (31A, 31HA)
- **Bulk**: DOT 406 cargo tanks for highway, DOT 407 for chemicals, IM 101/102 portable tanks

## Driver requirements
- CDL with **H** endorsement when placards required
- **N (tanker)** endorsement when in cargo tank > 1,000 gal
- Hazmat training under `§ 172.704`

## Segregation
- Avoid loading near oxidizers, organic peroxides, flammable gases — see segregation table at `§ 177.848`

## Documentation
- Shipping paper: proper shipping name, UN number, hazard class, packing group, quantity, ERG reference
- 24-hour emergency response phone

## Common errors
- Combustible liquids placarded as Class 3 unnecessarily, or vice versa
- IBC overfill (90% rule)
- Missing packing group on the shipping paper
- Drums not secured against shifting

name: Class 3 Fuel Tanker Specifics
body:
# Class 3 Fuel Tanker Specifics (Gasoline / Diesel / Ethanol)

Most Class 3 fuel haul in the United States involves gasoline, diesel, and ethanol blends. These loads use **DOT 406** cargo tanks and are subject to `49 CFR Parts 172–180`, EPA vapor recovery rules, and state-specific requirements.

## Common commodities
- **UN1203** Gasoline (Class 3, PG II)
- **UN1202** Diesel fuel / fuel oil (typically combustible liquid, NA1993 in some cases)
- **UN1170** Ethanol / Ethanol blends
- **UN3475** Ethanol gasoline mixture (>10% ethanol)
- **UN3473** Fuel cell cartridges, flammable liquid

## Cargo tank — DOT 406
- Multi-compartment configuration typical (3–5 compartments)
- MAWP typically 4 psi
- Vapor recovery piping
- Bottom loading and unloading via API valves
- Emergency shutoff valves

## Testing schedule on DOT 406
- **External visual** (V): annually
- **Internal visual** (I): every 5 years
- **Pressure test** (P): every 5 years
- **Leakage test** (K): annually
- **Lining inspection** (L): annually if lined
- **Pressure relief valve**: annually
- Test markings stenciled on the tank

## Loading at the rack
- Drive into bay, engine off (except for required PTO)
- Set chocks
- Bond and ground cable connected before opening any valve
- Driver attendance required (`§ 177.834`)
- Vapor recovery connected
- Top off to scheduled levels; do not exceed permitted outage

## Delivering to retail station
- Position truck to maintain clear escape route
- Driver remains within 25 feet of valves at all times
- Verify tank capacity at the station before opening
- No drop into wrong-grade tank (cross-drops are a major spill cause)
- Bonding/grounding to fill point

## Driver endorsements
- CDL with **N** (tanker) and **H** (hazmat)
- Or combined **X** endorsement
- TSA security threat assessment for H
- Recurrent hazmat training every 3 years (`§ 172.704`)

## Placarding
- **FLAMMABLE 3** with UN1203 or UN1202 on the placard
- All four sides of the cargo tank

## Spill response
- Stop the flow first
- Eliminate ignition sources
- Contain to drain protection (storm drains)
- Notify carrier dispatch
- National Response Center: 1-800-424-8802 for reportable spills
- State environmental hotline

## Common errors
- Cross-drops (premium gasoline into diesel tank or vice versa)
- Overfill (compartment over scheduled outage)
- Missing bonding cable
- Annual K test expired
- Driver away from vehicle during transfer
