Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 173.150** (Class 3 exceptions)
- **49 CFR § 178.345** (cargo tank construction)
- **49 CFR § 180.405** (testing)
- **49 CFR § 177.834**, **§ 177.837** (loading/unloading)

name: Class 4 Flammable Solids Pyrophoric
body:
# Hazmat Class 4 — Flammable Solids and Pyrophoric Materials

Class 4 includes substances that are flammable solids, spontaneously combustible, or dangerous when wet. Rules are in `49 CFR Parts 172–180`. The three divisions each behave differently and have separate handling rules.

## The three divisions
- **Division 4.1** — Flammable solids, self-reactive substances, polymerizing substances, solid desensitized explosives
- **Division 4.2** — Spontaneously combustible (pyrophoric or self-heating)
- **Division 4.3** — Dangerous when wet (emits flammable gases on contact with water)

## Common UN numbers
- **UN1325** Flammable solid, organic (4.1)
- **UN1944** Matches, safety (4.1)
- **UN1383** Pyrophoric metals (4.2)
- **UN1389** Alkali metal amalgam (4.3)
- **UN1428** Sodium (4.3)
- **UN1295** Trichlorosilane (4.3)
- **UN3208** Metallic substance, water-reactive (4.3)

## Placarding
- **FLAMMABLE SOLID** (4.1) — vertical red and white stripes
- **SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUSTIBLE** (4.2) — top white, bottom red
- **DANGEROUS WHEN WET** (4.3) — blue background, white flame
- All four sides of vehicle

## Storage and segregation (`§ 177.848`)
- 4.3 (water-reactive) kept away from any moisture
- 4.2 (pyrophoric) needs inert atmosphere or sealed packaging
- Avoid placing near Class 5 oxidizers
- Avoid placing near Class 3 flammable liquids

## Packaging
- Non-bulk: drums, jerricans, fiberboard or wooden boxes per UN spec
- IBCs sometimes authorized
- Bulk: limited; some materials require specific cargo tanks

## Driver requirements
- CDL with **H** endorsement
- TSA STA
- Hazmat training under `§ 172.704`
- Function-specific training on water-reactive handling if applicable

## Emergency response
- ERG Guides 133 (4.1), 135 (4.2), 138 (4.3)
- **Never** use water on Division 4.3
- Use dry chemical, sand, or special agents per ERG
- Evacuate downwind for spills generating flammable gases

## Common errors
- 4.3 packaging exposed to moisture in transit (truck leak, wet floor)
- Crews using water on a Division 4.3 spill
- Segregation violations with oxidizers (5.1)
- Loose packages allowing pyrophoric exposure

name: Class 5 Oxidizers Organic Peroxides
body:
# Hazmat Class 5 — Oxidizers and Organic Peroxides

Class 5 covers substances that intensify the combustion of other materials (oxidizers) and self-reactive organic peroxides. Rules are in `49 CFR Parts 172–180`. The two divisions behave differently and require strict segregation from flammable materials.

## The two divisions
- **Division 5.1** — Oxidizers (yield oxygen, intensify fire)
- **Division 5.2** — Organic peroxides (thermally unstable, may decompose violently)

## Common UN numbers
- **UN1942** Ammonium nitrate (5.1)
- **UN1454** Calcium nitrate (5.1)
- **UN1479** Oxidizing solid, n.o.s. (5.1)
- **UN2014** Hydrogen peroxide, aqueous solutions (5.1 or 8 depending on concentration)
- **UN3101** Organic peroxide type B, liquid (5.2)
- **UN3110** Organic peroxide type F, solid (5.2)

## Packing groups (5.1)
- **PG I**: strong oxidizer
- **PG II**: moderate oxidizer
- **PG III**: minor oxidizer

## Organic peroxide types (5.2)
- **Type A** — forbidden from transport
- **Type B–F** — authorized with increasing temperature controls
- Many require **temperature control** during transport (SADT — Self-Accelerating Decomposition Temperature)

## Temperature-controlled transport
- Organic peroxides requiring T-control must be shipped in equipment that maintains specified maximum temperature
- Emergency temperature also specified — if exceeded, emergency procedures triggered
- Driver monitoring and equipment alarms required

## Placarding
- **OXIDIZER 5.1** — yellow background, "O" flame symbol
- **ORGANIC PEROXIDE 5.2** — red and yellow halves, flame symbol
- All four sides

## Segregation (`§ 177.848`)
- **Never** load Class 5 with flammable liquids (3), flammable solids (4.1), or spontaneously combustible (4.2)
- Keep separated from organic combustibles
- Class 5 has more segregation requirements than most other classes

## Driver requirements
- CDL with **H** endorsement
- TSA STA
- Hazmat training (`§ 172.704`)
- Temperature monitoring procedure training for 5.2 T-controlled

## Emergency response
- ERG Guides 140–148 depending on material
- Oxidizer fires intensify with most fire suppressants — flood with water, large quantities
- Organic peroxide thermal runaway — evacuate, no firefighting
- Distance from fire critical

## Common errors
- Loading Class 5 with Class 3 flammable liquids (segregation violation)
- Temperature-control failure for Division 5.2
- Missing PG on shipping paper
- Wet packaging contaminating ammonium nitrate

name: Class 6 1 Toxic Substances
body:
# Hazmat Division 6.1 — Toxic Substances

Division 6.1 covers liquids and solids known or presumed to be toxic to humans. Rules under `49 CFR Parts 172–180`. Acute toxicity rather than corrosivity is the defining hazard.

## Definition (`§ 173.132`)
A material is Division 6.1 if it is known or presumed to cause death, serious injury, or human health damage if swallowed, inhaled (as dust/mist/vapor), or absorbed through skin.

## Packing groups
- **PG I**: high acute toxicity (oral LD50 ≤ 5 mg/kg, dermal ≤ 50 mg/kg, inhalation LC50 ≤ 200 ppm or 0.5 mg/L)
- **PG II**: medium
- **PG III**: low

## Inhalation Hazard (PIH liquid)
- Some Division 6.1 liquids that release toxic vapors at low concentrations qualify as **PIH liquids** (`§ 173.132(a)(1)(iii)`)
- PIH liquids assigned **Hazard Zone A or B** based on LC50 of vapor
- Trigger HMSP requirements and security plan obligations

## Common UN numbers
- **UN1051** Hydrogen cyanide (PIH Zone A)
- **UN1098** Allyl alcohol
- **UN1230** Methanol (also Class 3)
- **UN1593** Dichloromethane
- **UN1654** Nicotine
- **UN2810** Toxic liquid, organic, n.o.s.
- **UN2811** Toxic solid, organic, n.o.s.

## Placarding
- **POISON** or **TOXIC** placard
- **POISON INHALATION HAZARD** placard for PIH liquids
- All four sides; UN number on placard or orange panel

## Authorized packaging
- Non-bulk: drums, jerricans, IBCs, glass bottles per UN spec
- Bulk: DOT 407 cargo tank for many liquids; DOT 412 for corrosive subsidiary; portable tanks T-coded
- PIH liquid bulk packaging has specialized requirements

## Driver requirements
- CDL with **H** endorsement; TSA STA
- Hazmat training (`§ 172.704`)
- Security plan compliance (`§ 172.802`) for PIH and other security-sensitive materials

## Segregation
- Keep away from foodstuffs (`§ 177.841` poison rule — cannot transport with food)
- See segregation table at `§ 177.848`

## Emergency response
- ERG Guide 151–154 typical
- Respiratory protection critical
- Evacuation distances per ERG Table 1 for PIH

## Common errors
- Loading Division 6.1 with foodstuffs (`§ 177.841` violation)
- Missing PIH Hazard Zone on shipping paper
- No security plan for PIH carrier
- Wrong packing group on the document

name: Class 6 2 Infectious Substances
body:
# Hazmat Division 6.2 — Infectious Substances

Division 6.2 covers substances known or reasonably expected to contain pathogens capable of causing disease in humans or animals. Rules in `49 CFR Parts 172–180`, with significant overlap to **42 CFR** (CDC) and IATA/ICAO for air shipments.

## Categories under `§ 173.134`
- **Category A** — infectious substance capable of causing permanent disability, life-threatening or fatal disease (UN2814 humans, UN2900 animals only)
- **Category B** — infectious substance not meeting Category A criteria (UN3373 — Biological Substance, Category B)

## Common UN numbers
- **UN2814** Infectious substance, affecting humans (Category A)
- **UN2900** Infectious substance, affecting animals (Category A)
- **UN3373** Biological Substance, Category B
- **UN3245** Genetically modified microorganisms (when meeting infectious criteria)
- **UN3291** Regulated medical waste / clinical waste

## Packaging — triple packaging required (`§ 173.196`, `§ 173.199`)
1. **Primary receptacle** (leakproof, watertight)
2. **Secondary packaging** (leakproof, with absorbent material between primary and secondary)
3. **Outer rigid packaging** (cardboard, metal, plastic) with required markings

## Markings and labels
- **Category A**: full hazmat shipping paper, INFECTIOUS SUBSTANCE label, UN number, proper shipping name
- **Category B**: UN3373 mark (square-on-point diamond), no shipping paper required for ground if certain conditions met
- **Regulated medical waste (UN3291)**: Biohazard mark plus standard hazmat documentation

## Placarding
- Category A in bulk: **INFECTIOUS SUBSTANCE** placard required
- Category B: typically not placarded
- Regulated medical waste: placard at 1,001 lbs aggregate

## Driver requirements
- CDL with **H** endorsement for placarded loads
- Hazmat training (`§ 172.704`) — function-specific for infectious substance handling
- Bloodborne pathogen training (OSHA 1910.1030) for direct handling exposure

## Documentation (Category A)
- Shipping paper with proper shipping name, UN number, hazard class, quantity
- 24-hour emergency response phone number
- Emergency response information
- Special permits where applicable

## Exceptions
- Patient specimens minimally likely to contain pathogens may ship as **exempt human specimen** or **exempt animal specimen** with reduced requirements
- Cultures of pathogens always Category A or B based on risk group

## Common errors
- Category A shipped as Category B (missing labels, no shipping paper)
- UN3373 mark missing or wrong size
- Triple packaging missing absorbent
- Mailing infectious substances by USPS (USPS has separate rules and many infectious substances are prohibited)

- **49 CFR § 173.134** (Division 6.2 definition)

- **49 CFR § 173.199** (Category B packaging)

name: Class 7 Radioactive Materials
body:
# Hazmat Class 7 — Radioactive Materials

Class 7 (radioactive materials) is regulated jointly by **DOT** (`49 CFR Parts 172–178`) and the **Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)** (`10 CFR Parts 71, 73`). Carrier transport must satisfy both. This skill focuses on the DOT motor-carrier transport piece.

## Definition (`§ 173.403`)
Radioactive material has a specific activity greater than 70 Bq/g (0.002 µCi/g).

## Categories by transport index and surface dose
- **Excepted package** — very low activity (`§ 173.421`)
- **Industrial Package (IP-1, IP-2, IP-3)** — low specific activity / surface contaminated objects
- **Type A package** — moderate activity
- **Type B(U) and B(M)** — high activity (spent fuel, large sources)
- **Type C** — air transport for high activity

## Common UN numbers
- **UN2910** Excepted package — limited quantity
- **UN2912** Low specific activity (LSA-I)
- **UN2915** Radioactive material, Type A
- **UN2916** Radioactive material, Type B(U)
- **UN2917** Radioactive material, Type B(M)
- **UN2982** Radioactive material, n.o.s.

## Labels — three categories
- **RADIOACTIVE WHITE-I** — surface dose ≤ 0.5 mrem/h; TI = 0
- **RADIOACTIVE YELLOW-II** — surface dose ≤ 50 mrem/h; TI ≤ 1
- **RADIOACTIVE YELLOW-III** — surface dose > 50 mrem/h (up to 200 mrem/h); TI > 1
- Each label includes contents, activity, and transport index

## Placarding
- **RADIOACTIVE** placard required for any package bearing Yellow-III label or for exclusive use shipments
- All four sides

## Driver requirements
- CDL with **H** endorsement
- TSA STA
- Hazmat training (`§ 172.704`) including radioactive-specific function training
- Some shipments require **highway route controlled quantity** training and additional security

## Highway Route Controlled Quantity (HRCQ)
- Defined at `§ 173.403` — large quantities of certain isotopes
- Requires NRC license, prescribed routes (`§ 397.101`), escort and notification rules
- **CVSA Level VI** roadside inspection program applies

## Documentation
- Shipping paper with proper shipping name, UN number, hazard class 7, activity in becquerels, category of label, transport index, packing group, fissile excepted notation if applicable
- Emergency response info
- For HRCQ: NRC license, route plan, advance notification

## Emergency response
- ERG Guides 161–166
- Distance and shielding reduce exposure
- Time/distance/shielding fundamentals
- Notify state radiological emergency response

## Common errors
- Wrong category label (Yellow-II when surface dose exceeds threshold)
- Transport Index miscalculated
- Missing NRC license for HRCQ
- HRCQ off-route

Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

- **49 CFR § 173.403** (Class 7 definitions)
- **49 CFR § 173.421–§ 173.477** (radioactive packaging)

name: Class 8 Corrosive Specifics
body:
# Hazmat Class 8 — Corrosive Specifics

Class 8 (corrosive materials) covers substances that cause visible destruction or irreversible alterations of human skin or major damage to other freight or transport equipment. Rules in `49 CFR Parts 172–180`.

## Definition (`§ 173.136`)
A material is Class 8 if it:
- Causes full-thickness destruction of intact skin tissue in not more than 4 hours of contact, OR
- Has a corrosion rate on steel or aluminum exceeding 6.25 mm per year at test temperature

## Packing groups
- **PG I**: severe corrosive (destruction in ≤ 3 minutes)
- **PG II**: moderate (destruction > 3 min but ≤ 60 min)
- **PG III**: mild (destruction > 60 min but ≤ 4 hours)

## Common UN numbers
- **UN1789** Hydrochloric acid
- **UN1791** Hypochlorite solution (sodium hypochlorite / bleach)
- **UN1830** Sulfuric acid
- **UN1824** Sodium hydroxide solution
- **UN1779** Formic acid
- **UN2014** Hydrogen peroxide (also 5.1)
- **UN2796** Battery acid (sulfuric)
- **UN2789** Acetic acid

## Placarding
- **CORROSIVE** placard (black and white)
- All four sides
- UN number on placard or orange panel

## Authorized packagings
- **Non-bulk**: drums, jerricans, IBCs
- **Bulk**: DOT 412 cargo tank for high-pressure corrosive service; DOT 407 for lower-pressure corrosive
- Lining matched to commodity (rubber-lined for hydrochloric, stainless for some acids)

## DOT 412 testing
- External visual: annually
- Internal visual: 1–5 years depending on lining
- Pressure test: every 5 years
- Lining inspection: annually if lined

## Driver requirements
- CDL with **H** endorsement
- **N (tanker)** for cargo tanks > 1,000 gal
- Combined **X** endorsement covers both
- Hazmat training (`§ 172.704`)

## Segregation (`§ 177.848`)
- **Acids and bases must be separated** — reaction generates heat and toxic gases
- Avoid loading with cyanides (deadly hydrogen cyanide on contact)
- Avoid loading with Class 5 oxidizers

## PPE for handling
- Acid suit, face shield, chemical-resistant gloves
- Boots and apron for splash protection
- Eyewash station and safety shower at fixed facilities

## Emergency response
- ERG Guides 153–157
- Neutralize and contain — never use water on certain reactive acids without ERG guidance
- Vapor hazard from concentrated acids

## Common errors
- Acids and caustics on the same trailer (segregation violation)
- Missing or worn lining in DOT 412
- Driver no PPE during loading
- Sodium hypochlorite mixed with acid (lethal chlorine gas)

name: Class 9 Hazmat Elevated Temp Materials
body:
# Hazmat Class 9 — Elevated Temperature Materials

Elevated temperature materials (ETMs) are a subset of Class 9 (miscellaneous hazardous materials) that present a hazard solely because they are transported at high temperature. Rules in `49 CFR Parts 172–180`. Molten sulfur, molten aluminum, and hot asphalt are common examples.

## Definition (`§ 171.8`)
A material is an Elevated Temperature Material when, in transport:
- A **liquid** at or above 100°C (212°F), OR
- A **liquid with flash point > 38°C** transported intentionally heated at or above flash point, OR
- A **solid** at or above 240°C (464°F)

## Common ETM UN numbers
- **UN3257** Elevated temperature liquid, n.o.s., at or above 100°C and below flash point
- **UN3258** Elevated temperature solid, n.o.s., at or above 240°C
- **UN3256** Elevated temperature liquid, flammable, n.o.s.
- **UN2448** Sulfur, molten
- **UN1999** Tars, liquid
- **UN3257** also used for hot asphalt

## Marking
- The word **HOT** in a square-on-point marking, contrasting color on the package or vehicle
- For bulk shipments: **HOT** displayed on each side and each end of the vehicle

## Placarding
- Class 9 (with white and black vertical stripes top half) placard, OR
- The HOT mark in lieu of placard for ETM that is not otherwise hazardous (PHMSA-approved alternative)
- UN number on placard or orange panel

## Cargo tank requirements
- Tank must be designed for thermal expansion and pressure under heated conditions
- Insulation/heat retention systems for material temperature maintenance
- Pressure relief sized for fire conditions
- DOT 407 or appropriate specification for many ETMs

## Driver requirements
- CDL with **H** endorsement (when placarded)
- **N (tanker)** for bulk
- Hazmat training (`§ 172.704`) including thermal-hazard function training
- PPE for thermal exposure

## Documentation
- Shipping paper with proper shipping name including "ELEVATED TEMPERATURE LIQUID/SOLID" wording where applicable
- Hazard Class 9
- Approximate temperature of the material
- 24-hour emergency response phone

## Emergency response
- ERG Guide 128 typical for many ETMs
- Thermal burn hazard
- Steam explosion hazard if water contacts molten metal
- Ventilation for vapors

## Common errors
- Missing the HOT mark on bulk shipments
- Cargo tank not rated for elevated temperature
- Driver lacking thermal-hazard training
- Treating ETM as non-hazardous because the material itself is otherwise inert

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 171.8** (ETM definition)
- **49 CFR § 172.325** (HOT marking)
- **49 CFR § 172.504** (placarding)
- **49 CFR § 173.247** (transportation of molten materials)

name: Class 9 Miscellaneous Hazmat
body:
# Hazmat Class 9 — Miscellaneous Hazardous Materials

Class 9 is the catch-all for substances that present a hazard during transportation but do not fit any of Classes 1–8. Rules in `49 CFR Parts 172–180`. Lithium batteries, environmentally hazardous substances, and elevated-temperature materials are the largest Class 9 categories in commercial transport today.

## Common Class 9 materials
- **UN3480** Lithium-ion batteries
- **UN3481** Lithium-ion batteries packed with or in equipment
- **UN3090** Lithium metal batteries
- **UN3091** Lithium metal batteries packed with or in equipment
- **UN3171** Battery-powered vehicles or equipment
- **UN3082** Environmentally hazardous substance, liquid, n.o.s.
- **UN3077** Environmentally hazardous substance, solid, n.o.s.
- **UN1845** Dry ice (carbon dioxide, solid) — limited reg as Class 9
- **UN3257** Elevated temperature liquid
- **UN3245** Genetically modified organisms (when meeting criteria)

## Placarding
- **CLASS 9** placard (black and white striped top half, "9" at bottom)
- For ground transportation, Class 9 placard required when total weight ≥ 1,001 lbs of any hazmat — but Class 9 specifically only requires placards for bulk packagings on highway (`§ 172.504(f)(9)`)
- Marine and air have different placarding requirements

## Lithium battery transport — special focus
- Wattage and capacity thresholds determine packaging
- **Section II / IB / IA** rules for lithium batteries by size
- Damaged, defective, or recalled (DDR) batteries have separate UN numbers (UN3480 DDR, UN3091 DDR) and packaging
- Lithium battery mark required on certain packages (`§ 173.185`)

## Environmentally hazardous substances
- Marine pollutants flagged on the shipping paper
- Aquatic toxicity criteria from IMDG / GHS
- Marine pollutant mark required for bulk and some non-bulk (`§ 172.322`)

## Driver requirements
- CDL with **H** endorsement when placarded
- Hazmat training under `§ 172.704`
- Some Class 9 shipments below threshold may not require H endorsement

## Documentation
- Shipping paper with proper shipping name, UN number, Class 9
- Marine pollutant notation where applicable
- Battery shipper certification where required
- Emergency response phone

## Common errors
- Lithium battery shipments without the lithium battery mark
- Treating DDR batteries as standard lithium (separate packaging required)
- Missing marine pollutant flag on the shipping paper
- Dry ice shipped without ventilation consideration (CO2 asphyxiation risk)

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 173.140** (Class 9 definition)
- **49 CFR § 173.185** (lithium batteries)
- **49 CFR § 172.322** (marine pollutants)
- **49 CFR § 172.504** (placarding)

name: Cylinder Requirements 49Cfr 178
body:
# Cylinder Requirements (`49 CFR Part 178`)

DOT-specification cylinders are pressure vessels authorized to ship compressed gases and certain liquids under hazmat regulations. Specifications and inspection rules are in `49 CFR Part 178` Subpart C and `Part 180` Subpart C.

## Common DOT cylinder specifications
- **DOT 3A / 3AA** — steel seamless, high-pressure (oxygen, nitrogen, helium)
- **DOT 3AL** — aluminum seamless (medical oxygen, SCBA)
- **DOT 4BA / 4BW** — steel welded (propane, refrigerants)
- **DOT 4E** — aluminum welded
- **DOT 8 / 8AL** — acetylene cylinders (porous material inside)
- **DOT 39** — non-refillable (disposable) cylinders
- **UN cylinders** — ISO specs accepted under DOT (ISO 9809, ISO 11118, etc.)

## Required markings on cylinder
- DOT specification (e.g., DOT 3AA 2400)
- Serial number
- Owner identification
- Manufacturer ID
- Original test date and inspector mark
- Subsequent retest dates with inspector marks

## Requalification (retest) intervals
- **DOT 3A / 3AA**: every 5 years (hydrostatic) or 10 years with star marking
- **DOT 4BA / 4BW**: every 12 years (propane cylinders typically)
- **DOT 3AL**: every 5 years
- **DOT 8 (acetylene)**: every 10 years
- **Composite cylinders (3HT, FRP-1, FRP-2)**: every 3 years
- **DOT 39**: not refillable, single use

## Pre-shipment inspection (`§ 173.301`)
Before offering for transport, shipper must verify:
- Cylinder is authorized for the gas
- Cylinder requalification is current
- Valve protected (cap or guard)
- No visible damage, dents, gouges, or corrosion exceeding limits
- Pressure within authorized fill limits

## Loading on a vehicle (`§ 177.840`)
- Cylinders **secured against shifting** in any direction
- Valves protected
- Upright orientation for liquefied gases (with limited exceptions)
- Aggregate quantity may trigger placarding

## Damage limits (`§ 180.205`)
- Dents beyond depth thresholds → condemn or retest
- Corrosion: pit depth thresholds vary by spec
- Fire damage → cylinder must be condemned
- Arc burns → typically condemn

## Driver and training
- CDL with **H** endorsement when placarded
- Hazmat training (`§ 172.704`)
- Cylinder-specific function-specific training

## Common errors
- Expired requalification date
- Loose cylinders in the trailer (no securement)
- Wrong gas in cylinder not rated for it
- Damaged cylinder shipped
- Valve cap missing or broken

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR Part 178** Subpart C (cylinder specs)
- **49 CFR Part 180** Subpart C (cylinder requalification)
- **49 CFR § 173.301** (general packaging for compressed gases)
- **49 CFR § 177.840** (cargo restraint)

name: Dot Cargo Tank Specifications 406 407 412
body:
# DOT Cargo Tank Specifications — 406, 407, 412

The three most common cargo tank truck specifications cover flammable liquids, chemical liquids, and corrosive liquids. Construction rules are in `49 CFR Part 178` Subpart J; testing and qualification in `Part 180` Subpart E.

## DOT 406 — Flammable Liquids (low-pressure)
- **Service**: gasoline, diesel, ethanol, fuel oils
- **MAWP**: typically 4 psi (atmospheric service)
- **Construction**: aluminum or steel; multi-compartment common
- **Features**: emergency shutoff, vapor recovery, bottom-load adapters (API), pressure/vacuum relief
- **Predecessor**: MC 306 (still in service with grandfathered status)

## DOT 407 — Chemical Liquids (moderate-pressure)
- **Service**: a wide range of liquid chemicals — non-corrosive or mildly corrosive
- **MAWP**: typically 25–40 psi (or higher); higher than 406
- **Construction**: stainless steel, aluminum, or steel; insulated and heated options common
- **Features**: domes, manholes with emergency vents, bottom or top loading
- **Predecessor**: MC 307

## DOT 412 — Corrosive Liquids (high-pressure)
- **Service**: acids, caustics, sodium hypochlorite, hydrogen peroxide
- **MAWP**: variable, often 35–50 psi with high-pressure options
- **Construction**: stainless or rubber-lined steel
- **Features**: rubber, polyethylene, or other lining matched to commodity; corrosion-resistant valves
- **Predecessor**: MC 312

## Required tests by spec (`§ 180.407`)
| Test | DOT 406 | DOT 407 | DOT 412 |
|------|---------|---------|---------|
| External visual (V) | Annual | Annual | Annual |
| Internal visual (I) | 5 yr | 5 yr (or 2 yr lined) | 1–5 yr lined |
| Pressure test (P) | 5 yr | 5 yr | 5 yr |
| Leakage test (K) | Annual | Annual | Annual |
| Lining (L) | If lined | If lined | Annual if lined |
| Pressure relief (V) | Annual | Annual | Annual |
| Upper coupler | 5 yr | 5 yr | 5 yr |

## Test stenciling
- Each completed test stenciled on the right front of the tank
- Format: test type, date (month-year), inspector ID
- Roadside inspector verifies dates on stencil

## Driver requirements
- CDL with **N (tanker)** endorsement
- **H (hazmat)** endorsement when carrying hazmat
- Combined **X** endorsement
- Cargo tank-specific function training (`§ 172.704`)

## Common errors
- Expired stencil dates at roadside
- Wrong spec for the commodity (e.g., DOT 407 used for high-pressure corrosive)
- Damaged lining in DOT 412 not detected at annual L test
- Emergency discharge controls not operable
- Manhole gaskets failed

name: Emergency Equipment Required Hazmat
body:
# Emergency Equipment Required for Hazmat

Hazmat transport requires emergency equipment beyond the general CMV minimum under `Part 393`. Specific items are required by `49 CFR Parts 172–180` and by ERG references. This skill catalogs the equipment that must be on a hazmat vehicle.

## General CMV emergency equipment (`§ 393.95`)
- **Fire extinguisher** with UL rating
  - Single extinguisher: 5 B:C minimum if carrying hazmat
  - 10 B:C if carrying hazmat (one or more of various conditions)
- **Spare fuses** (or equivalent circuit protection)
- **Warning devices**: 3 bidirectional triangles OR 6 fusees + 3 liquid-burning flares

## Hazmat-specific fire extinguisher (`§ 393.95(a)`)
- For vehicles carrying hazmat requiring placards: **at least one 10 B:C** extinguisher OR two 5 B:C extinguishers
- Must be securely mounted; serviced annually with current tag

## Emergency response information (`§ 172.602`)
- ERG entry or equivalent for each material on board, OR
- Material-specific emergency response information document
- Must be **immediately accessible** to driver and emergency responders
- Typically in driver-side door pouch or designated holder

## Shipping papers (`§ 177.817`)
- On driver's seat when not driving, OR
- In holder on driver-side door when out of vehicle
- 24-hour emergency response phone number
- Cannot be locked away or buried

## Spill response materials (depending on commodity)
- **Cargo tank carriers**: spill kit with absorbents matched to commodity
- **Fuel haulers**: storm drain covers, sock booms
- **Acid carriers**: neutralizer and PPE
- **Cylinder transporters**: leak detection (soap solution, gas-specific)

## Personal Protective Equipment
- Eye protection
- Hand protection (chemical-resistant gloves for the commodity)
- Acid suit for corrosive bulk
- Respiratory protection for PIH

## Additional for specific operations
- **Bonding/grounding cable** for flammable liquid transfer
- **Wheel chocks** for cargo tank loading/unloading
- **Emergency shutoff knowledge** for cargo tanks
- **First aid kit** (not federally mandated for trucks but expected for hazmat carriers)

## Routing materials
- Hazmat route map for the trip (recommended)
- State-specific designated route information
- Bridge and tunnel restriction information

## What auditors look for
- Extinguisher in serviceable condition with current tag
- Triangles undamaged and accessible
- Shipping papers and emergency information present
- Hazmat training records for driver on file

## Common errors
- Expired extinguisher service tag
- Triangles missing or damaged
- Emergency response information buried in cab
- No 24-hour phone number on shipping paper
- Wrong commodity-specific spill kit

name: Emergency Response Guide Erg Usage
body:
# Emergency Response Guide (ERG) Usage

The **Emergency Response Guidebook** (ERG) is published jointly by **DOT (PHMSA), Transport Canada, SCT (Mexico), and CIQUIME (Argentina)**. It is referenced throughout `49 CFR Parts 172–180` as the default emergency response information for many hazmat materials. The 2024 edition is current as of this skill's publication.

## What the ERG is
- Pocket-sized guidebook for first responders
- Provides initial response guidance for the first 30 minutes of a hazmat incident
- Color-coded sections
- Updated every 4 years (2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2024)

## The four color sections
- **Yellow pages** — UN number index (numeric)
- **Blue pages** — proper shipping name index (alphabetical)
- **Orange pages** — Guide numbers (1–172) with response procedures
- **Green pages** — Table of initial isolation and protective action distances for PIH materials

## How to use during an incident
1. **Identify the material** — from placard UN number, shipping paper, or container marking
2. **Look up the UN number** in the Yellow pages, OR the shipping name in the Blue pages
3. **Note the Guide number** (orange pages)
4. **Turn to the orange pages** to read the Guide (potential hazards, safety distances, emergency response)
5. **For PIH materials**, also consult Green pages for isolation and downwind protection distances

## When ERG cross-reference is required
- ERG entry counts as **emergency response information** under `§ 172.602` for many materials
- More complex shipments may require Material Safety Data Sheets or written response plans
- 24-hour emergency response phone must still be provided regardless of ERG

## ERG must be accessible
- Carriers carrying hazmat typically keep a current ERG in each truck
- Many state inspectors will check for ERG presence
- Digital copies (PDF or apps) acceptable if accessible offline

## Updates between editions
- PHMSA publishes interim updates online
- New UN numbers introduced between editions may not appear in the current book
- Cross-reference PHMSA notices for new materials

## Apps and digital ERG
- **PHMSA ERG app** (free, iOS and Android)
- Many ELD vendors integrate ERG lookup
- Useful for finding materials quickly

## Common errors
- Using outdated ERG edition
- Driver cannot locate ERG quickly during inspection
- Looking up shipping name when UN number is faster
- Skipping the Green pages for PIH

## Training
- ERG familiarization should be part of `§ 172.704` general awareness training
- Drill scenarios: practice finding common materials in under 60 seconds

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 172.602** (emergency response information)
- **49 CFR § 172.604** (emergency response phone)
- **49 CFR § 172.704** (hazmat training)

name: Emergency Response Information Ergi
body:
# Emergency Response Information (ERI)

Emergency Response Information (often abbreviated ERI or ERGI for the document-related requirement) is mandated for nearly every hazmat shipment under `§ 172.600`–`§ 172.606`. It is distinct from the ERG itself — ERI is the documentation the carrier must produce on demand.

## What ERI must include (`§ 172.602`)
- **Basic description** of the hazmat (proper shipping name, hazard class, ID number)
- **Immediate hazards to health**
- **Risks of fire or explosion**
- **Immediate precautions** to be taken in the event of an incident
- **Immediate methods for handling fires**
- **Initial methods for handling spills or leaks** in the absence of fire
- **Preliminary first aid measures**

## Acceptable forms of ERI
- The **Emergency Response Guidebook** entry for that UN number, OR
- **Material Safety Data Sheet (SDS)** providing the equivalent information, OR
- A **written document** prepared by the carrier or shipper containing the required information
- Information may appear on the shipping paper itself

## Accessibility (`§ 172.600(c)`)
- Must be **immediately accessible** to the driver
- Maintained on the **same vehicle** as the hazmat
- Available to emergency responders at any time during transport
- Cannot be stored in a locked container that delays access

## Emergency response telephone number (`§ 172.604`)
- **24-hour, monitored** telephone number staffed by a person with knowledge of the hazards
- Must appear on the shipping paper
- Person answering must be able to provide emergency response information or contact someone who can
- Common providers: **CHEMTREC** (1-800-424-9300), **CHEMTEL**, **3E Company**, **INFOTRAC**

## CHEMTREC and similar registrations
- Carrier or shipper registers with the service
- The registration number appears on the shipping paper
- The service has the material information on file and routes calls 24/7

## What ERI is NOT
- Not a substitute for hazmat training
- Not a substitute for a security plan (`§ 172.802`)
- Not a substitute for SDS in the workplace (those serve OSHA's HazCom rule)

## Exceptions
- Limited quantities and ORM-D may have reduced ERI requirements
- Some small package shipments under specific rules
- Hazmat transported within a single facility under operator control

## Common errors
- ERI buried in glove box (not "immediately accessible")
- 24-hour phone number is the carrier's main line that goes to voicemail after hours
- SDS provided but missing key emergency information
- No registration with the emergency response provider listed on the shipping paper

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 172.600** (ERI applicability)
- **49 CFR § 172.602** (information required)
- **49 CFR § 172.604** (emergency phone number)
- **49 CFR § 172.606** (carrier responsibility)

name: Hazardous Materials Registration Phmsa
body:
# Hazardous Materials Registration with PHMSA

Offering or transporting certain hazmat in commerce requires annual registration with **PHMSA** under `49 CFR Subpart G of Part 107` (specifically `§ 107.601`–`§ 107.620`). This is in addition to FMCSA operating authority.

## Who must register (`§ 107.601`)
A person who offers for transportation or transports in commerce any of the following:
- **A highway-route-controlled quantity** of Class 7 radioactive
- **More than 25 kg of a Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosive**
- **More than 1 L per package of a "select agent" Division 6.1 material PIH Zone A**
- A hazmat shipment requiring placards under `Part 172` (with limited exceptions)
- A **bulk packaging** with capacity of 3,500 gallons or more of a liquid or gas
- A shipment in any non-bulk packaging of **5,000 lbs or more** of a single hazard class

## Who is exempt
- Government employees performing official duties
- Hazmat transported in a private motor vehicle for personal use
- Some small farmers under specific conditions

## Registration steps
1. Complete Form **PHMSA F 1000.1** (online preferred at phmsa.dot.gov)
2. Provide carrier information, hazmat activities, types of materials
3. Pay annual fee — varies by size of business (small business much lower than large)
4. Receive registration certificate and registration number
5. Renew annually by **July 1** for the registration year July 1 – June 30

## Annual fee structure (subject to change)
- **Small business** (under specified revenue/employee thresholds): lower fee tier
- **Not small business**: higher fee tier
- Additional administrative fee per year
- Multi-year registration available (pay 1, 2, or 3 years up front)

## Recordkeeping
- Maintain registration certificate at principal place of business
- Available for inspection by DOT
- Copy with shipping papers is not required but often kept in the truck

## Connection to other requirements
- Registration is **separate from** Hazardous Materials Safety Permit (HMSP) under `Part 385`
- Registration is **separate from** MC and DOT operating authority
- A carrier may need all three

## Common errors
- Missing the July 1 renewal deadline
- Wrong size classification (small vs not small) — affects fee
- Confusing PHMSA registration with HMSP
- Not registering when bulk capacity crosses 3,500 gallons

## Penalties
- Civil penalties for failure to register can exceed $80,000+ per day per violation
- Tracked through inspections and roadside checks

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- **49 CFR § 107.601** (registration requirement)
- **49 CFR § 107.612** (registration fees)
- **49 CFR § 107.620** (recordkeeping)
- **49 CFR Part 385** Subpart E (HMSP, separate)

name: Hazardous Materials Table 49Cfr 172 101
body:
# The Hazardous Materials Table (`§ 172.101`)

The **Hazardous Materials Table** at `49 CFR § 172.101` is the master reference that determines how nearly every hazmat is shipped. Every regulated material has an entry. Understanding the table's columns is essential to lawful hazmat transport.

## What the table does
For each hazardous material, the HMT specifies:
- The **proper shipping name**
- The **hazard class or division**
- The **identification number** (UN or NA)
- The **packing group**
- **Labels** required
- **Special provisions** (cross-references to `§ 172.102`)
- Authorized **packaging** (non-bulk and bulk) — references to `Part 173`
- **Quantity limits** for passenger aircraft, cargo aircraft, and rail
- **Vessel stowage** requirements

## How to read a row
Columns 1–10 (numbered in the regulation):
1. **Symbols** — A (air only), D (domestic only), I (international only), W (water shipment), G (generic name), + (proper shipping name not subject to change)
2. **Hazardous material descriptions and proper shipping names**
3. **Hazard class or division**
4. **Identification numbers**
5. **Packing group**
6. **Label codes**
7. **Special provisions** in `§ 172.102`
8. **Packaging authorizations**
   - 8A — exceptions
   - 8B — non-bulk packaging
   - 8C — bulk packaging
9. **Quantity limitations** (aircraft, rail)
10. **Vessel stowage**

## Selecting the right row
- Most specific entry takes priority over generic
- **N.O.S.** (not otherwise specified) entries used when no specific name fits
- For mixtures, use the most appropriate description
- Hazard class precedence rules apply when a material meets multiple class criteria (`§ 173.2a`)

## Worked example — UN1203 Gasoline
- Column 2: Gasoline
- Column 3: 3 (Class 3)
- Column 4: UN1203
- Column 5: II (Packing Group II)
- Column 6: 3 (flammable liquid label)
- Column 7: special provisions (e.g., 144, B1, T8)
- Column 8A: 150 (exceptions)
- Column 8B: 202 (non-bulk packaging)
- Column 8C: 242 (bulk packaging)
- Columns 9 and 10: limits for transport modes

## How to actually use it
1. Identify the material (chemical name, CAS number)
2. Find the proper shipping name in the table
3. Read across the row to get class, UN, PG, labels, packaging
4. Cross-reference the **special provisions** in `§ 172.102`
5. Cross-reference the **packaging sections** in `Part 173`
6. Build the shipping paper from this information

## Common errors
- Picking a generic (N.O.S.) entry when a specific entry exists
- Misreading the packing group column
- Ignoring special provisions that change packaging or quantity rules
- Using the air-only or water-only column for a highway shipment

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

- **49 CFR § 172.101** (the Hazardous Materials Table)

- **49 CFR § 173.2a** (classification of materials with multiple hazards)
- **49 CFR Part 173** (packaging)

name: Hazardous Waste Rcra Transport
body:
# Hazardous Waste — RCRA Transport

Hazardous waste transport is regulated jointly by **EPA under RCRA (40 CFR Parts 260–279)** and **DOT under HMR (49 CFR Parts 172–180)**. A carrier moving hazardous waste must comply with both. The defining document is the **Uniform Hazardous Waste Manifest** (EPA Form 8700-22).

## RCRA classification
A waste is hazardous under RCRA if it is:
- **Listed** (F-, K-, P-, U-list at 40 CFR § 261.31–§ 261.33), OR
- **Characteristic** — ignitable (D001), corrosive (D002), reactive (D003), or toxic (D004–D043)

## DOT classification of hazardous waste
- Most RCRA hazardous wastes ship as **Class 9** under DOT or as their underlying primary hazard class
- Proper shipping names often begin with "WASTE" (e.g., "Waste, flammable liquid, n.o.s.")
- UN numbers follow normal HMT lookup

## Carrier requirements
- **EPA ID Number** for the carrier (apply via EPA Form 8700-12 or state equivalent)
- DOT operating authority
- Hazmat training under `§ 172.704`
- CDL with **H** endorsement when loads are placarded
- Some states require additional state-level transporter permits

## The Uniform Hazardous Waste Manifest
- **EPA Form 8700-22** (with continuation sheet 8700-22A if needed)
- Tracks waste from cradle to grave
- Generator, transporter(s), and designated facility all sign
- Driver carries during transport
- Copies retained by each party per regulation (3 years generally)
- Most states now use **e-Manifest** through EPA's electronic system

## Required information on the manifest
- Generator EPA ID and address
- Transporter EPA ID and signature
- Designated facility EPA ID and address
- Waste descriptions per DOT shipping name + UN + class + PG
- Quantity, container type, codes
- Total weight
- Special handling instructions
- Emergency response phone

## Recordkeeping
- Generator: 3 years (`40 CFR § 262.40`)
- Transporter: 3 years (`40 CFR § 263.22`)
- TSDF: until receipt confirmed, then 3 years

## Spills and discharges
- Immediate response to contain
- Notify National Response Center (1-800-424-8802) if reportable quantity
- State environmental hotline
- Document the spill on the manifest

## Common errors
- Manifest not signed by all required parties
- Wrong proper shipping name for the waste
- Missing the EPA ID
- Generator's quantity does not match what's loaded
- e-Manifest not properly submitted

## Universal waste
- Reduced regulation for certain wastes (batteries, lamps, mercury thermostats, certain pesticides)
- 40 CFR Part 273
- Easier transportation rules but still hazardous waste

name: Hazmat Air Shipment Iata
body:
# Hazmat Air Shipment — IATA DGR

When hazmat moves by air, the shipment is governed by the **IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR)** and the ICAO Technical Instructions, which the U.S. references in 49 CFR § 171.22-171.24. The 49 CFR Parts 172-180 still apply to the surface leg, but the air-specific packaging, marking, and documentation are stricter.

## What's required
- Use **IATA DGR-compliant packaging** with UN performance markings rated for air transport.
- Apply the **Shipper's Declaration for Dangerous Goods** (IATA form), typically two signed originals.
- Mark and label per IATA — cargo aircraft only (CAO) label when applicable.
- The shipper (not the trucker) is normally responsible for IATA classification, but the motor carrier delivering to the airport must accept only properly prepared shipments.
- All persons handling the package must hold current **IATA DGR training** (recurrent every 24 months).

## How to comply
1. Confirm whether the goods are **forbidden** in air transport — many surface-legal materials cannot fly.
2. Verify the **passenger aircraft vs cargo aircraft only** quantity limits in IATA DGR Table 4.2.
3. Inspect the Shipper's Declaration against the package — UN number, PSN, class, packing group, and net quantity must match.
4. Reject any shipment with damaged packaging, missing labels, or an incomplete declaration.
5. Retain the declaration and air waybill copy for **2 years** under § 172.201(e).

## Common errors
- Treating surface placards as sufficient for the air leg.
- Driver signing the Shipper's Declaration — only the **shipper** signs it.
- Missing IATA-specific marks (orientation arrows on liquids, CAO label).
- Expired DGR training certificates for the dock worker handing the package off.

## What auditors look for
- Training records show IATA DGR module within the last 24 months for any employee preparing or accepting air shipments.
- Declarations match the surface shipping paper for the trucking leg.
- No surface-only packaging used on air-bound freight.

- `49 CFR Subpart H` — training

name: Hazmat Canada Cross Border Tdg
body:
# Hazmat Canada Cross-Border — TDG Reciprocity

Moving hazmat between the U.S. and Canada involves **two regulatory regimes**: 49 CFR Parts 172-180 on the U.S. side and the **Transportation of Dangerous Goods (TDG) Regulations** on the Canadian side. The two systems are largely harmonized through the UN Model Regulations, but the paperwork, marks, and driver credentials are not identical.

## What's required
- A **single shipping document** can be used if it satisfies both 49 CFR § 172.200 and TDG Part 3 (PSN, UN number, class, packing group, quantity, ERAP reference if applicable).
- **Placards** valid under either regime are accepted on both sides — DOT and TDG placards are visually equivalent.
- Driver must hold **TDG training certification** for the Canadian leg (TDG § 6) and **49 CFR Subpart H training** for the U.S. leg.
- Some Canadian shipments require an **Emergency Response Assistance Plan (ERAP)** number on the document — the U.S. has no exact equivalent.

## How to comply
1. Confirm the substance is legal in both countries — a few products differ in classification.
2. Issue a shipping paper that includes both U.S. and Canadian required data elements.
3. Verify the driver carries both TDG and 49 CFR training records, plus an H-endorsement CDL.
4. Confirm the carrier holds U.S. **DOT authority** and Canadian **NSC (National Safety Code)** registration.
5. Notify the **CANUTEC** emergency number (888-CAN-UTEC) and **CHEMTREC** as required — both should be listed on the document.

## Common errors
- Driver lacks TDG training and gets stopped at the border.
- Missing ERAP reference number on Canadian-required materials.
- Using only the English shipping paper when Quebec requires French.
- Forgetting to update the **5800.1 incident report** when a release occurs in transit between the two countries.

## What auditors look for
- Both U.S. and Canadian training records on file.
- Cross-border manifest matches U.S. and Canadian customs paperwork.
- Carrier registered with both FMCSA and applicable Canadian provincial regulators.

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

- `49 CFR § 172.200` — shipping papers
- `49 CFR Subpart H` — training
- **TDG Regulations** (Canada) Parts 3, 4, 6, 7

name: Hazmat Cargo Securement 49Cfr 393
body:
# Hazmat Cargo Securement

Hazmat freight is subject to the **general cargo securement rules in 49 CFR Part 393 Subpart I** (§§ 393.100-393.136) plus any commodity-specific requirements in Parts 172-180. The hazmat layer adds segregation rules, attendance rules, and container-specific tiedown standards on top of the baseline.

## What's required
- All cargo must be secured against **forward, rearward, sideways, and vertical movement** per § 393.102 working-load-limit math.
- **Cylinders** must be secured upright or laid down per § 173.301 and shipper instructions; valve protection caps in place.
- **Drums and IBCs** require tiedowns sized for the working load limit and edge protection where straps contact corners.
- **Segregation** under § 177.848 — incompatible hazmat must be physically separated even within the same load.
- **Cargo tanks** are governed by Part 178 (construction) and Part 180 (in-service inspection), not Part 393 securement.

## How to comply
1. Identify the commodity, packaging type, and any special securement notes in column 7 of the **§ 172.101 Hazardous Materials Table**.
2. Apply the general rule: number of tiedowns equals at least one for the first 5 ft and one for each additional 10 ft of article length.
3. Verify aggregate **working load limit (WLL) is at least 50% of cargo weight**.
4. Check the segregation table at § 177.848 before loading mixed hazmat.
5. Document pre-trip inspection of securement per § 392.9.

## Common errors
- Using **non-rated straps** or chains without legible WLL markings.
- Failing to segregate incompatible classes (e.g., oxidizers next to organic peroxides).
- Cylinders standing upright with no rack or bulkhead.
- Drums on pallets with shrink-wrap only — wrap is not a tiedown.

## What auditors look for
- Driver-vehicle inspection reports note securement check.
- Training records cover both general cargo securement and hazmat-specific handling.
- Roadside inspection history clear of § 393.100 and § 177.848 violations.

Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

name: Hazmat Cargo Tank Emergency Shutoff
body:
# Cargo Tank Emergency Shutoff

Cargo tank motor vehicles (CTMVs) carrying flammable, toxic, or compressed gases must have **emergency discharge control** systems that allow the driver or a third party to stop product flow during a release. The requirements live in `§ 173.315`, `§ 178.345-11`, and the loading/unloading rules at `§ 177.840`.

## What's required
- Tanks in **liquefied compressed gas service** (e.g., DOT 407/412 carrying chlorine, DOT 331 LPG) must have a **passive emergency shutoff** that closes the internal valve within 30 seconds of a fire or loss of control.
- **Off-truck remote shutoff** is required for many bulk gas deliveries — driver must be able to stop flow from at least 150 ft away.
- **Thermal activation** (a fusible element) closes the internal valve at a defined temperature (typically 250°F / 121°C).
- The system must be **tested and inspected** at intervals specified in `§ 180.407` (annual external, periodic internal).

## How to comply
1. Identify your tank specification (DOT 406/407/412, MC 330/331/338) and the commodity.
2. Check `§ 178.345-11` and the applicable specification subpart for the required shutoff type.
3. Train drivers to **test the remote shutoff before each loading and unloading** per `§ 177.840(p)`.
4. Log functional tests on the **driver-vehicle inspection report**.
5. Maintain shutoff test records with the cargo tank file for the life of the tank.

## Common errors
- Driver leaves the truck during loading without confirming the remote shutoff works.
- Fusible link painted over or damaged during paint touch-up.
- Annual external inspection missed the shutoff functional check.
- Missing or unreadable instruction placard at the operating station.

## What auditors look for
- Most recent `§ 180.407` inspection report on file with shutoff verification.
- Driver training records covering attendance and emergency shutoff use.
- Roadside inspection results clean of cargo tank discharge violations.

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

## CFR citations
- `49 CFR § 173.315` — compressed gases in cargo tanks
- `49 CFR § 177.840` — loading/unloading attendance and shutoff use
- `49 CFR § 178.345-11` — emergency discharge control
- `49 CFR § 180.407` — periodic inspection and test

name: Hazmat Cargo Tank Loading Rate Limits
body:
# Cargo Tank Loading Rate Limits

Cargo tank loading rate is regulated to prevent **static electricity buildup, overpressure, and overfill**. The controlling rules are in `§ 177.837` (loading flammable liquids), `§ 173.315` (compressed gases), and API RP 2003 (industry standard incorporated by reference for static control).

## What's required
- **Flammable liquid loading** must be done at a velocity that controls static — typically **not more than 1 m/s (3.3 ft/s)** during initial bottom loading until the fill pipe outlet is submerged.
- After the outlet is submerged, the rate may be increased to the maximum the system safely allows.
- The cargo tank, fill pipe, and loading rack must be **electrically bonded** and the tank **grounded** before loading begins per `§ 177.837(d)`.
- Engines off, no smoking, no cell phones within 25 ft of the loading point.
- Driver must be in attendance per `§ 177.834(i)`.

## How to comply
1. Read the shipper's loading procedure and the commodity's flash point.
2. Connect bonding cable before opening any valve.
3. Start the pump at the lowest rate, verify the splash-loading risk is gone (outlet submerged), then ramp up.
4. Watch the meter — stop at the calculated load weight minus the outage required for thermal expansion per `§ 173.24a`.
5. Disconnect bonding only after the dome cover is closed.

## Common errors
- Top-loading splash-fill of a flammable liquid (Class 3) without slow start.
- Bonding cable clipped to a painted surface — no metal-to-metal contact.
- Driver walks away to the office during loading.
- Loading too fast on a hot day and product expands past the safe fill volume.

## What auditors look for
- Written loading procedure available at the rack.
- Driver training records include static control.
- No history of overfill or release incidents tied to fast loading.

## How Compass surfaces this

name: Hazmat Cargo Tank Maintenance Schedule
body:
# Cargo Tank Maintenance Schedule

DOT-spec cargo tanks (MC 306/307/312, DOT 406/407/412, MC 330/331/338) require a layered **inspection and test schedule** under `49 CFR § 180.407`. The owner/operator is responsible for keeping the cargo tank fit for the commodity it carries.

## What's required
Four test families on a defined cadence:
1. **External visual inspection** — every **1 year** for most tanks.
2. **Internal visual inspection** — every **1, 2, or 5 years** depending on tank type and lining.
3. **Pressure test (hydrostatic or pneumatic)** — every **1, 2, or 5 years** depending on spec.
4. **Leak test** — every **1 year** for most service.
5. **Thickness test** — required for unlined tanks in corrosive service, frequency per `§ 180.407(i)`.

Additional checks: **lining inspection** annually for lined tanks, **vapor tightness (EPA Method 27)** for gasoline tanks every year.

## How to comply
1. Map each tank by **specification number** and **commodity** — the schedule depends on both.
2. Schedule tests with a **Registered Inspector (RI)** or **Registered Design Engineer** holding a current `§ 107.502` registration.
3. Display the **most recent test date markings** on the tank per `§ 180.415`.
4. Retain inspection reports for the **life of the tank** plus 1 year after sale per `§ 180.417`.
5. Tag any tank that fails — it cannot return to hazmat service until repaired and retested.

## Common errors
- Letting the annual external lapse on a parked tank that"s about to return to service.
- Test markings painted over during fleet refurbishment.
- Retiring an inspector and losing the test reports.
- Using an unregistered inspector — work is invalid.

## What auditors look for
- Inspection log per tank, by VIN, showing each required test.
- Registered Inspector ID on the report.
- Tank stencil matches the report date.

## How Compass surfaces this

name: Hazmat Cargo Tank Overfill Prevention
body:
# Cargo Tank Overfill Prevention

Overfill is a leading cause of bulk-liquid hazmat releases. The regulations require both a **calculated outage** before filling and **physical overfill protection** on certain tanks. Core sections: `§ 173.24a`, `§ 178.345-10`, and `§ 177.840`.

## What's required
- The driver or shipper must calculate the **maximum allowable fill volume** accounting for thermal expansion at the highest expected transit temperature per `§ 173.24a(d)`.
- DOT 406/407/412 cargo tanks loaded with flammable liquids require a **vapor-tight overfill prevention system** — typically a high-level sensor that signals the loading rack to stop, or an internal float that shuts the foot valve.
- The driver must be **in attendance** during loading and unloading per `§ 177.834(i)` and must observe the gauging.
- Outage requirements vary by **commodity flash point and tank insulation** — see `§ 173.24a(d)(1)`.

## How to comply
1. Look up the commodity's coefficient of thermal expansion and calculate ullage.
2. Confirm the **overfill alarm or shut-off** is wired and tested before opening the valve.
3. Watch the meter and the gauge — do not rely on a single point of measurement.
4. Stop loading when reaching the calculated safe volume, not when the truck is "full."
5. Document the load weight on the shipping paper.

## Common errors
- Filling to 100% capacity ignoring thermal expansion.
- Overfill sensor disconnected for service and not reconnected.
- Driver leaves the tank to handle paperwork while loading continues.
- Using a winter ullage in summer transit.

## What auditors look for
- Overfill device test log on the cargo tank file.
- Training records covering ullage calculation.
- No history of overfill spills reported on **DOT Form 5800.1**.

name: Hazmat Carrier Insurance Requirements
body:
# Hazmat Carrier Insurance Requirements

Financial responsibility for hazmat carriers is set by `49 CFR § 387.9` and FMCSA Form **MCS-90**. Minimum coverage depends on the **commodity class and quantity**, not just the carrier's authority.

## What's required
Minimums for for-hire and private carriers transporting hazmat in interstate commerce:
- **$5,000,000** — Class 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 explosives; Division 2.3 poison gases (Hazard Zone A or B); bulk Division 6.1 PG I Hazard Zone A.
- **$5,000,000** — bulk Class 7 highway-route-controlled radioactive material.
- **$1,000,000** — oil listed in `§ 172.101` and most other hazmat in quantities above the threshold.
- **$750,000** — non-hazmat for-hire over 10,001 lb GVWR (baseline).

File evidence of coverage with FMCSA as **Form BMC-91 or BMC-91X**, and the carrier must keep the **MCS-90 endorsement** on the policy.

## How to comply
1. Confirm the hazmat list on the operating authority matches the commodities actually hauled.
2. Verify the policy carries the MCS-90 endorsement — this is what triggers federal coverage if the insurer denies a claim.
3. File BMC-91 with FMCSA through the Unified Registration System.
4. Reissue evidence when the policy renews — lapses suspend operating authority.
5. Keep proof of insurance in each truck per `§ 387.7`.

## Common errors
- Carrying $1M when the commodity actually triggers $5M.
- Letting the BMC-91 lapse during a carrier switch — authority is revoked automatically.
- MCS-90 endorsement missing from the policy declarations.
- Hazmat endorsement on authority but no matching insurance on file.

## What auditors look for
- Current BMC-91 in the FMCSA system.
- Policy declarations page with MCS-90.
- Commodity scope on insurance matches scope on operating authority.

## How Compass surfaces this

name: Hazmat Carrier Osha Considerations
body:
# Hazmat Carrier OSHA Considerations

FMCSA covers the **truck and the road**. OSHA covers the **workplace and the worker**. A hazmat motor carrier sits in both jurisdictions: terminal yards, loading docks, repair shops, and driver tasks at the customer's site are OSHA-regulated even when the truck itself is under DOT.

## What's required
Key OSHA standards that touch hazmat carriers:
- **29 CFR § 1910.120 (HAZWOPER)** — emergency response training when employees may respond to a release.
- **29 CFR § 1910.1200 (Hazard Communication)** — Safety Data Sheets, container labeling, and employee training on chemicals used at the terminal (cleaners, lubricants, plus hazmat residues).
- **29 CFR § 1910.146 (Confined Space)** — required for tank entry during cleaning.
- **29 CFR § 1910.147 (Lockout/Tagout)** — for shop work on hazmat equipment.
- **29 CFR § 1904 (Recordkeeping)** — OSHA 300 log for occupational injuries (separate from FMCSA accident register).

## How to comply
1. Identify each site (terminal, shop, dispatch) and the OSHA standards that apply.
2. Build SDS access for every chemical used by employees.
3. Train terminal and shop workers on Hazard Communication and applicable PPE.
4. For employees who respond to spills, deliver the appropriate HAZWOPER tier (Awareness, Operations, Technician).
5. Maintain OSHA 300/300A logs separately from FMCSA records.

## Common errors
- Assuming DOT hazmat training covers OSHA HazCom — it does not.
- No SDS for products the driver actually handles.
- Confined space entry to clean a tank without a permit.
- OSHA 300 log not posted Feb 1 - Apr 30 each year.

## What auditors look for
- OSHA: SDS binder or system, training records, 300 log.
- DOT: hazmat training records under `§ 172.704`.
- No overlap or gaps between the two training programs.

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

- `29 CFR § 1904` — injury recordkeeping

name: Hazmat Carrier Recordkeeping 3 Years
body:
# Hazmat Carrier Recordkeeping — 3-Year Retention

Most hazmat documents have a **minimum 3-year retention** requirement, though specific records carry shorter or longer periods. The principal rule is `§ 172.704(d)` for training records and `§ 172.201(e)` for shipping papers.

## What's required (3-year items)
- **Hazmat training records** — kept for as long as the employee performs the function plus **90 days after termination**, per `§ 172.704(d)`. Industry practice retains for 3 years.
- **Shipping papers** for hazmat — **2 years** (carrier), **3 years** (offeror) for hazardous waste manifests under `§ 172.201(e)` and `40 CFR § 263.22`.
- **Hazardous waste manifests (uniform)** — **3 years** by EPA rule.
- **Cargo tank inspection records** — life of tank plus 1 year per `§ 180.417`.
- **Incident reports (Form 5800.1)** — **2 years** at the carrier per `§ 171.16(d)`.

## How to comply
1. Build a retention matrix by record type — training, shipping paper, manifest, tank, incident.
2. Tag each record with its **destruction-eligible date** at creation.
3. Store digitally with timestamps that can survive audit scrutiny.
4. Do not destroy records under audit hold or open litigation, even if past the minimum.
5. Cross-reference with state recordkeeping (waste manifest rules can be stricter).

## Common errors
- Treating all hazmat records as a single retention class — they vary.
- Destroying shipping papers at 1 year (FMCSA general DVIR rule) when the hazmat rule is 2.
- Losing training records when an employee transfers between functions.
- No backup of digital records.

## What auditors look for
- Producible records for the **full audit lookback window** (typically 6 months to 2 years).
- Training records show date, content, instructor, employee signature.
- Shipping papers retrievable by date or BOL number.

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

name: Hazmat Claim Handling Procedures
body:
# Hazmat Claim Handling Procedures

A hazmat-related claim can involve cargo damage, property damage, bodily injury, environmental cleanup, and regulatory fines — often simultaneously. Claim handling is not directly regulated by 49 CFR, but the **paper trail required by `§ 171.15`, `§ 171.16`, and `§ 172.201`** drives the claim file.

## What's required
- Immediate **notice to CHEMTREC (800-424-9300)** and **National Response Center (800-424-8802)** when a release meets the thresholds in `§ 171.15`.
- **DOT Form 5800.1** filed within 30 days of any reportable release per `§ 171.16`.
- Preserve **shipping papers, BOL, manifests, ELD data, dashcam, and DVIR** from the trip.
- Notify the carrier's insurer and the **MCS-90 underwriter** promptly.
- For hazardous waste, comply with the **uniform manifest discrepancy procedures** at `40 CFR § 263.21`.

## How to comply
1. Open a claim file the same day as the incident — number, driver, unit, commodity.
2. Pull and preserve all telematics and paper evidence within 24 hours.
3. Notify insurer and broker per policy timing requirements.
4. File 5800.1 by the **30-day deadline** even if the cleanup is still in progress.
5. Reconcile the **cleanup invoice, regulatory penalty, and cargo loss** within the claim file.
6. Schedule the **after-action review** (see related skill) within 30 days.

## Common errors
- No claim file opened because "it's small."
- Missing the 5800.1 deadline.
- Driver statement taken without legal review for criminal exposure.
- Settling with the shipper before the EPA cleanup invoice arrives.

## What auditors look for
- Claim file linked to the incident report and the accident register.
- 5800.1 on file with carrier copy of FMCSA acknowledgment.
- Evidence preservation log.

## How Compass surfaces this

name: Hazmat Classified But Exempt From Some Rules
body:
# Hazmat Classified But Exempt from Some Rules

Not every hazmat shipment triggers the full weight of 49 CFR. The HMR provide several **excepted, limited, and small quantity** categories that reduce or eliminate specific requirements while still requiring **proper classification**. The most-used exceptions live in `§ 173.150-173.156`.

## Common partial exceptions
- **Limited Quantity (LTD QTY)** — small inner packagings under `§ 173.150-173.155`. Exempt from placarding, shipping paper detail, and some labeling, but still subject to basic marking and training.
- **Excepted Quantity** — even smaller amounts per `§ 173.4a`. Wider relief from most HMR.
- **Consumer Commodity (ORM-D, now Limited Quantity by ground)** — retail-packaged goods.
- **Materials of Trade (MOT)** under `§ 173.6` — service technicians carrying small amounts for their own use; exempt from shipping paper, placard, and training requirements (basic awareness still needed).
- **De minimis** under `§ 173.4b` — very small amounts in strong outer packaging.
- **Agricultural operations** — limited relief for private farm use per `§ 173.5`.

## What stays required even with the exception
- **Correct classification** — you must still identify the UN number, class, and packing group.
- **Proper inner packaging** to the limit specified.
- **Outer package strength** to pass drop tests in `§ 178`.
- **Hazard communication training** appropriate to the exception used.
- **Incident reporting** if a release occurs.

## Common errors
- Claiming LTD QTY without checking that the per-package limit in Column 7 of the `§ 172.101` table allows it.
- MOT used by a for-hire carrier (it's only for in-service-of-the-business carriage).
- No driver training because "it's an exception" — basic awareness is still required.
- Mixing exception thresholds — LTD QTY rules ≠ Materials of Trade rules.

## How Compass surfaces this

name: Hazmat Customer Communication And Paperwork
body:
# Hazmat Customer Communication and Paperwork

The shipper, carrier, and consignee each bear part of the hazmat documentation chain. Clear customer communication prevents the most common DOT findings — incorrect shipping name, missing emergency contact, mismatched quantity, and undocumented residue.

## What the shipper must provide
- A **shipping paper** with the basic description from `§ 172.202`: UN number, PSN, hazard class, packing group, quantity.
- **Emergency response telephone number** that is monitored 24/7 per `§ 172.604`.
- **Emergency response information** per `§ 172.602` (either on the shipping paper or via ERG reference).
- **Shipper's certification** per `§ 172.204` — signed statement that the shipment is properly classified, described, packaged, marked, labeled, and in good condition.
- **Material Safety Data Sheet** or equivalent if needed for the receiving party.

## What the carrier must verify before accepting
1. Shipping paper is complete and signed.
2. Package marking and labeling match the description.
3. Quantity declared matches the bill of lading.
4. The emergency contact is **a person, not a generic mailbox**.
5. No prohibited or forbidden materials.

## What the consignee should expect
- Advance notice of delivery for restricted commodities.
- Confirmed unloading site, equipment, and **trained receiving personnel**.
- Copy of the shipping paper and SDS retained per their internal rules.

## Common errors
- Shipping paper says "Hazardous Material" without UN number — invalid.
- Customer's purchase order lists product weight that doesn't match the shipping paper.
- Emergency contact is the shipper's regular sales line — fails the 24/7 monitor test.
- Residue load (last-loaded) not disclosed to next consignee.

## How Compass surfaces this

name: Hazmat Cylinder Color Coding
body:
# Hazmat Cylinder Color Coding

Unlike paint schemes used in hospitals and laboratories, **DOT does not mandate a specific color for hazmat cylinders by gas type**. Color is industry convention (CGA C-9) and is not a substitute for required marks. The required identifiers are stamping, labels, and tags under `§ 172.301-172.304` and `§ 173.301`.

## What DOT actually requires on cylinders
- **UN/DOT specification marking** stamped into the metal (e.g., DOT-3AA, DOT-3AL, UN ISO 9809).
- **Proper shipping name and UN identification number** marked on the side of the cylinder per `§ 172.301`.
- **Hazard class label** per `§ 172.400` — diamond label appropriate to the gas.
- **Most recent requalification date** (test date and inspector mark) per `§ 180.213`.
- **Manufacturer serial number** and original test pressure.

## Industry color conventions (NOT regulatory)
- **Compressed Gas Association (CGA) Pamphlet C-9** offers recommended colors (medical oxygen green, nitrogen black, acetylene maroon, etc.).
- Following the color guide is **good practice and helps emergency responders**, but the DOT identifier is the label and UN number, not paint.

## Common errors
- Believing the color satisfies labeling requirements — it does not.
- Repainting a cylinder without restoring the stamped markings.
- Mixing medical and industrial color schemes (the two differ on some gases).
- Using a color-only system in place of a hazard class label.

## What auditors look for
- Required marks legible and present per `§ 172.301`.
- Requalification date current per `§ 180.209`.
- No prohibited cylinders in service.

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

name: Hazmat Cylinder Requalification
body:
# Hazmat Cylinder Requalification

DOT-spec compressed gas cylinders must be **periodically requalified** by a DOT-authorized retester. The cadence depends on cylinder specification and service. Rules sit in `§ 180.205-180.215`.

## What's required
- Requalification interval is set by the cylinder spec — typical examples:
  - **DOT-3A, 3AA** steel: **5 years** (or 10 years under § 180.209(b) star marking).
  - **DOT-3AL** aluminum: **5 years**.
  - **DOT-3HT** for aircraft service: **3 years**.
  - **Composite (DOT-CFFC)**: **5 years**, with a typical 15-year service life.
- Requalification involves **visual inspection, hydrostatic test, and external/internal examination** per the applicable Subpart C method.
- Tester must hold a **Requalifier Identification Number (RIN)** issued by PHMSA under `§ 107.805`.
- After passing, the cylinder is **stamped with the RIN and the requalification date** (month/year).

## How to comply
1. Build a cylinder roster with spec, serial, last test date, and next due date.
2. Refuse to fill any cylinder past its requalification due date.
3. Send cylinders to a registered requalifier well before due date.
4. Verify the returned cylinder has the new stamp.
5. Retain test reports per `§ 180.215`.

## Common errors
- Filling an expired cylinder — strict liability for the filler.
- Missing RIN stamp after retest.
- Confusing manufacture date with last test date.
- Using a foreign-spec cylinder without DOT special permit.

## What auditors look for
- Roster matches physical inventory.
- Test reports on file for every cylinder in service.
- Any condemned cylinders properly destroyed and logged.

## How Compass surfaces this

name: Hazmat Driver Attendance Rules 49Cfr 397 5
body:
# Hazmat Driver Attendance — § 397.5

A motor vehicle containing **Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives** must be **attended at all times** by its driver or another qualified representative. Other hazmat classes have lighter attendance rules but still cannot be left unattended in certain areas. The rule is `49 CFR § 397.5`.

## What "attended" means
Per `§ 397.5(d)`: the person attending the vehicle must be **awake, not in the sleeper berth, and within 100 ft of the vehicle with an unobstructed view of it**, OR in the vehicle's cab if it is not in a sleeper berth.

## What's required by class
- **Division 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 explosives** — attended at all times unless parked in a designated safe haven per `§ 397.5(b)`.
- **Other hazmat (including 1.4, 1.5, 1.6)** — attended in any place other than a safe haven, but unattended parking is allowed in approved locations.
- **Cargo tanks** with hazmat — attended during loading and unloading per `§ 177.834(i)`.
- **Bulk packagings** in general — special attendance during fueling and at terminals.

## Safe haven
A government-approved location for unattended parking — typically published by a state or local authority. The carrier must verify and document the location.

## How to comply
1. Brief drivers on which class triggers full-attendance rules.
2. Maintain a current safe-haven list per route.
3. Schedule routes so explosive loads do not need long unattended parking.
4. Use **team driver or relief driver** for cross-country explosive moves.
5. Document attendance for any DOT roadside or investigative inquiry.

## Common errors
- Driver naps in the sleeper berth while parked with 1.1 explosives.
- "Attended" by someone 200 ft away across the truck stop.
- Unattended fuel stop with cargo tank loaded.
- No safe-haven file — driver makes a judgment call.

## What auditors look for
- Written attendance policy referencing § 397.5.
- Training records for drivers carrying Division 1.1/1.2/1.3.
- Safe haven list and route plans.

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.

name: Hazmat Driver Citizenship Immigration Tsa
body:
# Hazmat Driver Citizenship, Immigration, and TSA Threat Assessment

To hold the **H endorsement** on a CDL, a driver must pass the **TSA Hazmat Threat Assessment Program (HTAP)** under `49 CFR Part 1572`. The program is run by TSA, but it's a precondition for the FMCSA-recognized hazmat endorsement.

## What's required
- Driver must be a **U.S. citizen, U.S. national, or lawful permanent resident** to pass HTAP per `49 CFR § 1572.105`.
- **Asylees, refugees, and non-immigrant aliens** are disqualified from HTAP — they cannot hold the H endorsement.
- TSA conducts a **fingerprint-based criminal history records check** for permanent and interim disqualifying offenses listed in `§ 1572.103`.
- Endorsement is valid for the duration of the CDL but the **threat assessment must be renewed** when the driver renews the endorsement (typically every 5 years).
- A driver with a non-U.S. CDL (e.g., Canadian) carrying hazmat in the U.S. requires alternative TSA-approved screening.

## How to comply
1. Verify citizenship/immigration status before sponsoring the driver to pursue the H endorsement.
2. Have the driver complete the TSA enrollment online and visit an enrollment center for fingerprints.
3. Maintain a copy of the **TSA Determination of Threat Assessment letter** in the DQ file.
4. Track the H endorsement expiration date — when it expires, the driver cannot legally haul placardable hazmat.
5. Document re-enrollment well before expiration.

## Common errors
- Hiring a lawful permanent resident and assuming they qualify without TSA verification.
- Letting H endorsement lapse — driver continues hauling hazmat unlawfully.
- Missing the **disqualifying offense list** that goes beyond CDL disqualifications.
- No record of the TSA determination in the DQ file.

## What auditors look for
- Current H endorsement on the CDL copy in the DQ file.
- Evidence the driver completed TSA HTAP (Determination letter).
- Renewal cycle documented.

## How Compass surfaces this
Searchable in Compass Ask. Runs against carrier fleet data when invoked from the relevant tracker. Read-only; no actions without explicit user approval.
